definition: Identity/card semantic projection: NFC and whitespace-normalized id, label, learning_takeaway and card; exact scope/entity_kind; sorted unique aliases/domains; owner/primary_domain/primary_subfield from central selection v3. Excludes card versions, source/evidence/relationship metadata, locators, timestamps and validation/audit bookkeeping. It is a canonical content projection, not a claim that arbitrary paraphrases have identical hashes.

records.label: Homeostasis
records.learning_takeaway: Understand stable internal conditions as ongoing sensing and correction rather than complete constancy.
records.card: Homeostasis keeps internal conditions within workable ranges through continuous adjustment. Sensors detect changes, and responses can oppose those deviations through negative feedback. Stability therefore does not mean that temperature, pressure or other values never move; it means regulation limits their departures from suitable conditions.

records.label: Presupposition
records.learning_takeaway: Recognize information an utterance presents as already accepted, such as prior activity implied by stopping it.
records.card: A presupposition presents information as already taken for granted. Saying that a restaurant stopped charging extra for guacamole assumes that it used to charge extra. Listeners can therefore learn something from the background of an utterance as well as from the change it explicitly announces.

records.label: Sensory memory
records.learning_takeaway: Distinguish very brief sensory persistence from longer-term storage.
records.card: Sensory memory briefly holds information from sights, sounds and other sensory events. In the Atkinson–Shiffrin model, this fleeting store precedes short-term memory. The distinction explains why a sensory trace can exist momentarily without becoming something retained for later conscious recall.

records.label: Spacing effect
records.learning_takeaway: Separate encounters with course material over time while keeping total study time comparable.
records.card: The spacing effect concerns better retention when study encounters are spread out rather than crowded together. The IES guide recommends returning to important material after a delay, including through reviews or quizzes. The useful interval depends on how long the knowledge must be retained, not one universal schedule.

records.label: Engineering
records.learning_takeaway: Turn problems into tested solutions through iterative design, prototyping, and evaluation.
records.card: Engineering turns a problem into a workable solution through design, construction, and testing. A prototype makes an idea concrete enough to evaluate. When a test reveals shortcomings, engineers revise the design and test again, so improvement is part of the process rather than an afterthought.

records.label: Conservation of energy
records.learning_takeaway: Track energy transfers and transformations without confusing total energy with mechanical energy alone.
records.card: In a mechanical system, energy can change form or cross its boundary without being created or destroyed. Mechanical energy alone can decrease when nonconservative forces act. Choosing the system and included energy forms prevents energy transferred into heat from looking like unexplained loss.

records.label: Go
records.learning_takeaway: Connect surrounding space with the capture of groups that lose every liberty.
records.card: Go players place stones on grid intersections to surround space. Connected stones share liberties: empty neighboring intersections along the grid lines. When an opponent occupies every liberty, the whole connected string is captured, linking local fights over stones with the larger struggle for territory.

records.label: Homology
records.learning_takeaway: Algebraic groups distinguish cycles that bound regions from cycles detecting holes in a space.
records.card: Homology converts topological features into algebraic objects by comparing cycles with boundaries. In a plane with two punctures, a loop surrounding both holes can represent the sum of loops surrounding them separately. The algebra records which closed paths enclose genuine holes rather than filled regions.

records.label: Glass
records.learning_takeaway: Disordered atomic arrangements help explain why glass softens over a range of temperatures.
records.card: Glass lacks the regular internal arrangement of a crystal. In silica glass, silicon–oxygen tetrahedra form a disordered structure. Its low thermal expansion helps it tolerate rapid temperature changes, while transparency to visible and ultraviolet light makes this particular glass useful in optical equipment.

records.label: Sestina
records.learning_takeaway: Six recurring end-words move through a fixed sequence of stanzas and an envoi, creating variation through repetition rather than a conventional rhyme scheme.
records.card: A sestina repeats six end-words through six stanzas in a prescribed changing order, then gathers them in a short envoi. Its formal pressure comes from recurring words rather than a conventional rhyme scheme. New contexts can make the same words carry different associations.

records.label: Figure–ground (perception)
records.learning_takeaway: See why a single image can reverse between an object and its background.
records.card: Figure–ground organization separates a focal object from its background. In the familiar vase-and-faces image, the same boundary can outline a white vase or two dark faces. Changing which region counts as the figure changes what the image seems to depict.

records.label: Availability heuristic
records.learning_takeaway: Explore how accessible examples substitute for broader evidence in judgment.
records.card: The availability heuristic uses readily accessible examples or recent experiences to guide judgment. That shortcut can be misleading when the easiest case to recall is poorly suited to the decision. Accessibility supplies an answer quickly, but does not establish that the example is representative.

records.label: Geodetic datum
records.learning_takeaway: Coordinate measurements require a shared reference framework; horizontal position and height can rely on different datums.
records.card: A geodetic datum supplies a reference framework for measuring positions. Coordinates become meaningful when their reference is known, and horizontal position and height may use different datums. This is why matching numbers alone does not ensure that two geographic measurements identify the same location.

records.label: Dovetail joint
records.learning_takeaway: Connect interlocking pins and tails with a choice about whether the joint is visible at the front.
records.card: Dovetail joints connect boards through interlocking pins and tails. Through dovetails show the joint on both faces, while half-blind versions hide it from the front, as in a drawer. The same joining principle can therefore support different choices about how much of the construction remains visible.

records.label: Caldera
records.learning_takeaway: Explain a volcanic depression through loss of support above a draining magma reservoir.
records.card: A caldera is a volcanic depression associated with collapse above a magma reservoir. At Kīlauea in 2018, magma draining toward lower-elevation vents removed support beneath the summit, which repeatedly subsided. The example connects a surface hollow with changes in the volcano’s internal plumbing.

records.label: ENIAC
records.learning_takeaway: Explore why electronic calculation speed coexisted with days of wiring and switch-setting for a new problem.
records.card: ENIAC performed calculations electronically, yet setting it up for a new problem could take days of connecting wires and adjusting switches. Its history separates calculation speed from programming effort. Maintaining nearly 18,000 vacuum tubes created another practical challenge that technicians gradually learned to handle more efficiently.

records.label: Centripetal force
records.learning_takeaway: Circular motion requires an inward net force; tension, friction, or gravity can provide it.
records.card: Centripetal force is the inward net force required for uniform circular motion, not a new kind of physical interaction. Depending on the situation, friction, tension, or gravity can supply it. The force continually changes the direction of velocity while the object’s speed remains constant.

records.label: Tempera
records.learning_takeaway: Tempera binds pigment in a water-soluble medium; in modern art-historical usage the term commonly points to egg-yolk painting.
records.card: Tempera binds colored pigment in a water-soluble medium. In modern art-historical usage, the word commonly refers to egg-yolk painting, though its broader meaning includes other binders. Paying attention to that distinction prevents a familiar medium label from hiding differences in how a paint was made.

records.label: Trolley problem
records.learning_takeaway: Compare driver and bystander versions rather than assuming one explanation settles both.
records.card: The trolley problem asks whether redirecting a lethal threat from five people toward one is permissible. Changing the decision-maker from driver to bystander challenges explanations based simply on doing versus allowing harm. The variants probe moral distinctions rather than supply an agreed algorithm for sacrifice.

records.label: Subduction
records.learning_takeaway: Connect the descent of an oceanic plate with earthquakes, accretion and volcanic arcs.
records.card: At a subduction zone, one tectonic plate descends beneath another. Material can be scraped from the descending plate, while fluids released at depth help generate magma above it. The same plate boundary can therefore produce coastal mountain building and a separate inland belt of volcanoes.

records.label: Markov chain
records.learning_takeaway: Conditional on the current state, the next-state distribution does not depend on earlier history.
records.card: A Markov chain models successive states whose future depends on the present state rather than the full earlier path. This is a conditional-independence assumption, not a promise of certainty. A random walk gives a simple example: the current position supplies the state for the next step.

records.label: Heat engine
records.learning_takeaway: Extract work from heat flowing between reservoirs while rejecting part of the input energy.
records.card: A cyclic heat engine takes energy from a hot source, converts part into useful work, and rejects the rest to a cooler sink. A power plant’s steam can drive a generator while discarded heat goes to water or air. Both outputs belong in its energy accounting.

records.label: Jet engine
records.learning_takeaway: Compress incoming air, add heat, and accelerate exhaust to produce thrust while turbines power the compressor.
records.card: A jet engine generates thrust by accelerating expelled fluid. In a turbojet, incoming air is compressed and heated; hot gas turns a turbine that powers the compressor, then exits through a nozzle. This couples internal energy conversion with momentum delivered to the exhaust.

records.label: Map projection
records.learning_takeaway: Flattening Earth trades off shape, area, distance and direction, so projection choice should follow a map’s purpose.
records.card: A map projection converts locations on Earth’s curved surface to a flat map. That transformation changes some combination of area, shape, distance and direction. Choosing a projection means deciding which distortions are acceptable for the geographic extent and purpose of the map.

records.label: Counterpoint
records.learning_takeaway: Distinguish simultaneous melodic lines from a melody with accompaniment.
records.card: Counterpoint combines two or more melodic lines sounding at the same time. A listener can follow their separate motion while also hearing the resulting texture. This differs from organizing the music principally as one foreground melody with accompaniment, a contrast the textbook calls contrapuntal versus homophonic.

records.label: James Webb Space Telescope
records.learning_takeaway: A multilayer sunshield limits incoming infrared radiation so the distant space observatory can study faint targets.
records.card: The James Webb Space Telescope uses a five-layer sunshield to limit infrared radiation arriving from the Sun, Earth, and Moon. It observes early cosmic history from an orbit around the Sun near the second Sun–Earth Lagrange point, rather than circling close to Earth.

records.label: Ecological succession
records.learning_takeaway: Trace community change after disturbance while allowing surviving organisms to shape recovery.
records.card: Ecological succession describes changes in a community through time, often after disturbance. Research at Mount St. Helens showed that surviving organisms and other biological legacies strongly affected recovery. Different places followed different trajectories, challenging the idea that every recovering landscape passes through one fixed sequence.

records.label: Chemical equilibrium
records.learning_takeaway: At equilibrium forward and reverse reactions continue at equal rates; composition stays constant.
records.card: Chemical equilibrium is a dynamic balance: forward and reverse reactions continue at equal rates. Reactant and product concentrations therefore stay constant, but need not equal one another. A stable-looking mixture can still contain molecules continually changing into other species.

records.label: Historical linguistics
records.learning_takeaway: Track changes through competing variants rather than treating a language as fixed across generations.
records.card: Historical linguistics studies how languages change over time. Some variants remain stable alternatives, while others spread and replace older patterns. Comparing such changes can reveal shifts in pronunciation, grammar, or social influence, without assuming that every difference between today's speakers represents a change in progress.

records.label: Central limit theorem
records.learning_takeaway: For independent identically distributed finite-variance observations, normalized sums approach a normal distribution.
records.card: For independent, identically distributed observations with finite nonzero variance, the central limit theorem describes their growing sum after centering and rescaling. Its distribution approaches a normal distribution even when individual observations are not normal. The result concerns a limit, not exact normality for every small sample.

records.label: Metallic bonding
records.learning_takeaway: Delocalized electrons connect metal structure with conductivity and malleability.
records.card: Metallic bonding holds metal atoms together through delocalized electrons rather than separate localized bonds between fixed pairs. That electronic structure helps explain electrical and thermal conduction. It also allows many metals to deform under a hammer instead of shattering like a brittle ionic crystal.

records.label: Hindsight bias
records.learning_takeaway: Distinguish knowing an outcome from having predicted it beforehand.
records.card: Hindsight bias is the tendency to see a known outcome as having been predictable beforehand. Learning what happened changes the perspective from which an earlier decision is judged. Confidence after the event can therefore be mistaken for foresight that was never actually demonstrated.

records.label: Zeeman effect
records.learning_takeaway: External magnetic fields split spectral lines, allowing astronomical field strengths to be inferred.
records.card: The Zeeman effect splits atomic energy levels and spectral lines when an external magnetic field is present. Measuring the resulting line separation provides information about the field. Astronomers use this connection to infer magnetic activity on the Sun from its light.

records.label: Guru Granth Sahib
records.learning_takeaway: Sikh hymns are accorded the authority of the living Guru; honoring the scripture is distinguished from worshipping it as an object.
records.card: The Guru Granth Sahib is Sikh scripture accorded the authority of the living Guru. Its hymns guide congregational and everyday devotion. Reverence for the text’s authority is distinguished from worshipping the physical book: Sikh worship is directed toward God through the divine word.

records.label: Enjambment
records.learning_takeaway: A sentence can continue beyond a line break, setting grammatical movement against the visible or audible boundary of the verse.
records.card: Enjambment carries a sentence or phrase beyond the end of a verse line. Syntax keeps moving where the visible line stops, creating an interaction between grammatical sense and poetic arrangement. The break can therefore affect pacing or emphasis without functioning as a full sentence boundary.

records.label: En passant
records.learning_takeaway: Understand the pawn capture available only immediately after a neighboring two-square advance.
records.card: An en passant capture answers a pawn's two-square first advance. An opposing pawn beside its destination may capture it as though it had moved only one square. The opportunity exists only on the immediately following move; waiting forfeits this particular capture.

records.label: Coevolution
records.learning_takeaway: Recognize reciprocal evolutionary effects rather than merely two species changing at the same time.
records.card: Coevolution occurs when interacting species influence one another’s evolution. A change in one partner can alter the selection pressures faced by the other, prompting a reciprocal response. Merely finding two species together, or observing both change, does not by itself demonstrate this evolutionary feedback.

records.label: Chemical kinetics
records.learning_takeaway: Measure how reaction speed depends on concentrations and temperature rather than inferring it from stoichiometry.
records.card: Chemical kinetics investigates how quickly reactions occur and what changes their speed. Experiments vary reactant concentrations to determine a rate law. Its exponents are measured properties, so copying coefficients from the balanced chemical equation generally does not establish the reaction rate.

records.label: Herschel Space Observatory
records.learning_takeaway: Cryogenically cooled detectors opened far-infrared and submillimeter views of cold star-forming material.
records.card: Herschel studied the cool Universe in far-infrared and submillimeter light. Detectors in its cameras and high-resolution spectrometer were cooled close to absolute zero. These instruments let astronomers examine forming stars and galaxies and trace water and other material involved in planetary systems.

records.label: Cognitive dissonance
records.learning_takeaway: Explore responses to discomfort when commitments and behavior conflict.
records.card: Cognitive dissonance is discomfort associated with inconsistent beliefs, attitudes or behavior. Someone who smokes while believing smoking is harmful may reduce the conflict by quitting or by discounting the evidence. Resolving the discomfort can therefore involve changing behavior or changing its interpretation.

records.label: Sfumato
records.learning_takeaway: Gradual tonal transitions soften painted contours so forms emerge without sharply drawn outlines.
records.card: Sfumato softens painted forms through gradual tonal transitions instead of sharply outlined edges. The effect can make contours appear smoky or elusive. Looking at how one tone passes into another reveals a technique in which a boundary is suggested rather than firmly drawn.

records.label: Sociology
records.learning_takeaway: Connect everyday interactions with patterned relationships and institutions at larger social scales.
records.card: Sociology studies patterns in how people interact, form groups, and organize societies. It connects small encounters with larger institutions and historical conditions. A conflict between work and family responsibilities, for example, can be examined as more than one person's private failure to manage time well.

records.label: International Phonetic Alphabet
records.learning_takeaway: Use a cross-language sound notation to avoid inconsistencies between ordinary spelling and pronunciation.
records.card: The International Phonetic Alphabet provides a shared notation for speech sounds across languages. It avoids relying on ordinary spelling, where one letter can represent different sounds and one sound can have several spellings. Transcriptions can be broad or include finer detail, depending on the analyst's purpose.

records.label: Atomic clock
records.learning_takeaway: Tune an oscillator to an atomic resonance, then count its cycles to define elapsed time.
records.card: An atomic clock uses an atomic transition to stabilize an oscillator. In a cesium beam clock, atoms interact with microwaves, and their final states reveal whether the frequency is correctly tuned. Counting the stabilized microwave cycles then turns a repeatable atomic process into a measure of elapsed time.

records.label: Chocolate bloom
records.learning_takeaway: Recognize fat bloom as one kind of pale chocolate coating caused by fat reaching the surface.
records.card: One form of chocolate bloom occurs when fat moves toward the surface and later crystallizes into a pale coating. Warm storage can encourage this migration. Understanding fat bloom links a visible change in appearance with the movement of cocoa butter, without assuming every pale chocolate coating has that cause.

records.label: F1 hybrid
records.learning_takeaway: Distinguish a deliberate parental cross from the variable offspring produced by saving seed from that hybrid.
records.card: An F1 hybrid is the first generation produced by crossing distinct parental lines. In crop varieties, that cross can combine useful traits, but saved seed from the hybrid need not reproduce the same combination. Later offspring can vary, even when the original hybrid plants seemed very consistent.

records.label: Dual graph
records.learning_takeaway: Exchange faces and vertices of an embedded planar graph; the embedding can affect the resulting dual.
records.card: In a planar embedding, a dual graph turns faces into vertices and connects them across shared edges. The original placement matters: different embeddings of a planar graph can produce different duals. For suitable polyhedral graphs, the construction exchanges vertex and face roles while preserving edge count.

records.label: Analytical chemistry
records.learning_takeaway: Turn measurements of reactions and separated products into estimates of a sample’s composition.
records.card: Analytical chemistry turns measurements into information about a sample’s composition. A titration uses a known reagent to estimate a concentration; gravimetric analysis weighs a separated component. The key is relating a measurable change to the amount of the substance being investigated.

records.label: Data compression
records.learning_takeaway: Reduce representation size by replacing repeated strings and assigning economical symbol codes.
records.card: Data compression represents information using fewer bits. Lossless methods preserve everything needed to reconstruct the original: DEFLATE, for example, replaces repeated byte strings with references and encodes symbols economically. Its combination shows that exploiting repetition and shortening frequent symbols are different routes to smaller representations.

records.label: Under the Wave off Kanagawa
records.learning_takeaway: Hokusai uses perspective and framing to make Mount Fuji appear as a small triangular form within the much larger wave.
records.card: Hokusai’s Under the Wave off Kanagawa makes Mount Fuji appear as a small triangular form within a towering wave. The contrast depends on perspective and framing. Looking between the mountain and the water reveals how the print organizes apparently unequal scales within one view.
records.primary_subfield: Works, movements and historical design cases

records.label: Incomplete contracts
records.learning_takeaway: Recognize that important behavior may be unmeasurable, unverifiable, unforeseen, or too costly to specify in an enforceable agreement.
records.card: A contract is incomplete when it leaves relevant actions or future circumstances outside enforceable terms. Some details are too costly to specify; others are difficult for a court to verify. Incompleteness can therefore persist even when both parties care about the outcome and have signed a detailed agreement.

records.label: Social network
records.learning_takeaway: Represent people and relationships to inspect how local connections shape access to wider social worlds.
records.card: A social network represents people or other social actors through the relationships connecting them. Looking at those links reveals patterns that a list of individuals misses. Some positions connect otherwise separate circles, while others sit inside densely linked groups, creating different opportunities for information and cooperation.

records.label: Centimorgan
records.learning_takeaway: Distinguish recombination frequency from a fixed number of DNA base pairs.
records.card: A centimorgan measures genetic recombination, not a fixed physical length of DNA. Two nearby markers separated by one centimorgan have about a one-percent chance of being separated by recombination in meiosis. Equal genetic distances therefore need not correspond to equal numbers of DNA bases.

records.label: History
records.learning_takeaway: Accounts of the past depend on interpreting evidence in its setting; apparently conflicting documents can illuminate the same historical concern.
records.card: History investigates the past by interpreting surviving evidence. A document’s statements become more useful when its author, audience and circumstances are considered. Comparing sources can reveal why people described events differently, rather than reducing historical inquiry to choosing the account that sounds most convincing.

records.label: Organizational design
records.learning_takeaway: Choose responsibilities and coordination structures that connect individual work to an organization's purposes.
records.card: Organizational design arranges roles, responsibilities, and coordination so people's work fits together. An organization chart describes part of that arrangement, but managers also decide how information and resources should move. The choices influence who can make decisions and how separate activities contribute to shared purposes.

records.label: Computer security
records.learning_takeaway: Control who can use or modify stored information through architectural protection and authentication mechanisms.
records.card: Computer security concerns who can use or change a system and its stored information. Protection mechanisms turn that goal into checks on access and authority. A secure design must consider unusual paths such as recovery and maintenance, because ordinary successful use may never expose an unintended access route.

records.label: Silk Road
records.learning_takeaway: Overlapping routes and merchant intermediaries carried luxury goods together with religious, artistic and musical traditions across Eurasia.
records.card: The Silk Road was an interconnected set of routes linking Eurasian societies through trade and travel. Merchants carried ideas and practices as well as goods. Sogdian communities show how commercial intermediaries could also transmit religions, languages and artistic traditions between regions.

records.label: Political science
records.learning_takeaway: Examine how rules and participants' choices shape collective decisions involving government.
records.card: Political science examines collective choices and conflicts, especially those involving government. A useful analysis asks which rules apply, what circumstances participants face and what choices they make. The same formal rule can produce different outcomes when the surrounding conditions or participants' strategies change.

records.label: Mechanical resonance
records.learning_takeaway: Repeated forcing near a natural frequency can accumulate a large oscillation from small pushes.
records.card: Mechanical resonance occurs when repeated forcing near a system’s natural frequency produces a large response. Small, well-timed pushes can make a swing travel higher because energy is added repeatedly. Damping limits the response and changes how sharply the system favors a particular driving frequency.

records.label: Morphology
records.learning_takeaway: Analyze how form-and-meaning units combine into words, including words expressing sentence-like meanings.
records.card: Morphology studies how words are built from smaller units of form and meaning. English cats combines cat with a plural ending, while some languages pack sentence-like information into one word. The order and combination of these pieces are constrained, rather than being freely interchangeable.

records.label: Phonology
records.learning_takeaway: Study how a language organizes and combines sound or sign units beyond their physical production.
records.card: Phonology studies the patterns that organize a language's sounds or signs. Physical units cannot necessarily combine in every order, and neighboring units may change their realization. An important task is distinguishing meaning-changing contrasts from different pronunciations that speakers treat as versions of the same unit.

records.label: Talmud
records.learning_takeaway: Rabbinic law and commentary preserve argument and non-legal material together, making disagreement part of the text’s form.
records.card: The Talmud combines Jewish legal traditions with rabbinic discussion and material beyond law. It preserves argument as part of its textual form, rather than presenting only a list of final rules. Recognizing this layered structure helps explain why studying it involves following reasoning and disagreement.

records.label: Chemical bond
records.learning_takeaway: Attractive interactions hold particles together; ionic solids demonstrate how charged ions produce material properties.
records.card: Chemical bonds hold atoms or ions together in larger structures. In an ionic solid, opposite charges attract and constrain the ions’ motion. When the solid melts or dissolves, those ions can move, helping explain why electrical conductivity changes with the material’s state.

records.label: Erie Canal
records.learning_takeaway: The canal taught engineers to trade longer routes against aqueduct construction while coordinating a huge earthwork project.
records.card: The Erie Canal became a training ground for practical engineering while much construction relied on people and horses. Engineers learned to compare routing around a valley with carrying water across it on an aqueduct. Its history links infrastructure design with earthmoving, materials, and coordination of a large workforce.
records.primary_subfield: Transport systems and engineered case studies

records.label: Genetic drift
records.learning_takeaway: Distinguish chance differences in reproduction from selection favoring a useful trait.
records.card: Genetic drift changes how common gene variants are through chance differences in which individuals reproduce. A variant can become common or disappear without providing an advantage. This distinguishes random sampling across generations from natural selection, which links reproductive differences to traits affecting success.

records.label: Control engineering
records.learning_takeaway: Use measured response and corrective action to make engineered systems follow desired behavior.
records.card: Control engineering designs how systems follow desired behavior. In a feedback example, a motor-speed controller compares a target with measured speed and adjusts its output. Designing the controller requires attention to the response over time, including persistent error and overshoot.

records.label: Memory
records.learning_takeaway: Distinguish encoding, retaining and recovering information rather than treating memory as a recording.
records.card: Memory involves several activities rather than a single recording process. Encoding organizes incoming information, storage retains it, and retrieval brings it back for use. Remembering a fact later therefore depends on more than exposure: the information must have been encoded and remain accessible when needed.

records.label: Fatigue (material)
records.learning_takeaway: Repeated sub-yield loads can initiate and grow cracks even when one application appears harmless.
records.card: Material fatigue accumulates damage under repeated loading, sometimes below the ordinary yield point. In metals, local flaws can concentrate deformation and develop into cracks that grow over many cycles. A load that appears harmless once can therefore become dangerous when repeatedly applied to the same component.

records.label: Integrated pest management
records.learning_takeaway: Combine identification, prevention and selective interventions rather than treating every organism as a pest.
records.card: Integrated pest management combines identification, monitoring, prevention and selective control. Finding an organism does not automatically justify spraying: its identity and the likelihood of damage matter. The approach uses evidence to decide whether action is needed and which available method fits the particular problem.

records.label: Anchoring effect
records.learning_takeaway: Investigate how an initial focal value can steer subsequent judgment.
records.card: Anchoring occurs when one piece of information receives disproportionate weight in judgment. A house hunter may fixate on an initial spending figure and overlook what that amount actually buys. The focal value narrows consideration even when other relevant information is available.

records.label: String harmonic
records.learning_takeaway: Compare lightly touching an open string with touching a separately stopped string.
records.card: Lightly touching a string at a suitable point suppresses vibrations incompatible with a node there, bringing out a higher mode. Natural harmonics use an open string. Artificial harmonics combine stopping the string with a second light touch, giving the player access to different starting pitches.

records.label: Informal organization
records.learning_takeaway: Trace the emergent personal connections that influence how work actually gets done beyond the organization chart.
records.card: An informal organization consists of relationships that emerge as people work and interact. Colleagues learn whom they trust, consult, or depend on, creating a network that may not match official reporting lines. These connections can help coordination or obstruct it, depending on how they develop.

records.label: Buoyancy
records.learning_takeaway: A fluid’s pressure gradient produces an upward force equal to displaced fluid weight, even on sinking objects.
records.card: In a static fluid under gravity, pressure increases with depth, producing buoyancy equal to the weight of displaced fluid. Buoyancy still acts on an object released from rest to sink: its weight exceeds that upward force, so it initially accelerates downward.

records.label: Motivation crowding theory
records.learning_takeaway: Examine how external rewards can weaken or strengthen intrinsic motivation under different conditions.
records.card: External rewards can change intrinsic motivation rather than simply adding to it. Expected tangible rewards may weaken interest in an activity, while praise or an unexpected reward can have different effects. The finding depends on the reward and context, so payment does not invariably destroy enjoyment.

records.label: Atacama Large Millimeter Array
records.learning_takeaway: A high, dry antenna array observes cold dusty regions and adjusts angular resolution through antenna spacing.
records.card: ALMA combines many antennas on a high, dry plateau in Chile to observe millimeter and submillimeter radiation. These wavelengths reveal cold clouds where stars form, while atmospheric water vapor can absorb them. Changing antenna spacing lets the array adjust the angular detail it can resolve.

records.label: Adjacency matrix
records.learning_takeaway: Encode graph edges in a matrix while recognizing that vertex relabeling changes the matrix, not the graph.
records.card: An adjacency matrix records which pairs of graph vertices are connected. For a simple undirected graph, entries are zero or one, the diagonal is zero, and the matrix is symmetric. Renumbering the vertices changes the matrix’s layout while preserving the underlying graph.

records.label: Panama Canal
records.learning_takeaway: Gravity-fed lock chambers lift ships to an inland lake rather than requiring a sea-level passage.
records.card: The Panama Canal’s original locks raise ships toward Gatun Lake using gravity-fed water. Large culverts distribute flow through many openings in each chamber floor, helping control turbulence. This engineering arrangement turns a difference in water elevation into a controlled means of lifting and lowering floating vessels.
records.primary_subfield: Transport systems and engineered case studies

records.label: Gene duplication
records.learning_takeaway: Explore how extra gene copies can alter dosage and contribute to genomic evolution.
records.card: Gene duplication produces an extra copy of a gene or DNA segment. Such changes have contributed to genome evolution, but they can also cause disease. Duplication of the human PMP22 gene, for example, is a common cause of one form of Charcot–Marie–Tooth neuropathy.

records.label: Source-monitoring error
records.learning_takeaway: Recognize a remembered detail whose origin has been confused.
records.card: A source-monitoring error confuses where remembered information came from. Someone might remember seeing a film accurately but assign that experience to the wrong companion. The mistake concerns the memory's origin or context, showing why recognizing a familiar detail does not guarantee correct attribution.

records.label: Sympathetic resonance
records.learning_takeaway: Understand how shared harmonics transfer vibration through a guitar bridge.
records.card: An untouched guitar string can vibrate when another string is plucked. Harmonic components pass through the bridge and excite a compatible resonance in the second string. The apparent response at a distance therefore involves transferred mechanical energy and matched frequencies, not a second deliberate pluck.

records.label: Testing effect
records.learning_takeaway: Use effortful recall with corrective feedback as a learning activity rather than treating quizzes only as measurement.
records.card: The testing effect is the finding that recalling studied material can strengthen later retention, rather than merely measure it. Closed-book questions ask learners to retrieve an answer instead of rereading it. Corrective feedback helps when recall fails, making quizzes useful as learning activities as well as assessments.

records.label: Constitution (politics)
records.learning_takeaway: Understand how basic rules assign governmental powers, duties and limits.
records.card: A political constitution sets out basic principles governing public power, including institutional structure, governmental duties and people's rights. Those principles need not appear in a single document. Constitutional arrangements can combine written provisions with other sources, so a state's constitution is more than a document's title.

records.label: Water activity
records.learning_takeaway: Distinguish available water from total moisture when reasoning about food stability.
records.card: Water activity compares the equilibrium water-vapor pressure above a food with that above pure water at the same temperature. It differs from total moisture content because some water is tightly associated with food components. This distinction helps explain why foods containing water can support microbes differently.

records.label: El Niño–Southern Oscillation
records.learning_takeaway: Connect changes in equatorial Pacific winds and ocean temperatures with distant weather patterns.
records.card: El Niño–Southern Oscillation couples tropical Pacific ocean conditions with the atmosphere. El Niño weakens the usual trade winds and changes warm-water distribution and upwelling; La Niña strengthens the winds. These shifts can alter weather far from the Pacific, linking a regional ocean pattern with wider climate effects.

records.label: Economics
records.learning_takeaway: Connect choices under scarce resources with the gains and coordination problems of specialization and exchange.
records.card: Economics studies how people and societies make choices when resources are limited. Specialization can increase what people produce, but it also makes them depend on exchange and coordination. Studying those choices includes asking how information, incentives, and institutions affect whether the potential gains are actually realized.

records.label: Feature (archaeology)
records.learning_takeaway: A hearth, soil stain or posthole is evidence that must be recorded in place rather than collected as a portable artifact.
records.card: An archaeological feature is a nonportable trace of human activity, such as a hearth or posthole. Excavators record it where it occurs rather than lifting it out like a complete object. Its shape and position help preserve evidence of an earlier activity.

records.label: Catalysis
records.learning_takeaway: A regenerated catalyst changes the reaction pathway and can reduce the activation barrier.
records.card: A catalyst accelerates a reaction by providing an alternative mechanism with a lower activation barrier. It participates in intermediate steps but is regenerated overall. Changing the route can make a transformation faster without changing the identities of its initial reactants and final products.

records.label: Photoelectric effect
records.learning_takeaway: Light above a threshold frequency ejects electrons whose maximum energy is measured with a stopping potential.
records.card: In ordinary single-photon photoemission, light above a threshold frequency ejects electrons from a metal. The stopping voltage measures their maximum kinetic energy. At fixed frequency, brighter illumination can increase photocurrent without increasing that maximum energy, separating electron number from energy per electron.

records.label: Second moment of area
records.learning_takeaway: Material farther from the neutral axis contributes disproportionately to a cross-section’s bending resistance.
records.card: The second moment of area measures how cross-sectional material is distributed about a chosen axis. Contributions grow with the square of distance from that axis. Together with elastic modulus, this geometric quantity influences bending stiffness; it is not the same as the mass moment of inertia.

records.label: Database
records.learning_takeaway: Organize related tables and indexes so stored information can be queried and updated consistently.
records.card: A database organizes stored information so programs can retrieve and change it systematically. Tables can hold related records, while indexes help find selected entries. SQLite illustrates another useful feature: transactions group changes so applications can treat several updates as a coherent operation.

records.label: Euler characteristic
records.learning_takeaway: A topological invariant connects combinatorial counts with the number and type of surface holes.
records.card: The Euler characteristic packages a space’s structure into a number. For a finite triangulation of a closed surface, vertices minus edges plus faces gives this invariant. A sphere and a torus have different values, revealing a distinction that persists when either surface is smoothly reshaped.

records.label: Crystal structure
records.learning_takeaway: Describe a solid through a repeating unit cell and its spatial arrangement.
records.card: A periodic crystal structure is a repeating pattern of atoms. Its ordered arrangement extends through space rather than ending at the edge of a drawn box. Describing the repeating cell and atomic positions separates the geometry of repetition from the substance occupying it.

records.label: Burden of proof
records.learning_takeaway: Compare who must prove a proposition with how much proof the proceeding requires.
records.card: The burden of proof concerns who must establish a proposition and what standard their evidence must meet. In US criminal cases, the prosecution must prove guilt beyond reasonable doubt; most civil claims use preponderance of evidence. Different proceedings therefore demand different levels of evidentiary persuasion.

records.label: Hinduism
records.learning_takeaway: Diverse deities, texts and practices are woven through Hindu traditions, whose forms change across regions and diaspora communities.
records.card: Hindu traditions encompass diverse deities, texts and forms of practice that change across regions and communities. Puja offers one entry point: worship can involve images, offerings and visual encounters with a deity. Exploring a particular practice makes that diversity more concrete than assuming one universal religious routine.

records.label: Topspin
records.learning_takeaway: See how topspin permits a faster shot to dip back into court.
records.card: Topspin helps a tennis ball dip into the court after clearing the net, allowing a faster shot to remain in play. Producing it depends on the racket's upward motion relative to the incoming ball, its tilt, and the ball's existing motion and spin.

records.label: Psychology
records.learning_takeaway: Understand how observable behavior and reports support inferences about mental processes.
records.card: Psychology studies mind and behavior through empirical methods. Mental processes are not directly visible, so researchers draw inferences from behavior, biological indicators and people's reports. A claim about thought becomes scientifically testable by connecting it to observations that could support or challenge an explanation.

records.label: Mamluk
records.learning_takeaway: Enslaved boys were trained and later freed into military households whose loyalty and rivalry could determine political succession.
records.card: Mamluks were enslaved recruits trained for military service who could later be freed into powerful households. In the Mamluk Sultanate, ties to commanders and fellow soldiers shaped political loyalties. Rival households could therefore influence succession as well as the conduct of warfare.

records.label: Gardening
records.learning_takeaway: See soil cover as one of the ways gardeners manage the growing conditions around plants.
records.card: Gardening involves shaping the conditions in which plants grow. A mulch layer, for example, can conserve soil moisture, suppress weeds and alter temperature around roots. Such choices show that caring for plants includes managing their immediate environment, as well as sowing, planting or tending the plants themselves.

records.label: Fermentation
records.learning_takeaway: Recognize food fermentation through microbial products that change flavor, texture and keeping qualities.
records.card: Food fermentation uses microorganisms to transform a food’s ingredients. Products such as acids can change flavor and texture and, under suitable conditions, help inhibit spoilage. The culinary practice depends on the organisms and process conditions, rather than treating every uncontrolled microbial change as desirable fermentation.

records.label: Urban heat islands
records.learning_takeaway: Distinguish hot built surfaces from warmer urban air and identify their different measurements.
records.card: Buildings and paved surfaces absorb and later release heat, while reduced vegetation limits shade and evaporative cooling. These differences can make urban areas warmer than their surroundings. Surface temperatures and air temperatures describe related but distinct heat-island patterns, so the measurement being compared matters.

records.label: Confirmation bias
records.learning_takeaway: Recognize selective attention to information supporting an existing belief.
records.card: Confirmation bias makes evidence supporting an existing belief easier to notice than evidence challenging it. Someone convinced a teacher is unfriendly may remember curt exchanges while overlooking pleasant ones. The resulting impression can feel well supported because counterexamples received less attention.

records.label: Oral history
records.learning_takeaway: An interview becomes a usable historical source through preparation, recording, preservation and access arrangements, with attention to the narrator’s perspective.
records.card: Oral history turns recorded recollections into historical sources through preparation, interviewing, preservation and arrangements for access. The narrator’s perspective remains part of the evidence. Researchers therefore contextualize the account and, when possible, check factual statements against other information.

records.label: Archaeology
records.learning_takeaway: Study material traces alongside their find circumstances to reconstruct human activity rather than treating an object as an isolated collectible.
records.card: Archaeology reconstructs human lives from material remains, including objects, traces of structures and environmental evidence. A find gains meaning through its location and associations. Recording those circumstances lets researchers connect a surviving object with the activities that produced or used it.

records.label: Food history
records.learning_takeaway: Following the movement of crops such as maize, potatoes and cacao reveals how familiar diets are products of historical migration and exchange.
records.card: Food history traces how familiar meals emerge from changing production, exchange and habits of eating. Crops such as maize, potatoes and cacao traveled far beyond their American origins. Following those movements reveals that everyday diets preserve histories of migration and contact.

records.label: Citizens' assemblies
records.learning_takeaway: Explore informed public deliberation whose recommendations remain advisory in Ireland.
records.card: Citizens' assemblies bring selected members of the public together to learn, hear contrasting evidence and deliberate on a policy question. In Ireland's process, participants discuss in small groups and make recommendations. Those recommendations are advisory: elected institutions retain responsibility for deciding legislation and government policy.

records.label: Worker cooperatives
records.learning_takeaway: Separate worker ownership and selection of managers from the day-to-day hierarchy that may still coordinate production.
records.card: Worker cooperatives place ownership with the people working in the enterprise. Worker-owners can choose those who manage everyday operations, so democratic oversight need not eliminate a workplace hierarchy. The important distinction is to whom managers are accountable, not whether every operational decision is made by everyone together.

records.label: Public health
records.learning_takeaway: Connect community-wide prevention with safer water, vaccination and protection from health hazards.
records.card: Public health works to prevent illness and protect health across communities. Vaccination, safer environments and reducing exposure to hazards can change risks before an individual needs treatment. Its population focus connects personal health with shared conditions, policies and collective actions that affect many people at once.

records.label: Linguistics
records.learning_takeaway: Investigate language through systematic observations rather than treating preferred usage as an empirical rule.
records.card: Linguistics investigates how people actually use language, rather than simply declaring which usages they ought to prefer. Researchers compare patterns and test possible explanations against observations. A word that sounds impossible in a language can be informative evidence about its structure, even when no rule was explicitly taught.

records.label: Peer learning
records.learning_takeaway: Develop understanding by explaining reasoning to other learners and considering their explanations.
records.card: Peer learning develops understanding through exchanges between learners. Explaining why an answer seems right and listening to another person's reasoning can expose gaps that solitary work misses. Peer Instruction provides one structured classroom example, but the broader activity is not limited to that particular voting-and-discussion sequence.

records.label: Bread baking
records.learning_takeaway: Connect dough structure and microbial gas production with the rise of bread.
records.card: Bread dough needs both expanding gas and a structure that can retain it. In wheat bread, yeast produces gas while hydrated flour proteins form a stretchy gluten network. Baking expands the pockets and sets the dough, connecting fermentation, material structure and heat in one everyday craft.

records.label: Chess
records.learning_takeaway: Understand why checkmate ends play without capturing the king.
records.card: Chess ends in checkmate when the opposing king is attacked and no legal move can remove the threat. The king is never actually captured. A different ending, stalemate, occurs when a player has no legal move but their king is not attacked.

records.label: Shogi
records.learning_takeaway: Explain the piece-reuse feature of shogi through a directly supported broad-game overview, leaving the perpetual-check exception to its separate rule card.
records.card: Shogi is Japanese chess with a distinctive form of piece reuse. Captured pieces become reserves for their captor. Instead of moving a piece already on the board, a player can spend a turn returning a captured piece to play on their own side.

records.label: Backgammon
records.learning_takeaway: Connect dice-limited movement with the race to remove all fifteen checkers.
records.card: Backgammon combines a race with obstacles. Each player moves fifteen checkers according to dice rolls, aiming to gather them in the home board and remove them. Landing on a lone opposing checker sends it to the bar, where it must re-enter before other checkers move.

records.label: Contract bridge
records.learning_takeaway: See how bidding fixes a partnership's trick-taking target before play.
records.card: In contract bridge, four players form two partnerships. Bidding establishes a contract specifying a number of tricks and a trump suit, or no trumps. During play, one partner's cards are exposed as dummy, and the declarer chooses cards from both partnership hands.

records.label: Woodworking
records.learning_takeaway: See joining wood as a way to build objects whose size and behavior differ from a single solid piece.
records.card: Woodworking shapes and joins wood into useful or decorative objects. Adhesive bonds, for example, let separate pieces share loads and form structures that a single piece could not easily provide. Understanding the material and the joint together helps explain why successful making involves more than choosing a shape.

records.label: Weaving
records.learning_takeaway: Distinguish the held warp from the interlacing weft that creates woven cloth.
records.card: Weaving interlaces two sets of threads to build cloth. The warp is held on the loom under tension, while the weft passes over and under it. Separating those roles helps explain how a loom organizes many individual strands into a stable, patterned textile structure.

records.label: Color theory
records.learning_takeaway: Color relationships include changes caused by neighboring colors and by colors seen immediately beforehand.
records.card: Color theory examines relationships among colors and the effects those relationships can produce. A color’s appearance depends partly on its surroundings and on what was seen before it. Comparing these situations reveals why choosing a color is also choosing a context in which viewers will encounter it.

records.label: Epistemology
records.learning_takeaway: Investigate what distinguishes knowledge, justified belief and other forms of cognitive success.
records.card: Epistemology investigates knowledge, justification, understanding and other kinds of cognitive success. It asks how evidence should constrain belief and what separates knowing from merely being right. Different approaches examine individual reasoning, sensory experience or the social interests that influence which evidence receives attention.

records.label: Religious studies
records.learning_takeaway: The academic study of religion uses multiple methods, and different definitions change which practices or institutions enter its questions.
records.card: Religious studies examines religion through historical, social and interpretive methods. What researchers count as religion affects which practices and institutions enter their questions. Comparing definitions and methods therefore matters alongside learning about any one tradition’s beliefs, texts or ceremonies.

records.label: Islam
records.learning_takeaway: Commitments to God, Muhammad and the Qur’an coexist with differing interpretations of leadership, scripture and religious practice.
records.card: Islamic religious life is shaped by commitments to God, Muhammad and the Qur’an, while communities differ in interpretation and practice. Prayer offers a concrete entry point: preparation and orientation connect shared commitments with repeated bodily actions performed in many different settings.

records.label: Judaism
records.learning_takeaway: Jewish religious life connects sacred texts and monotheistic traditions with collective history, culture and changing communal practices.
records.card: Jewish life connects sacred texts and religious practice with collective history, culture and changing communities. Scriptural interpretation offers one way to explore these connections. The Talmud’s preserved arguments, for example, show how teaching can develop through discussion rather than only through a single final statement.

records.label: Buddhism
records.learning_takeaway: Buddhist traditions share reference to Buddha, Dharma and Sangha while interpreting and practicing these commitments in diverse ways.
records.card: Buddhist traditions look to Buddha, Dharma and Sangha: the awakened teacher, the teaching and the community. Those shared points of reference coexist with varied practices and interpretations. Beginning with the community’s relationship to teaching helps make that diversity visible without reducing Buddhism to one uniform routine.

records.label: Shinto
records.learning_takeaway: Kami are enshrined and venerated in diverse jinja; visits, festivals and protective objects connect sacred places with everyday life.
records.card: Shinto shrine traditions center on the veneration of kami in places called jinja. Visits, festivals and sacred objects connect these places with ordinary life. An ofuda taken home, for example, can extend a shrine relationship into the household through an object treated with religious reverence.

records.label: Distributed systems
records.learning_takeaway: Coordinate machines through messages while preserving shared results despite some machine failures.
records.card: Distributed systems spread computation across machines that communicate over a network. Keeping their work coordinated becomes difficult when messages are delayed or machines fail. Replicated state machines offer one approach: replicas agree on commands and execute them deterministically in the same order to maintain matching results.

records.label: Cryptography
records.learning_takeaway: Combine keyed encryption and authentication to protect message confidentiality, integrity, and peer identity.
records.card: Cryptography uses keyed mathematical techniques to protect information and verify messages or participants. Encryption can hide content, while authentication and integrity mechanisms help detect impersonation or alteration. TLS illustrates how several cryptographic tools are combined into a communication protocol rather than relying on secrecy of the design.

records.label: Probability
records.learning_takeaway: Represent uncertainty through outcomes, numerical likelihoods, and distributions whose total probability is one.
records.card: Probability studies uncertain outcomes by assigning them numerical likelihoods and organizing those likelihoods into distributions. A distribution can describe individual possible values or a continuous range. Cumulative probability combines the possibilities up to a threshold, connecting uncertainty about outcomes with quantities that can be compared.

records.label: Graph theory
records.learning_takeaway: Separate a network’s underlying connections from the way its vertices and edges are drawn or labeled.
records.card: Graph theory studies structures made of vertices and connecting edges. A graph’s drawing or numbering can change without altering its connections. An adjacency matrix provides one numerical representation, making it possible to analyze the same underlying network through different arrangements of symbols.

records.label: Topology
records.learning_takeaway: Study connectivity and properties preserved by continuous changes rather than exact lengths or angles.
records.card: Topology studies properties of spaces preserved by continuous, reversible changes of shape. Stretching a circle into an ellipse changes lengths but preserves its connected loop. Focusing on such structure lets mathematicians compare objects without treating every geometric distortion as a fundamentally new space.

records.label: Information theory
records.learning_takeaway: Measure communication choices without treating message meaning as the engineering quantity.
records.card: Information theory measures the choices involved in sending messages and the limits of communication systems. In Shannon's formulation, a message is selected from possible alternatives; its personal meaning is a separate question. Using base-two logarithms measures those choices in bits.

records.label: Physics
records.learning_takeaway: Use common laws of matter, energy, space, and time to connect laboratory and cosmic phenomena.
records.card: Physics seeks common explanations for matter, energy, motion, and interactions across scales. The gravity governing a galaxy’s stars is connected with the gravity involved in water flowing through a dam. Such links let a few tested principles explain phenomena that initially seem unrelated.

records.label: Optics
records.learning_takeaway: Explain image formation and light guidance through refraction and related behavior at material boundaries.
records.card: Optics studies light’s behavior and its interactions with materials. Refraction offers a concrete example: a ray can change direction when it enters a medium where light travels at a different speed. The same principle helps explain lenses, distorted underwater views, and optical-fiber systems.

records.label: Chemistry
records.learning_takeaway: Connect observable changes in matter with particle-level explanations and chemical representations.
records.card: Chemistry connects observable substances with the particles and interactions that explain their behavior. A visible change can be described through a molecular model and represented by a formula or equation. Moving among these descriptions helps make sense of experiments.

records.label: Geology
records.learning_takeaway: Read Earth’s materials and landscapes as evidence of processes and planetary history.
records.card: Geology investigates Earth’s materials, physical processes and history. Rocks preserve evidence of earlier conditions, while tectonics, weathering and erosion continue to change landscapes. Reading a place geologically means connecting what is visible today with the processes and timescales that produced it.

records.label: Oceanography
records.learning_takeaway: Connect ocean chemistry, life, seafloor history and water movement as interacting research areas.
records.card: Oceanography studies the ocean through its water movement, chemistry, living communities and seafloor history. These perspectives overlap: circulation can move nutrients that influence marine life. Field observations, experiments and models connect the ocean’s physical setting with the organisms and chemical processes operating within it.

records.label: Genetics
records.learning_takeaway: Connect inherited DNA variation with environmental influences rather than treating genes as destiny.
records.card: Genetics studies inheritance and variation, including how genes interact with the environment. A DNA difference can influence a trait without determining it alone. Studying genes alongside behavior and surroundings helps explain why genetic information is only part of the story of health.

records.label: Ecology
records.learning_takeaway: Connect organisms’ distribution and abundance with living and nonliving surroundings.
records.card: Ecology investigates how organisms interact with one another and with their surroundings. A butterfly’s food plant, predators and climate can all shape where it survives. Moving between individuals, populations and communities helps researchers connect small interactions with larger patterns of abundance and distribution.

records.label: Material culture
records.learning_takeaway: A trade token’s imagery and product list provide evidence of commercial life and how a coffee house represented itself.
records.card: Material culture examines social life through objects and their uses. A coffee-house trade token, for example, advertised goods while presenting a particular image of the business. Its wording and pictures let a small commercial object become evidence about consumption, exchange and public identity.

records.label: Human geography
records.learning_takeaway: Social life, economies and settlement patterns can be studied through their relationships to locations and environments.
records.card: Human geography studies how communities, cultures and economies relate to places and environments. Questions about settlement, movement or work become spatial questions: where activities occur, how places connect and how people shape their surroundings. Different methods reveal different parts of those relationships.

records.label: Cartography
records.learning_takeaway: Making a map requires selecting features and symbols to communicate spatial relationships for a particular use.
records.card: Cartography turns spatial information into maps through choices about selection, symbols and presentation. A map made to compare population rates may look very different from one designed for navigation. Thinking about its purpose helps explain both what a map emphasizes and what it leaves out.

records.label: Cultural landscapes
records.learning_takeaway: Terraces, gardens and sacred sites show how communities shape environments and give them practical or symbolic meaning.
records.card: Cultural landscapes record relationships between people and their environments. Cultivation, settlement, engineering and sacred practices can give a place its visible form and meaning. Reading terraces or water channels as cultural evidence connects practical land use with the institutions and values that sustained it.

records.learning_takeaway: Explore a three-movement performance that directs attention toward ambient sound.
records.card: John Cage's 4′33″ directs attention toward sounds already present around a performance. The John Cage Trust's official app makes this idea concrete by recording ambient sound in three movements. The example shifts attention from supplying a new melody to noticing the listening environment itself.

records.label: A Mathematical Theory of Communication
records.learning_takeaway: See how Shannon's 1948 paper separated message selection from semantics to formulate an engineering theory.
records.card: Shannon's 1948 paper, A Mathematical Theory of Communication, framed communication as selecting and reproducing messages from possible alternatives. It separated that engineering problem from what messages mean to people. Its logarithmic measure also explained why base-two units could conveniently be called bits.

records.label: A Sunday on La Grande Jatte
records.learning_takeaway: Seurat organized separate, contrasting strokes into a large composition that became a central demonstration of Neo-Impressionist optical-mixture aims.
records.card: Seurat’s A Sunday on La Grande Jatte arranges separate colored strokes within a large composition. The Met describes it as a major demonstration of Neo-Impressionist technique. It offers a case for comparing visible brushwork with the optical effects the movement’s artists hoped to achieve.
aliases: A Sunday Afternoon on the Island of La Grande Jatte
records.primary_subfield: Works, movements and historical design cases

records.label: Absolute sensory threshold
records.learning_takeaway: Interpret detection threshold as a probability under controlled conditions.
records.card: An absolute sensory threshold is usually defined as the stimulus intensity detected on half of repeated presentations under specified conditions. It is therefore a probabilistic measurement, not a magical boundary below which detection never happens. The testing conditions matter when comparing how sensitive different observers appear.

records.label: Access control list
records.learning_takeaway: Associate an object with a list of principals authorized to access it.
records.card: An access control list associates a protected object with the principals permitted to use it. When access is requested, that object-centered list helps determine authority. This differs from a capability system, where a principal presents an unforgeable ticket naming the object and conveying access authority.

records.label: Achieved status
records.learning_takeaway: Identify social positions acquired through activity or choice, while separating the position from its expected behaviors.
records.card: An achieved status is a social position acquired through activity or choice, such as becoming a nurse. The term distinguishes its route of acquisition from an ascribed position. Status names the position; role describes the patterns of behavior expected of someone who holds it.

records.label: Acid-base indicator
records.learning_takeaway: Different colors of a weak acid and its conjugate base report the solution’s pH range.
records.card: An acid–base indicator has differently colored acid and base forms. Changing pH shifts their relative amounts, producing a visible transition rather than an infinitely sharp switch. An indicator therefore reports a range of acidity, and its useful color interval depends on its own acid–base equilibrium.

records.label: Acid-base titration
records.learning_takeaway: Use controlled neutralization and a pH curve to determine acid or base concentration.
records.card: An acid–base titration uses a reagent of known concentration to measure an unknown acid or base. Tracking pH reveals progress toward stoichiometric equivalence. The equivalence point is not always neutral: titrating a weak acid with a strong base typically leaves a basic solution.

records.label: Activation energy
records.learning_takeaway: Relate the energy barrier between reactants and the transition state to successful molecular collisions.
records.card: In a collision model, activation energy marks the barrier reactants must overcome to reach a transition state. Collisions can fail even when molecules meet: insufficient energy prevents productive rearrangement. A higher barrier leaves fewer collisions energetic enough to react at a given temperature.

records.label: Actuarially fair insurance
records.learning_takeaway: Separate a premium equal to expected claims from one that also funds operating expenses and profit.
records.card: Actuarially fair insurance charges a premium equal to the expected claim payment for the relevant risk group. It is a benchmark, not necessarily the price an insurer can sustainably offer. Administration, other business costs, and profit require additional funding beyond that expected-claims amount.

records.label: Adagio for Strings
records.learning_takeaway: Hear how a 4–3 suspension delays resolution in Barber's work.
records.card: Samuel Barber's Adagio for Strings provides a textbook example of a 4–3 suspension. A prepared note becomes dissonant against the bass before resolving downward by step. The numbers describe the suspension and resolution as interval classes, so compound intervals can receive the same analytical label.

records.label: Adaptive optics
records.learning_takeaway: Rapidly reshape a flexible mirror to compensate for atmospheric distortion of incoming starlight.
records.card: Adaptive optics counters atmospheric blurring by measuring distortion and rapidly changing the shape of a flexible mirror. The corrections help incoming light reach a sharper focus. A ground-based telescope can therefore recover detail that its aperture permits but turbulent air would otherwise obscure.

records.label: Additive minimalism
records.learning_takeaway: Track growth by gradually extending repeated musical patterns.
records.card: Additive minimalism develops music by expanding repeated material in small steps. In Glass's examples, repetitions may be added or chords given extra subdivisions. The listener can follow a process of gradual growth rather than waiting for an entirely new theme to replace the existing pattern.

records.label: ADH-dependent aquaporin trafficking
records.learning_takeaway: Explain how reversible water-channel insertion changes collecting-duct water recovery.
records.card: Antidiuretic hormone increases the number of aquaporin water channels in the kidney’s collecting-duct cell membranes. Water can then leave the forming urine along an osmotic gradient. With less hormone, fewer channels are inserted, less water is recovered and the urine can remain more dilute.

records.label: Adjacency pair
records.learning_takeaway: See how an initial conversational action makes a specific kind of response relevant, such as an answer after a question.
records.card: An adjacency pair links two conversational actions, such as a question and its answer or an invitation and its response. Once the first action occurs, a particular kind of second action becomes relevant. An appropriate response can also show whether the listener understood what the first speaker meant.

records.label: Adverse selection
records.learning_takeaway: See how privately known risk changes which people seek insurance and can push low-risk buyers out.
records.card: Adverse selection can arise when insurance buyers know more about their own risk than the insurer. A pooled premium may attract high-risk buyers while discouraging lower-risk ones. The changing mix can then raise average claims, making coverage harder to price even before anyone changes their behavior.

records.label: Aflaj irrigation landscapes of Oman
records.learning_takeaway: Five protected systems display how water sources, channels, agriculture, defensive buildings and shared management shaped arid settlements.
records.card: Five protected Omani aflaj systems connect water sources, channels, cultivated land and settlement. Their structures also reveal arrangements for sharing and protecting scarce water. Looking across the systems shows how technical infrastructure and collective management together shaped inhabited landscapes in an arid region.

records.label: Aflaj water-sharing settlements
records.learning_takeaway: Gravity-fed water channels and timed access support permanent settlement and require communities to coordinate maintenance and distribution.
records.card: Aflaj water systems use gravity-fed channels to distribute water through arid settlements and agricultural land. Sharing access requires arrangements for timing, upkeep and allocation. Their geography is therefore institutional as well as hydraulic: reliable flow depends on people maintaining both channels and rules.

records.label: Agha Shahid Ali
records.learning_takeaway: Ali promoted the traditional ghazal in English through poetry and anthology editorship, emphasizing the autonomy of its couplets.
records.card: Agha Shahid Ali helped bring the classical ghazal into English-language poetry and edited Ravishing DisUnities. The Academy’s account emphasizes his understanding of autonomous couplets and the anthology’s varied formal fidelity. His work offers a case for studying poetic adaptation across languages.

records.label: Ait-Ben-Haddou
records.learning_takeaway: Compact earthen dwellings and communal facilities inside walls show how a pre-Saharan trading post organized defense and shared life.
records.card: Ait-Ben-Haddou groups earthen houses and communal facilities inside defensive walls along a former pre-Saharan trade route. Its compact arrangement shows collective settlement in built form. Examining the whole ksar connects domestic life with shared spaces, defense and the movement of goods through the region.

records.label: Akhand path
records.learning_takeaway: Readers work in successive shifts so the entire Guru Granth Sahib can be read without interruption.
records.card: An akhand path is an uninterrupted reading of the Guru Granth Sahib. Readers take successive turns so the recitation continues through the entire scripture. The practice combines sustained attention to the text with shared responsibility, making continuity possible through the coordinated participation of several people.

records.label: Al Ain oasis landscape
records.learning_takeaway: Tombs, settlement remains and irrigation works record long-term sedentary life at a desert crossroads.
records.card: Al Ain’s oasis landscape brings tombs, settlement remains and irrigation works into a long record of life at a desert crossroads. These different kinds of evidence connect burial, habitation and water management. Together they reveal how communities sustained settled activity within an arid environment.

records.label: Allocation concealment
records.learning_takeaway: Explain why recruiters must not know the next treatment assignment before enrollment.
records.card: Allocation concealment keeps the next trial assignment unknown until enrollment is settled. If recruiters can predict the group a person will enter, they may selectively include participants and undermine randomization. This protection operates at recruitment, whereas blinding addresses knowledge of treatment after assignment.

records.label: Allomorph
records.learning_takeaway: Recognize different forms of one morpheme, with variants conditioned by sounds or specific lexical roots.
records.card: Allomorphs are different forms expressing one morpheme. English a and an vary with the following sound, while plural forms show both predictable sound changes and word-specific patterns. Recognizing the shared grammatical function helps distinguish this variation from entirely different morphemes that merely resemble each other.

records.label: Allophone
