records.learning_takeaway: Recognize physically different pronunciations treated as realizations of a single abstract phoneme.
records.card: Allophones are physically different realizations of one phoneme. In many North American English varieties, the consonant in atom differs from the aspirated consonant in atomic, yet both are analyzed as versions of /t/. Their distribution depends partly on the surrounding sounds and stress pattern.

records.label: Alternative splicing
records.learning_takeaway: Explain how different exon combinations produce multiple related transcripts from one gene.
records.card: A gene’s RNA can be assembled in different ways by joining different combinations of exons. Alternative splicing therefore produces related RNA transcripts from one gene, and these can encode proteins with different structures or functions. One gene need not yield just one protein product.

records.label: Altitude effects on baseball pitches
records.learning_takeaway: Explore why thinner air weakens a spinning baseball's curvature, other factors equal.
records.card: A curveball's behavior depends partly on the air around it. In NASA's simplified model, lower air density weakens the aerodynamic deflection of a spinning pitch, all else equal. High-altitude conditions can therefore make a curveball travel along a straighter path.

records.label: Ambulatory blood pressure monitoring
records.learning_takeaway: Distinguish repeated measurements during ordinary activity from one clinic reading.
records.card: Ambulatory blood pressure monitoring collects repeated readings while a person goes about ordinary life, usually over twenty-four hours. A worn monitor is returned after the recording period. This provides a pattern across time and circumstances, rather than relying only on one measurement taken in a clinic.

records.label: Amicus curiae
records.learning_takeaway: Understand how a nonparty can contribute a brief to a court's consideration.
records.card: In US court practice, an amicus curiae is a nonparty offering arguments or information through a brief. An interest in the case does not make the contributor a litigant. Each court's applicable rules govern when and how such outside submissions may be made.

records.label: Anadiplosis
records.learning_takeaway: The closing word of one unit becomes the opening word of the next, linking statements into a chain.
records.card: Anadiplosis repeats the end of one clause or line at the beginning of the next. The shared wording acts as a hinge between units, allowing the second statement to grow from the first. Its chained position differs from repeating all beginnings or all endings.

records.label: Anamorphosis
records.learning_takeaway: A deliberately distorted image becomes recognizable from a particular viewing position, as the stretched skull in Holbein’s Ambassadors does from the lower right.
records.card: Anamorphosis deliberately distorts an image so that it becomes recognizable from a particular viewing position or arrangement. Holbein’s stretched skull in The Ambassadors resolves from an oblique angle. The viewer’s position therefore becomes part of how the image is constructed and encountered.

records.label: Anaphora (rhetoric)
records.learning_takeaway: Repeating initial words across phrases or lines can build rhythmic and emotional accumulation.
records.card: Rhetorical anaphora repeats a word or phrase at the beginnings of successive units. The shared opening creates a recognizable pattern while later words accumulate differences. It can shape momentum or emphasis, whether the units are poetic lines, clauses or statements in a longer passage.

records.label: Angular momentum
records.learning_takeaway: Rotational momentum depends on linear momentum and position relative to a chosen origin.
records.card: For a classical particle, angular momentum combines linear momentum with position relative to a chosen origin. Even straight-line motion can have angular momentum about a point away from that path. A different origin changes the lever arm, so this quantity is not defined by speed alone.

records.label: Anonymization in Song examinations
records.learning_takeaway: Numbers replaced candidates’ names and clerks recopied answers to reduce recognition through identity or handwriting.
records.card: Song examination procedures could replace candidates’ names with numbers and have clerks recopy their answers. These steps reduced clues supplied by identity and handwriting. The practice shows a historical attempt to make assessment depend more on the submitted work than on recognizing its author.

records.label: Apical dominance
records.learning_takeaway: Connect growth at a shoot tip with suppression of lateral buds and the effects of pruning.
records.card: A growing shoot tip can suppress the development of lateral buds. Apical dominance involves hormonal signals, including auxin from the tip, while cytokinins can favor bud growth. Removing the tip changes that balance, helping explain why pruning can encourage a plant to branch.

records.label: Apostrophe (rhetoric)
records.learning_takeaway: A speaker directly addresses an absent person, an abstraction or a nonhuman thing, creating an imagined listener.
records.card: Rhetorical apostrophe directly addresses an absent person, an abstraction or something nonhuman as if it could listen. The address creates a speaker’s imagined relationship with its recipient. It is a figure of speech, distinct from the punctuation mark that shares its name.

records.label: Apple Inc.
records.learning_takeaway: Examine a historically documented separation of product ownership, component sourcing, and final assembly across firms and countries.
records.card: Apple's historical iPhone supply-chain example in The Economy separates product ownership, component manufacturing, and final assembly across different firms and countries. The case shows why calling a product American or Chinese can conceal several distinct production roles, rather than identifying one place where all its value was created.
records.primary_subfield: Economic history and documented business cases

records.label: Appoggiatura
records.learning_takeaway: Follow an expressive non-chord note approached by leap and resolved by step.
records.card: An appoggiatura is a non-chord tone approached by a leap and left by a step. It is usually accented, placing the dissonance on a strong moment before resolution. The resolving step can go upward or downward; the expressive effect does not require one fixed direction.

records.label: Archaeological context
records.learning_takeaway: An object’s location, associations and chronological, social and cultural setting determine what historical inferences it can support.
records.card: Archaeological context includes where a find lay, what accompanied it and its chronological, social and cultural setting. These relationships constrain interpretation. The same object can support different historical explanations when found in different associations, which is why documenting its surroundings matters.

records.label: Archaeological cross-dating
records.learning_takeaway: Matching evidence across archaeological contexts can place otherwise undated finds in a relative sequence.
records.card: Archaeological cross-dating compares evidence from different contexts to establish their relative ages. A recognizable pattern at one site can be compared with another, or across layers within a site. The comparison links sequences without necessarily giving either context an exact calendar date.

records.label: Archaeological seriation
records.learning_takeaway: Changes in the relative popularity of artifact styles allow assemblages to be arranged into a relative chronological sequence.
records.card: Seriation arranges archaeological evidence into a relative sequence by tracking changes in artifact styles. Styles rise and fall in popularity, producing overlapping periods of use. Comparing those patterns can order assemblages, even when the method alone supplies no precise calendar date.

records.label: Archaeological stratigraphy
records.learning_takeaway: In undisturbed deposits, the ordering of layers supplies relative evidence for the sequence of human activities.
records.card: Archaeological stratigraphy uses the sequence of deposited layers to investigate earlier human activity. In an undisturbed sequence, lower layers generally precede those above. The qualification matters: rearranged deposits cannot automatically be read as a simple oldest-to-newest stack.

records.label: Archival provenance
records.learning_takeaway: Keeping records grouped by their creating person or organization preserves relationships that would disappear if unrelated origins were mixed.
records.card: Archival provenance keeps records connected to the person or organization that created them. Records from different origins are not simply mixed because they discuss the same subject. Preserving that grouping helps researchers reconstruct the activities and relationships that generated the documents.

records.label: Area and territory scoring in Go
records.learning_takeaway: Compare counting occupied points with counting territory plus prisoners.
records.card: Territory scoring counts enclosed empty points and captured stones; area scoring counts enclosed points and stones still occupying the board. That difference changes whether filling your own territory costs a point. AGA rules use pass stones to permit territory-style counting within an area-scoring framework.

records.label: Area cartogram
records.learning_takeaway: Resizing geographic units according to a quantity displays that variable directly, at a cost to familiar shape or adjacency.
records.card: An area cartogram resizes places according to a chosen quantity, such as population. Geographic area becomes a visual measure of that variable instead of land size. The transformation can make comparisons striking, while distorting familiar shapes or spatial relationships that help readers recognize places.

records.label: Argo
records.learning_takeaway: Explore how buoyancy-changing floats repeatedly profile the ocean and return data by satellite.
records.card: Argo floats repeatedly move through the ocean to measure conditions such as temperature and salinity. Pumping oil into an external bladder changes volume without changing mass, allowing a float to rise or sink. On a typical profiling cycle, it surfaces to transmit data, then descends again.

records.label: Arrhenius equation
records.learning_takeaway: Use temperature-dependent rate measurements to infer activation energy under the Arrhenius model.
records.card: The Arrhenius equation connects a reaction’s rate constant with temperature and activation energy. Measuring rates at several temperatures can reveal the barrier through a graph of logarithmic rate constant against inverse temperature. This inference assumes the reaction follows the Arrhenius model over that range.

records.label: Arterial blood gas testing
records.learning_takeaway: Distinguish blood oxygenation, carbon-dioxide removal and acid-base measurements in one arterial sample.
records.card: An arterial blood gas test analyzes a blood sample for oxygen, carbon dioxide and pH. These measurements address oxygenation, removal of carbon dioxide and acid–base balance together. Unlike a light-based pulse-oximeter reading, the test requires blood from an artery and supplies information beyond oxygen saturation.

records.label: Artesian aquifer
records.learning_takeaway: Explain why confined water rises in a well but may not flow out at the surface.
records.card: An artesian aquifer holds groundwater under pressure beneath relatively impermeable layers. Water in a well tapping it can rise above the aquifer’s top, but water flows out at the surface only if the pressure level is high enough. Depth alone does not make a well artesian.

records.label: Ascending open auction
records.learning_takeaway: Reveal progressively higher offers until only one bidder remains willing to pay the rising price.
records.card: An ascending open auction raises the price while bidders remain active or drop out. When only one bidder remains willing to continue, that bidder wins. Unlike sealed bids, the process makes others' continued participation visible, so the sequence itself can convey information during the auction.

records.label: Asch's conformity experiments
records.learning_takeaway: Examine public agreement with a clearly mistaken majority in a particular experimental setting.
records.card: In Asch's line-judgment experiments, participants heard a group give an obviously wrong answer before responding aloud. Many agreed with the group at least once. Dissenting allies and private responding changed conformity, showing that agreement depended partly on the social arrangement of the task.

records.label: Ascribed status
records.learning_takeaway: Identify social positions assigned without personal choice and the expectations attached to them.
records.card: An ascribed status is a social position assigned without the person's choosing it, such as being someone's child. The status comes with expectations and relationships. It describes how the position is acquired, which is different from the behavior people perform while occupying that position.

records.label: Assembling perspective
records.learning_takeaway: Examine how gatherings form and act through observable component processes instead of treating a crowd as one mind.
records.card: The assembling perspective examines what people in crowds actually do: gather, orient together, move, speak, or manipulate objects. It shifts attention toward component actions and the lifecycle of gatherings. This makes coordination observable, though critics argue that focusing so closely on actions can miss wider cultural context.

records.label: Astronomical interferometry
records.learning_takeaway: Combine separated antennas as one telescope and vary their spacing to change angular resolution.
records.card: Astronomical interferometry combines signals from separated antennas so they operate together as an observing instrument. In ALMA, changing antenna configurations changes the maximum separation and the angular detail the array resolves. The arrangement turns carefully coordinated measurements into a larger effective observing baseline.

records.label: Astronomical seeing
records.learning_takeaway: Turbulent air continually redirects starlight, blurring ground-based images and making stars twinkle.
records.card: Astronomical seeing describes the blurring produced when starlight crosses turbulent air. Patches with different temperatures bend rays differently, and moving air continually changes those paths. The resulting image shifts and blurs; related fluctuations can also make stars appear to twinkle when seen from the ground.

records.label: Atlas linguistique de la France
records.learning_takeaway: See how mapped transcriptions from many places make regional language variation inspectable.
records.card: The Atlas linguistique de la France turned regional speech observations into maps. Around the turn of the twentieth century, fieldwork gathered detailed transcriptions from hundreds of French locations. The atlas shows how systematically placing comparable forms on maps can make geographical variation visible rather than merely listing local words.

records.label: Atmospheric perspective
records.learning_takeaway: Changing color and tone as a landscape recedes can represent the effect of atmosphere and create pictorial depth.
records.card: Atmospheric perspective suggests distance by changing the color and tone of receding forms. A landscape can gradually shift from foreground to background as though intervening air alters its appearance. The painter creates depth through these transitions rather than relying only on the geometry of drawn edges.

records.label: Atmospheric river
records.learning_takeaway: Connect a concentrated corridor of water-vapor transport with both useful precipitation and flood risk.
records.card: An atmospheric river is a concentrated corridor of water vapor moving through the atmosphere. When it reaches land, that moisture can fall as rain or snow. Such events supply useful water, but stronger or persistent landfalls can also produce flooding, so their effects depend on the event.

records.label: Atomic commit
records.learning_takeaway: Make a transaction appear all-or-nothing even though storage writes happen sequentially and can be interrupted.
records.card: Atomic commit makes a transaction's changes appear all-or-nothing, even though storage writes occur sequentially. SQLite uses recovery mechanisms to preserve that appearance across crashes or power failures under documented storage assumptions. The guarantee concerns which changes take effect, rather than requiring hardware to write everything simultaneously.

records.label: Atrial natriuretic peptide
records.learning_takeaway: Explain how cardiac stretch signals the kidneys to lose sodium and water.
records.card: Stretch of the heart’s atria can stimulate release of atrial natriuretic peptide. The signal promotes sodium and water loss through the kidneys and suppresses hormones that retain them. It connects increased cardiac filling with a response that helps reduce excess circulating volume.

records.label: Augmented sixth chord
records.learning_takeaway: Follow two chromatic voices approaching the dominant from opposite semitone directions.
records.card: An augmented sixth chord contains notes a semitone below and above the dominant scale degree. The raised fourth moves upward while the lowered sixth moves downward toward dominant pitches. This characteristic voice-leading explains the chord family's predominant role in the cited tonal framework.

records.label: Authentication rate limiting
records.learning_takeaway: Constrain failed online guesses while balancing attack resistance against legitimate users being locked out.
records.card: Authentication rate limiting restricts repeated failed login attempts. A verifier might impose waiting periods or disable an authenticator after too many failures. These controls make online guessing harder, but designers must also consider attackers who deliberately trigger the limit to lock out legitimate users.

records.label: Autochrome
records.learning_takeaway: A layer of colored starch grains acts as a filter in a glass photographic plate, producing a color transparency rather than an ordinary monochrome print.
records.card: Autochrome makes a color transparency on glass using a screen of tiny colored starch grains. Light passes through this filtering layer as part of the photographic process. The resulting color image depends on the arrangement of the grains, not simply on coloring a monochrome print afterward.

records.label: Bach's Fugue in C minor, BWV 847
records.learning_takeaway: Trace full subject entries alternating with development through fragmented motives.
records.card: Bach's C-minor fugue from the first Well-Tempered Clavier offers a compact lesson in contrapuntal development. Its opening exposition introduces the subject in every voice. Episodes then work with smaller fragments of subjects and countersubjects, allowing recognizable material to generate passages without a complete subject statement.

records.label: Bach's Invention in C major, BWV 772
records.learning_takeaway: Recognize inversion and rhythmic augmentation within one tightly developed keyboard work.
records.card: Bach's C-major Invention shows how a short idea can sustain development. The opening notes return with their melodic direction inverted, and fragments also appear in rhythmic augmentation. These transformations preserve recognizable material while changing its contour or the amount of time it occupies.

records.label: Back-calculation anti-windup
records.learning_takeaway: Feed saturation information back into a controller’s integrator so it unwinds toward an achievable output.
records.card: Back-calculation anti-windup feeds information about an actuator’s saturation back into a controller’s integrator. The feedback unwinds internal demand that the actuator cannot realize. This helps the controller return to its usable range more quickly after saturation, rather than waiting for accumulated error to disappear unaided.

records.label: Bali’s subak cultural landscape
records.learning_takeaway: Linked forests, water temples, canals and terraces demonstrate how a volcanic island’s watersheds are organized through farming and ritual.
records.card: Bali’s protected subak landscape links forests, water temples, canals and rice terraces across volcanic watersheds. These components show how farming and ritual organization work through the same environment. The place makes an irrigation institution visible through the connected spaces and structures that sustain it.

records.label: Bank of England
records.learning_takeaway: Trace the transition from a privately owned government banker to a nationalized central bank.
records.card: The Bank of England began in 1694 as a privately owned bank helping finance the government. It also accepted public deposits, and much later was nationalized. Its history shows that a public financial role and private ownership can coexist, rather than central banking always beginning with government ownership.
records.primary_subfield: Economic history and documented business cases

records.label: Bar entry in backgammon
records.learning_takeaway: Understand why a hit checker must return before other pieces can move.
records.card: A lone backgammon checker hit by an opponent goes to the bar. Its owner must bring barred checkers back into the opponent's home board before moving other pieces. If the dice offer no open entry point, the player's turn is lost.

records.label: Baroreflex
records.learning_takeaway: Trace a blood-pressure change from arterial stretch receptors to rapid cardiac and vascular responses.
records.card: When arterial pressure rises, stretch-sensitive baroreceptors increase their signaling to the brainstem. Reflex changes reduce cardiac output and relax peripheral vessels, helping oppose the rise. Falling pressure produces responses in the other direction. The baroreflex links mechanical stretch to rapid cardiovascular adjustment.

records.label: Bauhaus sites in Weimar, Dessau and Bernau
records.learning_takeaway: This ensemble links Bauhaus teaching and social ambitions to buildings whose structural frames, glass surfaces and basic forms reworked the relation between use and architectural expression.
records.card: The Bauhaus sites in Weimar, Dessau and Bernau connect teaching and social ambitions with built experiments in modern design. Structural frames, glass surfaces and simplified forms helped express new approaches to use and construction. The ensemble lets an educational movement be studied through particular buildings and spaces.
records.primary_subfield: Works, movements and historical design cases

records.label: Bayeux Tapestry
records.learning_takeaway: The Bayeux Tapestry’s narrative is embroidered in wool on joined linen panels rather than woven as a pictorial tapestry.
records.card: Despite its familiar name, the Bayeux Tapestry is embroidery rather than a woven pictorial tapestry. Wool stitches form the narrative on joined linen panels. Examining the stitched surface offers a concrete way to distinguish applied needlework from an image created by weaving.
records.primary_subfield: Works, movements and historical design cases

records.label: Bearing off in backgammon
records.learning_takeaway: Explore the conditions for removing checkers and using an oversized die roll.
records.card: Bearing off removes checkers from a backgammon board, but only after all your active checkers reach your home board. A roll normally removes a checker from its matching point. An oversized roll can remove the highest remaining checker when no checker occupies a higher point.

records.label: Beemster Polder
records.learning_takeaway: Reclaimed lake land was laid out with a geometric grid that coordinated fields, roads, canals and settlement.
records.card: Beemster’s reclaimed lakebed was organized through a geometric network of fields, roads, canals and settlement. Its regular pattern expresses both a design ambition and the practical need to manage water. The landscape shows how engineering and planned land division can structure everyday agricultural space together.

records.label: Benthic macroinvertebrate bioassessment
records.learning_takeaway: Read aquatic-community composition as an integrated record of environmental stress.
records.card: Bottom-dwelling aquatic invertebrates differ in their tolerance of pollution and other stress. Because many move little, the community found at a site can reflect conditions over time. Bioassessment uses this living evidence to complement a water sample that captures only the moment it was collected.

records.label: Betweenness centrality
records.learning_takeaway: Measure how much shortest-path traffic passes through a node or edge rather than simply counting its immediate contacts.
records.card: Betweenness centrality measures a node's or edge's share of shortest paths between other points in a network. When several shortest paths exist, their contribution is divided. This highlights potential intermediary positions that simple neighbor counts miss, while remaining a model of routes rather than a measurement of actual message traffic.

records.label: Bias facings
records.learning_takeaway: Finish a curved fabric edge using a narrow strip whose bias orientation allows it to conform to the curve.
records.card: A bias facing uses a narrow strip of fabric cut on the bias to finish a curved edge. The strip can be shaped to follow the curve without the bulk of a wider facing. Its usefulness comes from how the fabric direction allows the finish to conform.

records.label: Bicameralism
records.learning_takeaway: Understand two-chamber lawmaking through the qualified Commons–Lords example.
records.card: Bicameralism organizes a legislature into two chambers. In the United Kingdom, the Commons and Lords normally both pass a bill before it becomes law, but the Parliament Acts create specified exceptions. The example shows that two chambers need not possess equal or unrestricted blocking powers.

records.label: Binary search
records.learning_takeaway: Exploit sorted keys to find a record with logarithmic rather than full-scan search effort.
records.card: Binary search exploits an ordered collection instead of inspecting every entry. It repeatedly narrows the range that could contain a requested key. SQLite's row lookup illustrates the payoff: search effort grows logarithmically with the number of records, rather than in proportion to the entire table.

records.label: Biochemical oxygen demand
records.learning_takeaway: Use microbial oxygen consumption as an indicator of biodegradable organic loading.
records.card: Biochemical oxygen demand measures the oxygen microorganisms consume while breaking down organic material under specified conditions. A high demand can help explain why a water body loses oxygen even when it initially contains plenty. The measure concerns consumption, rather than simply the oxygen concentration at one moment.

records.label: Bipartite graph
records.learning_takeaway: Two vertex classes with only cross-class edges are equivalent to two-colorability and absence of odd cycles.
records.card: A bipartite graph divides its vertices into two groups with edges only between groups. This is equivalent to coloring the vertices with two colors without same-colored neighbors. An odd cycle prevents such a division, while graphs containing no odd cycles permit it.

records.label: Blanching vegetables before freezing
records.learning_takeaway: Explain a brief heat treatment as a way to slow enzyme-driven quality loss during frozen storage.
records.card: Briefly heating vegetables before freezing can slow or stop enzymes that would otherwise degrade flavor, color and texture during storage. This blanching step protects quality, but its duration depends on the vegetable and its size. Too little or too much heating can undermine the intended result.

records.label: Blocking knitted fabric
records.learning_takeaway: Set a knitted piece’s dimensions and even its fabric using a method suited to the yarn.
records.card: Blocking shapes a knitted piece and evens its fabric using moisture, sometimes with steam. The method should suit the yarn and its care instructions. Testing a swatch first helps reveal how the material responds before trying to bring a finished garment to its intended dimensions.

records.label: Body-centered cubic structure
records.learning_takeaway: A cubic cell with one central atom has two atoms per cell and eight nearest neighbors.
records.card: A monatomic body-centered cubic crystal has atoms at a cube’s corners and one at its center. Sharing corner atoms with neighboring cells gives two atoms per conventional cell. Each atom has eight nearest neighbors, illustrating how the arrangement determines local coordination.

records.label: Body plethysmography
records.learning_takeaway: Distinguish measuring residual lung volume from measuring only air that can be exhaled.
records.card: Body plethysmography measures lung volumes, including air that remains after a person breathes out as fully as possible. Testing takes place in an enclosed booth. This adds information beyond the air a person can blow through a spirometer, helping distinguish different aspects of lung function.

records.label: Bohr effect
records.learning_takeaway: Explain why lower pH promotes oxygen unloading from hemoglobin.
records.card: Hemoglobin releases oxygen more readily when its surroundings become more acidic. This pH-dependent change in oxygen affinity is the Bohr effect. It helps connect local chemical conditions with oxygen unloading, rather than treating hemoglobin as a container that releases oxygen at one fixed rate.

records.label: Bolting
records.learning_takeaway: Recognize premature flowering as a shift that can reduce the edible quality of a leafy or root crop.
records.card: Bolting is a crop’s shift into flowering earlier than the grower wants. In cool-season vegetables, heat or long days can help trigger it, depending on the crop and its history. Once reproductive growth begins, the quality of leaves or roots harvested for food can decline.

records.label: Bond (finance)
records.learning_takeaway: Treat a bond as an issuer's debt promise to pay specified interest and principal, with default still possible.
records.card: A financial bond is a debt security: investors lend money to an issuer under specified payment terms. Those terms typically cover interest and repayment of principal at maturity. The issuer can default, so a contractual promise to repay differs from a guarantee of receiving the money.

records.label: Borel–Cantelli lemma
records.learning_takeaway: If event probabilities have a finite sum, infinitely many occurrences have probability zero.
records.card: The first Borel–Cantelli lemma links a sum of event probabilities with what happens over an infinite sequence. If that sum is finite, only finitely many of the events occur with probability one. An endless list of possible events therefore need not produce endlessly many actual occurrences.

records.label: Borsuk–Ulam theorem
records.learning_takeaway: A continuous map from an n-sphere to n-dimensional space identifies some antipodal pair.
records.card: The Borsuk–Ulam theorem guarantees that a continuous map from an n-dimensional sphere to n-dimensional Euclidean space gives the same output at some antipodal pair. For an ordinary sphere, any two continuous real-valued measurements therefore agree simultaneously at a pair of opposite points.

records.label: Bretton Woods Conference
records.learning_takeaway: See how 1944 negotiations combined adjustable exchange-rate commitments with new institutions for payments support and reconstruction.
records.card: The Bretton Woods Conference in 1944 combined negotiations over exchange-rate stability with plans for new international institutions. The IMF would support countries facing payments imbalances, while a reconstruction bank had a different task. The resulting system linked adjustable national currencies to a dollar convertible into gold.
aliases: United Nations Monetary and Financial Conference
records.primary_subfield: Economic history and documented business cases

records.label: Brewster’s angle
records.learning_takeaway: At a particular dielectric reflection angle, reflected light is fully polarized.
records.card: For unpolarized light striking an ideal nonabsorbing dielectric interface, Brewster’s angle makes the reflected light fully linearly polarized. The angle depends on the refractive-index ratio. This helps explain why rotating polarized sunglasses changes the glare seen from surfaces such as water or glass.

records.label: Broadbalk Wheat Experiment
records.learning_takeaway: Use a persistent untreated comparison to interpret crop responses to fertilizer over many years.
records.card: Broadbalk compares wheat grown under different nutrient treatments across many years. An unfertilized strip maintained since 1843 provides a persistent reference against which fertilized plots can be read. The experiment shows how a long-lived control helps separate treatment effects from the changing background of agricultural seasons.

records.label: Brooklyn Bridge
records.learning_takeaway: Steel suspension cables reduced dead load while trusses were designed to resist deck oscillations.
records.card: The Brooklyn Bridge’s suspension design changed from iron to steel to reduce dead load. Its main cables bundle thousands of galvanized steel wires, while stiffening trusses were intended to limit deck oscillations. The bridge combines flexible suspension with structural elements designed to control unwanted movement.
records.primary_subfield: Transport systems and engineered case studies

records.label: Brouwer fixed-point theorem
records.learning_takeaway: Every continuous self-map of a closed finite-dimensional ball leaves at least one point fixed.
records.card: Brouwer’s fixed-point theorem states that every continuous map from a closed finite-dimensional ball into itself leaves at least one point fixed. The map may move most points dramatically. Continuity and keeping the whole image inside that same ball are essential conditions of the claim.

records.label: Brown v. Board of Education
records.learning_takeaway: Explore the constitutional rejection of state-mandated racial segregation in public education.
records.card: Brown v. Board of Education rejected state-imposed racial segregation in US public education under equal protection. The Court treated separate schooling as inherently unequal, rather than asking only whether physical facilities matched. The decision challenged a legal framework of separation, although implementing desegregation required further proceedings and resistance persisted.

records.label: Buffer capacity
records.learning_takeaway: Buffers with equal pH can resist different acid loads because their total concentrations differ.
records.card: Buffers with nearly the same pH can tolerate very different additions of acid or base. Buffer capacity depends on how much of the conjugate pair is present. Increasing both components together can raise capacity while approximately preserving their ratio-dependent initial pH.

records.label: Buffer solution
records.learning_takeaway: A weak conjugate acid-base pair consumes small additions of strong acid or base.
records.card: A buffer contains a weak acid and its conjugate base, or an analogous weak-base pair. Added strong acid or base is converted into weaker species, limiting the pH change. This resistance has limits: a buffer does not keep its pH fixed under unlimited additions.

records.label: Bumpless transfer
records.learning_takeaway: Track the active manual signal internally before switching to automatic control to avoid a sudden output jump.
records.card: Bumpless transfer avoids an abrupt commanded-output jump when switching from manual to automatic control. One implementation lets the automatic controller track the manual signal and adjust its internal state before taking over, aligning the two outputs at the switching moment.

records.label: Buon fresco
records.learning_takeaway: Painting into freshly applied wet plaster makes the timing of plaster preparation part of the painting process.
records.card: Buon fresco paints onto freshly applied wet plaster. The wall’s preparation and the painter’s timing are therefore inseparable: the surface must still be suitable when the pigment is applied. Work proceeds in manageable fresh sections rather than treating the entire wall as an indefinitely available canvas.

records.label: Burnside’s lemma
records.learning_takeaway: Count symmetry classes by averaging the number of objects fixed by each group action.
records.card: Burnside’s lemma counts distinct objects when symmetries make some appearances equivalent. For a finite group acting on a finite set, count the objects fixed by each symmetry and average those counts. The answer is the number of orbits, avoiding the mistake of treating every rotated appearance as new.

records.label: Cadential six-four chord
records.learning_takeaway: Understand why an inverted tonic sonority can perform a dominant function.
records.card: A cadential six-four contains the notes of a tonic triad with its fifth in the bass, yet commonly functions as part of a dominant arrival. Before the following dominant chord, its pitch content and its harmonic role therefore point in different analytical directions.

records.label: Caesura
records.learning_takeaway: A pause within a poetic line can divide its movement without coinciding with the line ending.
records.card: A caesura is a pause within a line of verse. It can divide the line’s movement without ending the line itself, making an internal break audible or meaningful. Attending to caesuras distinguishes the rhythm of a sentence from the poem’s outer line boundaries.

records.label: Canal lock
records.learning_takeaway: Controlled filling or draining changes a chamber’s water level to move floating vessels between elevations.
records.card: A canal lock raises or lowers a vessel by changing the water level inside an enclosed chamber. Water enters or leaves through controlled passages while gates retain it. At Panama, gravity supplies the water movement, turning a difference in elevation into a controlled transfer between levels.
records.primary_subfield: Transport systems and engineered case studies

records.label: Candidate-understanding repair
records.learning_takeaway: Offer a possible interpretation of the prior message and ask the original speaker to confirm or correct it.
records.card: Candidate-understanding repair offers a possible interpretation and asks the original speaker to confirm or correct it. Repeating a guessed phrase with questioning intonation can make the proposed solution explicit. The task differs from simply asking for clarification: the speaker can often resolve the trouble with a short confirmation.

records.label: Canon (scriptural collection)
records.learning_takeaway: A religious community identifies a bounded set of authoritative texts; the Catholic list illustrates one particular canon rather than every tradition’s collection.
records.card: A scriptural canon identifies writings recognized as authoritative within a religious tradition. The Catholic list of biblical books provides one specific example. Studying a canon means asking which texts belong to the collection and how that authority is understood, without assuming every community recognizes the same boundaries.

records.label: Canonical equivalence in Unicode
records.learning_takeaway: Recognize a precomposed accented character and its decomposed sequence as the same abstract character.
records.card: Unicode can represent the same abstract character in different ways, such as a precomposed accented letter or a letter followed by a combining accent. Canonical equivalence identifies these alternatives as fundamentally equivalent. Normalization allows software to compare their representations consistently.

records.label: Canonical Huffman coding
records.learning_takeaway: Reconstruct a Huffman codebook from ordered code lengths using deterministic code assignment.
records.card: Canonical Huffman coding determines the actual codewords from ordered symbol lengths. Codes of equal length receive consecutive values, with shorter codes preceding longer ones. DEFLATE uses these rules so a decoder can reconstruct the codebook from lengths rather than receiving every codeword explicitly.

records.label: Capability-based security
records.learning_takeaway: Represent authority with unforgeable object-specific tickets that a principal presents to obtain access.
records.card: Capability-based security represents authority with an unforgeable ticket for a particular object. Presenting the ticket demonstrates permission to access that object. This organizes protection around what a principal possesses, rather than asking every object to maintain a list of all principals allowed to use it.

records.label: Carnot cycle
records.learning_takeaway: A reversible cycle sets the maximum heat-engine efficiency between two specified thermal reservoirs.
records.card: The Carnot cycle is an ideal reversible heat-engine cycle operating between two thermal reservoirs. Its efficiency sets an upper bound for engines working between those temperatures. Real irreversibilities reduce performance, making the cycle a reference limit for comparison rather than a promise about a practical machine.

records.label: Cascade control
records.learning_takeaway: A fast inner loop rejects local disturbances while a slower outer loop commands its setpoint.
records.card: Cascade control nests a fast inner feedback loop inside a slower outer one. The outer controller sets the inner loop’s target, while the inner loop helps reject local disturbances before they spread through the plant. Speed separation matters; stacking two controllers does not ensure this benefit.

records.label: Cascadia Subduction Zone
records.learning_takeaway: Explain the paired coastal and volcanic ranges produced by the descending Juan de Fuca Plate.
records.card: In the Cascadia Subduction Zone, the Juan de Fuca Plate descends beneath North America. Scraped-off material helps build coastal ranges, while deeper processes support the Cascade volcanic arc inland. The region shows how one convergent boundary can produce distinct landscape features at different distances.

records.label: Castling
records.learning_takeaway: Distinguish permanent loss of castling rights from temporary obstacles.
records.card: Castling moves a king and rook in one turn, but permission depends on more than empty squares. Moving the king or the relevant rook permanently loses that castling right. Pieces between them or attacks on the king's starting, crossing or destination square can temporarily prevent it.

records.label: Catalan numbers
records.learning_takeaway: The same integer sequence counts polygon triangulations and related recursive combinatorial structures.
records.card: Catalan numbers appear when counting ways to triangulate a regular polygon with fixed vertices using noncrossing diagonals. The same sequence arises in tree-enumeration problems. Such repeated appearances suggest a useful strategy: translate one counting problem into another structure whose possibilities are already understood.

records.label: Center of percussion in a tennis racket
records.learning_takeaway: Explore how recoil and rotation can cancel motion at a particular supporting point.
records.card: An impact makes a tennis racket both recoil and rotate. At a particular supporting point, those motions can cancel. The corresponding impact location is its center of percussion. Adding the hand's mass shifts this relationship, so a freely suspended racket does not reproduce every playing condition.

records.label: Chair by Ruth Asawa
records.learning_takeaway: In the 1965 lithograph Chair (TAM.1558-II), patterned marks and unmarked spaces both delineate chairs, making negative space an active part of the composition.
records.card: Ruth Asawa’s 1965 lithograph Chair (TAM.1558-II) lets furniture emerge from patterned marks and from unmarked areas between them. Some chairs appear through the marks; others through their absence. The work offers a case for examining how positive and negative areas organize a composition.
records.primary_subfield: Works, movements and historical design cases

records.label: Chandra X-ray Observatory
records.learning_takeaway: Special paired mirrors allow Chandra to image high-energy X-rays that ordinary optical designs cannot focus.
records.card: Chandra’s X-ray telescope uses four pairs of precisely shaped mirrors. X-rays that would penetrate an ordinary face-on mirror can reflect at grazing angles, so the optics resemble nested barrels. Extremely smooth, aligned, iridium-coated surfaces guide the radiation into sharp images of energetic cosmic environments.

records.label: Chantale Cenerini
records.learning_takeaway: Learn from her account of documenting community stories while respecting distinct local Michif and Métis language histories.
records.card: Chantale Cenerini describes documenting stories with Michif and Métis communities as work that can preserve language, family histories, and locally valued knowledge. Her account emphasizes learning each community's linguistic history first. A shared national identity does not mean every community uses the same language.

records.label: Chebyshev’s inequality
records.learning_takeaway: Finite variance bounds large deviations from the mean without requiring a particular distribution shape.
records.card: Chebyshev’s inequality bounds large deviations from a mean using variance. For a positive deviation threshold, the probability of reaching or exceeding it is at most the variance divided by the threshold squared. The bound applies without assuming a normal distribution, provided the variance is finite.

records.label: Chemigram
records.learning_takeaway: Chemigrams manipulate photosensitive paper with resists and photographic chemicals in full light, allowing chemical interaction and chance to shape the image.
records.card: A chemigram creates an image by manipulating photographic paper with chemicals and substances that resist them. Working in full light lets materials such as oils or varnishes shape the reaction. Chance and direct intervention can both influence marks without a camera recording an external scene.

records.label: Chiasmus
records.learning_takeaway: A statement reverses the arrangement of paired elements, producing a crossing pattern that can sharpen contrast.
records.card: Chiasmus reverses the arrangement of paired elements into a crossing pattern. The effect depends on their order rather than simply on repeating a sound. When identical words recur in reverse order, the pattern takes the more specific form often called antimetabole.

records.label: Chimerism
records.learning_takeaway: Distinguish cell populations derived from different zygotes from mosaicism within one zygote.
records.card: Chimerism means that genetically distinct cell populations within one individual originated from different fertilized eggs. Mosaicism instead arises among descendants of a single fertilized egg. The distinction concerns the populations’ origins, even when both situations produce a body containing more than one cellular genome.

records.label: Chinese imperial examinations
records.learning_takeaway: In the Song case, literary and Confucian examinations offered a route into government, but most candidates never became officials.
records.card: Chinese imperial examinations linked literary and Confucian learning with entry into government. In the Song period, growing candidate numbers competed for limited posts, and most never became officials. This example exposes both a route to advancement and strong constraints on success.
aliases: Civil service examinations in imperial China

records.label: Chintz in global trade
records.learning_takeaway: Washable, colorfast Indian cottons were adapted to foreign tastes and prompted European restrictions and domestic imitation.
records.card: Indian painted and printed cottons attracted overseas buyers because their colors endured washing and their designs could be adapted to different tastes. European demand encouraged imitation and restrictive import policies. A textile’s commercial history therefore reveals both shared fashions and competition between producers.

records.label: Chlor-alkali process
records.learning_takeaway: Electrolyzing brine produces chlorine and sodium hydroxide through competing electrode reactions.
records.card: The chlor-alkali process uses electrolysis of brine to produce chlorine and sodium hydroxide. Water participates in the electrode chemistry alongside dissolved ions. This makes the aqueous process different from simply decomposing molten sodium chloride, showing why the solvent matters to industrial electrochemistry.

records.label: Chocolate tempering
records.learning_takeaway: Connect controlled cocoa-butter crystallization with gloss, snap and contraction as chocolate sets.
records.card: Tempering chocolate encourages cocoa butter to form a suitable stable crystal structure. That preparation helps the finished chocolate set with gloss, a clean snap and useful contraction. Simply letting melted chocolate become cold does not necessarily produce the same arrangement of crystals or the same finish.

records.label: Choosing a titration indicator
records.learning_takeaway: Match an indicator’s color-transition interval to the steep pH change near equivalence.
records.card: Choosing a titration indicator means matching its color-change interval to the steep part of the pH curve near equivalence. An indicator that changes earlier can give a premature stopping signal; one suitable for a strong acid may fail for a weak acid.

records.label: Choropleth mapping
records.learning_takeaway: Shading geographic areas by a rate or ratio reveals spatial comparisons while differing area sizes can influence visual attention.
records.card: A choropleth map shades geographic areas according to an attribute such as a rate or ratio. The pattern lets readers compare regions, but large areas can attract disproportionate attention. Using appropriate normalized values helps prevent population size from masquerading as the phenomenon being compared.

records.label: Christian typological interpretation
records.learning_takeaway: Earlier scriptural events are read as anticipations of later ones, while Catholic teaching also preserves the earlier texts’ intrinsic value.
records.card: Christian typological interpretation reads earlier scriptural people or events as anticipations of later ones. Catholic teaching uses this approach to connect the Testaments while also affirming the earlier texts’ intrinsic value. The interpretive link therefore does not require treating the earlier narrative as meaningless on its own.

records.label: Chromatic polynomial
records.learning_takeaway: Count proper vertex colorings for each palette size using a graph-associated polynomial.
records.card: A finite undirected graph’s chromatic polynomial counts its proper vertex colorings for any specified number of available colors. Adjacent vertices must receive different colors, and color names are distinguishable. Evaluating the polynomial answers many counting questions rather than only finding the fewest necessary colors.

records.label: Circumstantial moral luck
records.learning_takeaway: Ask how unchosen situations expose people to different moral tests.
records.card: Circumstantial moral luck concerns the unchosen situations that test a person's character. Someone placed in a brutal political environment may face choices another person never encounters. The philosophical problem is whether differing moral assessments are justified when the opportunity for wrongdoing itself depended on luck.

records.label: Claim preclusion
records.learning_takeaway: Understand why a resolved cause of action generally cannot be litigated again.
records.card: In US litigation, claim preclusion generally prevents repeating a cause of action after a final judgment on its merits. A losing plaintiff cannot simply sue the same defendant again on that claim; a winning plaintiff likewise cannot start another suit just to obtain additional recovery.

records.label: Clapping Music
records.learning_takeaway: Hear how discrete rhythmic rotations create changing alignments without a gradual tempo drift.
records.card: In Steve Reich's Clapping Music, rhythmic alignment changes through discrete rotations of a repeated pattern. One performer maintains the original pattern while the other moves to the next alignment on a measure's downbeat. Unlike Piano Phase, the transition does not require gradually speeding up.

records.label: Clarinet overblowing at the twelfth
records.learning_takeaway: Compare a clarinet's next register with a flute's octave using boundary conditions.
records.card: A simple clarinet model is a cylindrical pipe closed at one end, which supports an odd-harmonic sequence. Its next resonance is therefore near three times the fundamental, a musical twelfth higher. Real clarinets depart from the ideal cylinder, but the model explains their characteristic register jump.

records.label: Clay drying shrinkage
records.learning_takeaway: Explain shrinkage before firing through particle packing as inter-particle water leaves the clay.
records.card: Wet clay shrinks as water between its particles leaves and the particles pack closer together. If different parts dry unevenly, they can shrink by different amounts and develop cracks as the piece stiffens. This drying change occurs before the separate transformations produced by firing in a kiln.

records.label: Cliché-verre
records.learning_takeaway: A drawn, painted or scratched glass plate acts as a negative for exposing light-sensitive paper.
records.card: Cliché-verre turns a drawing on a transparent plate into a photographic printing surface. Marks painted or scratched on glass control the light reaching sensitized paper beneath it. The result joins hand-made lines with photographic exposure rather than recording a scene through a camera lens.

records.label: Cluny Abbey
records.learning_takeaway: Its monumental church and rich decoration show how an influential Benedictine community made elaborate worship visible in architecture.
records.card: Cluny’s great Benedictine church combined monumental scale with rich decoration and elaborate liturgy. Its architecture made a community’s worship visible and spatially impressive. The example shows how monastic religious priorities could shape artistic patronage and building, alongside the disciplined routines of life within the abbey.

records.label: Coannular exhaust nozzle
records.learning_takeaway: Route engine-core and fan exhaust through concentric outlets to combine their flows.
records.card: A coannular nozzle provides concentric outlets for two exhaust streams. In a turbofan, core flow leaves the central passage while fan air exits through a surrounding annulus. Their interaction affects thrust and noise, showing why the arrangement of outlets matters as well as the flow within them.

records.label: Coastal strip-land division at Grand Pré
records.learning_takeaway: Long agricultural divisions along the coast preserve a settlement pattern alongside the separately maintained marsh-drainage system.
records.card: Grand Pré preserves long agricultural land divisions alongside its coastal marsh reclamation works. The pattern records how settlers organized access and farming space, while dykes and drainage addressed water. Reading these features together distinguishes the geometry of landholding from the engineering that made cultivation possible.

records.label: Coastal upwelling
records.learning_takeaway: Connect offshore displacement of surface water with rising cold nutrient-rich water.
records.card: When winds move coastal surface water away, colder water can rise from below to replace it. This upwelling often brings nutrients into sunlit waters and supports high biological productivity. The process connects a change in water movement with conditions that can benefit marine food webs.

records.label: Coinsurance
records.learning_takeaway: Split a covered loss by percentages so the insured party retains part of each covered cost.
records.card: Coinsurance divides a covered cost by percentages between an insurer and the insured party. If coverage pays eighty percent, the other share remains with the policyholder. This differs from a deductible's initial threshold and a copayment's fixed charge for a covered service.

records.label: Colca
records.learning_takeaway: Inka state storehouses combined regional collection and redistribution with storage designed to exploit natural airflow.
records.card: Colcas were Inka state storehouses for food, textiles and other goods collected from different regions. Their placement and construction could use natural airflow to help preserve supplies. Clusters of storehouses supported redistribution, including when harvests were poor or officials needed stored resources.

records.label: Collagraph
records.learning_takeaway: Materials glued onto a support create a textured printing surface that can be inked and pressed onto paper.
records.card: A collagraph builds a printing surface by attaching materials to a support. Their textures can hold or distribute ink that is then transferred to paper. The assembled surface functions as a matrix, which distinguishes the resulting print from a collage whose attached materials remain the finished image.

records.label: Collective behavior
records.learning_takeaway: Study noninstitutionalized group activity while distinguishing a shared gathering from a formally regulated organization.
records.card: Collective behavior involves group activity that is not governed through an established institution's rules. Crowds, dispersed publics, and shared fashions can take different forms. Studying these episodes does not require assuming that participants lose reason; sociological theories also examine coordination, interpretation, and newly developing norms.

records.label: Columbian Exchange
records.learning_takeaway: Post-1492 transfers of plants, animals, people and disease reshaped societies across the Atlantic in unequal and often destructive ways.
records.card: The Columbian Exchange names the movements of plants, animals, people and diseases between the Americas and other regions after 1492. New crops changed diets, while disease and coercive colonial relationships brought devastating consequences. Exchange here describes connected transformations, not an equal bargain.

records.label: Columnar jointing
records.learning_takeaway: Connect contraction during cooling with polygonal fractures in volcanic rock.
records.card: Cooling lava can contract and fracture into columns separated by polygonal joints. Seen from above, the cracks may resemble a honeycomb. Columnar jointing records a material response to cooling, distinguishing these fractures from a structure that necessarily formed through later faulting or folding.

records.label: Combining equilibrium constants
records.learning_takeaway: Reverse, scale, or add reaction equations to derive the corresponding transformed equilibrium constants.
records.card: At a common temperature, equilibrium constants follow the algebra of reaction equations. Reversing a reaction takes the reciprocal of its constant; multiplying coefficients raises the constant to that power. Adding reactions multiplies their constants, letting a difficult equilibrium be assembled from known ones.

records.label: Combustion analysis
records.learning_takeaway: Infer elemental composition from measured carbon dioxide and water produced by complete combustion.
records.card: Combustion analysis can determine the carbon and hydrogen content of a hydrocarbon sample. Complete combustion produces carbon dioxide and water, which are collected separately. Their measured masses reveal how much of each element was present and can establish the compound’s empirical formula.

records.label: Common ground in communication
records.learning_takeaway: Use mutually taken-for-granted knowledge, beliefs, and assumptions as the shared basis for coordinated communication.
records.card: Common ground consists of knowledge, beliefs, and assumptions participants take to be mutually shared. It gives them a starting point for coordination, but is updated as they communicate. Two people separately knowing the same fact is not automatically the same as recognizing it as shared between them.

records.label: Common-value auction
records.learning_takeaway: Distinguish shared underlying value from bidders' differing information about that value.
records.card: In a common-value auction, the object has the same underlying value to bidders, but they may estimate it differently. A jar of coins is a simple example. Winning can then reveal that one's estimate was unusually optimistic, so the information contained in winning matters for sensible bidding.

records.label: Community-led language reclamation
records.learning_takeaway: Let communities' own language histories and goals guide locally tailored reclamation work rather than assuming one shared language.
records.card: Community-led language reclamation begins with a community's own history and goals. Cenerini's Michif case explains that Métis communities do not all share one language, so a uniform national approach can miss local identities. Learning what people speak and value shapes which reclamation work makes sense there.

records.label: Compatibility equivalence in Unicode
records.learning_takeaway: Treat certain stylistic or presentation variants as equivalent while recognizing potentially meaningful distinctions lost by folding.
records.card: Compatibility equivalence connects Unicode forms that may differ in presentation, such as a circled numeral and its ordinary digit. Compatibility normalization can fold these distinctions. That can help comparison, but blindly applying it may erase formatting or mathematical distinctions that matter in context.

records.label: Competitive exclusion principle
records.learning_takeaway: Explain why competing for all the same limiting resources can prevent stable coexistence.
records.card: Two species competing for exactly the same limiting resources cannot indefinitely occupy the same niche under the competitive exclusion principle. Laboratory comparisons with Paramecium illustrate one competitor displacing another. Coexistence becomes more plausible when species differ in resource use, habitat or feeding time.

records.label: Complementary distribution
records.learning_takeaway: Recognize nonoverlapping sound environments without assuming this alone proves that the sounds share one phoneme.
records.card: Two sounds have complementary distribution when they occur in nonoverlapping environments. That can help identify allophones, but it is not enough by itself: English /h/ and /ŋ/ also occupy different environments for many speakers. Phonetic similarity and broader patterns help determine whether sounds belong together.

records.label: Complete mediation
records.learning_takeaway: Check authority for every access, including recovery and maintenance paths rather than only ordinary operation.
records.card: Complete mediation requires checking authority for every access to every protected object. The requirement includes initialization, recovery, and maintenance, not only the usual operation path. A bypass can undermine an otherwise careful permission system, so identifying the source of each request is part of the problem.

records.label: Compton Gamma-Ray Observatory
records.learning_takeaway: Four complementary instruments surveyed gamma rays and mapped radioactive aluminum in the Milky Way.
records.card: The Compton Gamma-Ray Observatory combined four instruments sensitive to different gamma-ray energies. It mapped radioactive aluminum across the Milky Way and provided evidence pointing toward distant origins for gamma-ray bursts. The mission demonstrates how high-energy observations can trace processes unavailable to ordinary visible-light surveys.

records.label: Concurrent legislative powers in Germany
records.learning_takeaway: See how federal action can displace state legislative authority within a shared competence.
records.card: In Germany's concurrent legislative sphere, the Länder generally may legislate while the Federation has not exercised its power. Federal legislation can therefore change the space for state action. Article 72 also permits departures in specified fields, so concurrency does not mean either unrestricted coexistence or uniform federal exclusion.

records.label: Conditional amnesty in South Africa's TRC
records.learning_takeaway: See why political context alone did not guarantee amnesty without full disclosure.
records.card: Amnesty before South Africa's TRC was conditional, not automatic for politically connected violence. In a 1997 decision, Henry Khanyile's application failed because the committee found he had withheld relevant facts. The case shows why political context did not remove the requirement for full disclosure.

records.label: Conditional expectation
records.learning_takeaway: Average a random quantity while retaining the information supplied by another variable or sigma-algebra.
records.card: Conditional expectation averages an integrable random quantity while retaining specified information, such as another variable’s value. The result can itself vary with that information rather than being one fixed number. Its mathematical definition preserves the appropriate averages over events recognizable from the conditioning information.

records.label: Confidence and supply agreement
records.learning_takeaway: Distinguish supporting a government on specified matters from joining its coalition.
records.card: A confidence and supply agreement allows one party to support another on specified parliamentary matters without forming a coalition government together. New Zealand's electoral authority distinguishes these arrangements from parties joining government. The distinction shows that keeping a government functioning need not mean sharing its entire program.

records.label: Connecting concrete and abstract representations
records.learning_takeaway: Explicitly map familiar objects or examples onto abstract symbols so knowledge can transfer beyond surface features.
records.card: Connecting concrete and abstract representations means explicitly showing how familiar examples correspond to symbols or general concepts. Without that bridge, learners may manipulate a formula yet struggle to apply it elsewhere. Comparing several representations can direct attention away from surface details toward the underlying relation.

records.label: Constituency tests
records.learning_takeaway: Combine replacement and movement evidence to identify word groups that behave as sentence units.
records.card: Constituency tests investigate which words behave together as a unit inside a sentence. Replacing a group with a pronoun or moving it can supply evidence for a phrase. Different tests offer complementary clues, so a sentence's visible sequence alone need not reveal its internal structure.

records.label: Constitutive moral luck
records.learning_takeaway: Examine responsibility for dispositions shaped partly by unchosen development and inheritance.
records.card: Constitutive moral luck concerns traits and dispositions shaped partly by factors people did not choose, including inheritance and upbringing. If those traits influence action, judging someone's character also raises a question about control. The issue is responsibility for who one has become, not merely what happens afterward.

records.label: Construct validity
records.learning_takeaway: Ask whether an operational measure captures the intended psychological concept.
records.card: Construct validity asks whether a measure actually captures the concept it is intended to represent. A procedure can produce consistent scores yet miss its intended target. The challenge is therefore more than repeatability: it is connecting an observable measurement to the psychological idea being studied.

records.label: Constructed treatment wetland
records.learning_takeaway: Treat wastewater with deliberately arranged vegetation, soils and microbial processes.
records.card: A constructed treatment wetland uses wetland plants, soils and associated microorganisms as part of an engineered water-treatment system. Water-quality improvement depends on these natural processes working within a designed setting. The vegetation is therefore part of the treatment approach, not merely decoration around a pond.

records.label: Constructive vote of no confidence
records.learning_takeaway: Understand why Germany requires choosing a successor while removing the Chancellor.
records.card: Germany's constructive vote of no confidence requires the Bundestag to elect a successor Chancellor by a majority of its members while seeking the incumbent's dismissal. Opposition must therefore agree on a replacement, not merely on rejection. Article 67 also requires forty-eight hours between motion and election.

records.label: Convergent evolution
records.learning_takeaway: Explain similar functions that evolved separately rather than being inherited from a shared ancestor.
records.card: Convergent evolution produces similar features in separate evolutionary lineages. Bird and bat wings both serve flight, but their wing structures arose independently. Their underlying forelimbs still share ancestry, showing that the answer depends on which feature and evolutionary level a comparison is examining.

records.label: Conversational acknowledgment
records.learning_takeaway: Provide brief verbal or gestural evidence of understanding, often without taking over the speaking turn.
records.card: A conversational acknowledgment gives brief evidence that a listener is following or understanding, often without taking the speaking turn. Responses such as yeah or a head nod can serve this function. Their role is feedback within coordination, rather than necessarily endorsing the truth of everything the speaker says.

records.label: Conversational implicature
records.learning_takeaway: Distinguish a contextually suggested conclusion from a necessary implication by checking whether it can be cancelled.
records.card: A conversational implicature is an interpretation suggested by context rather than guaranteed by the sentence's truth. Hearing that a customer sighed might suggest annoyance, yet the speaker can add that the customer was relieved. This cancellability helps distinguish an implicature from a necessary entailment.

records.label: Conversational turn-taking
records.learning_takeaway: Coordinate alternating speakers partly by anticipating possible turn endings rather than waiting only to react after silence.
records.card: Conversational turn-taking coordinates who speaks and when. Experiments with conversation fragments show that listeners can anticipate turn endings, supporting accounts that involve preparation before silence arrives. Such laboratory tasks isolate useful cues, but do not establish how every transition is managed in natural conversation.

records.label: Coordinating graphics and verbal explanations
records.learning_takeaway: Place relevant verbal explanations alongside the visual elements they explain so learners can connect representations.
records.card: Coordinating graphics with verbal explanations helps learners connect what an image shows with the process being described. Relevant labels can sit close to the visual elements they explain. Decorative or overly detailed pictures may distract instead, so the principle concerns meaningful integration rather than adding images indiscriminately.

records.label: Coral bleaching
records.learning_takeaway: Distinguish stress-driven loss of symbiotic algae from immediate coral death.
records.card: Stressed corals can lose the symbiotic algae living in their tissues, leaving them pale or white. This bleaching also removes an important food source. A bleached coral is not necessarily dead, but prolonged stress makes recovery harder and can ultimately lead to death.

records.label: Coriolis force
records.learning_takeaway: A rotating frame describes apparent trajectory bending through an inertial force absent from the inertial-frame account.
records.card: The Coriolis force appears when motion is described from a rotating reference frame. A path can seem to bend sideways because the observer’s coordinate system is turning. An inertial-frame description accounts for the same motion without assigning this apparent force a separate physical interaction.

records.label: Countersubject
records.learning_takeaway: Identify recurring counterpoint accompanying successive subject entries.
records.card: A countersubject is recurring counterpoint that accompanies a fugue's subject. Its identity matters: the composer brings back recognizable accompanying material when the subject returns, rather than inventing completely different counterpoint each time. The same countersubject can appear in different voices as the texture changes.

records.label: Covalent network solid
records.learning_takeaway: A continuous covalent-bond network helps explain the hardness and high melting temperatures of diamond-like solids.
records.card: A covalent network solid contains atoms joined in an extended web of covalent bonds. Disrupting that network requires breaking bonds, rather than merely separating intact molecules. Such solids often have high melting temperatures; diamond illustrates the hardness that extensive covalent bonding can produce.

records.label: Cover crops
records.learning_takeaway: Distinguish a crop grown for soil cover and ecosystem functions from one grown primarily for harvest.
records.card: Cover crops are grown primarily to keep living vegetation on the soil and provide conservation benefits, rather than as the main harvested crop. Their roots and residues can reduce erosion and add organic matter. Timing and management determine how those functions fit around the farm’s other crops.

records.label: Covering index
records.learning_takeaway: Include search and output columns in an index so a query need not consult the original table.
records.card: A covering index contains every column a particular query needs, including its output columns. The database can answer that query from the index without looking up matching rows in the original table. Whether an index covers a query therefore depends on that query's requested information.

records.label: Creep (materials)
records.learning_takeaway: Time-dependent deformation can accumulate at elevated temperature even below a material’s usual yield stress.
records.card: Creep is deformation that accumulates under sustained loading over time. In metals and ceramics at elevated temperatures, it can become important even below the usual yield stress. Components such as turbine blades must therefore be assessed for service duration and temperature, not only their initial deformation.

records.label: Critical damping
records.learning_takeaway: Tune the linear damping threshold for rapid nonoscillatory return to equilibrium.
records.card: For a displaced linear spring–mass system released from rest, critical damping returns it toward equilibrium as quickly as possible without oscillation. It marks the threshold between oscillatory and nonoscillatory response; simply adding more damping makes the return slower rather than always improving the result.

records.label: Critical point of a fluid
records.learning_takeaway: At the end of liquid-vapor coexistence, the liquid-gas boundary disappears and pressure alone cannot liquefy hotter gas.
records.card: A fluid’s critical point marks the end of the liquid–vapor coexistence boundary. As it is approached, the distinction between the two phases disappears. Above the critical temperature, applying more pressure cannot produce a separate liquid phase, although the fluid can become dense.

records.label: Crop rotation
records.learning_takeaway: Disrupt recurring crop-pest associations by changing the crop grown in a field over time.
records.card: Crop rotation changes the crops grown in a field through a planned sequence over time. This can interrupt recurring pest associations and diversify how the field is used. It is a preventive management practice, rather than simply moving an existing pest after it has become a problem.

records.label: Crystal vacancy
records.learning_takeaway: A missing atom at a regular lattice site is a structural defect distinct from an interstitial impurity.
records.card: A crystal vacancy is an unoccupied position where an atom or ion normally belongs in a lattice. It differs from an interstitial defect, where a particle occupies a gap between regular positions. Both disturb an otherwise repeating internal arrangement of particles.

records.label: Curveball aerodynamics
records.learning_takeaway: Connect spin-generated sideways force with a curved pitch trajectory.
records.card: A spinning baseball can experience a sideways aerodynamic force that bends its path. NASA's simplified curveball model links the curvature to spin, speed and air density. It treats the path as a circular arc when drag and the resulting changes in the force are neglected.

records.label: Cyanotype
records.learning_takeaway: Light acts on iron-salt-coated paper, and washing develops the characteristic blue image.
records.card: Cyanotype uses light-sensitive iron salts to produce a characteristic blue image. Exposure and washing make the image visible on a prepared surface. Because the process can record objects placed directly on paper, it can join photographic chemistry with close observation of a specimen’s shape.

records.label: Damped harmonic motion
records.learning_takeaway: Dissipation removes oscillator energy so its amplitude declines rather than continuing indefinitely.
records.card: In a weakly damped spring–mass system, oscillations lose energy and their amplitude declines. A common low-speed model makes the damping force proportional to velocity and opposite to motion. Under that model, the oscillating displacement fits inside a shrinking exponential envelope.

records.label: Darshan
records.learning_takeaway: Seeing a deity’s image can be a devotional encounter; visual presence matters in temples and in debates over online worship.
records.card: Darshan concerns the devotional encounter of seeing a deity, commonly through an image. The visual interaction can be central to puja rather than merely decorative. Debates about internet worship make this emphasis especially visible by asking how an encounter changes when the image is mediated online.

records.label: Dasymetric mapping
records.learning_takeaway: Ancillary information reallocates aggregate population away from uninhabited areas instead of assuming uniform density within census boundaries.
