records.primary_subfield: Transport systems and engineered case studies

records.label: Horizontal gene transfer
records.learning_takeaway: Distinguish DNA exchange outside parent-to-offspring inheritance from ordinary reproduction.
records.card: Genetic information can move between cells outside ordinary parent-to-offspring inheritance. In prokaryotes, transformation takes up environmental DNA, transduction uses viruses, and conjugation transfers DNA through cell contact. Horizontal gene transfer therefore offers several routes for acquiring genetic material without reproducing a whole new organism.

records.label: Horticultural grafting
records.learning_takeaway: Join a selected shoot variety to a different root system so each contributes different traits.
records.card: Grafting joins a selected shoot, or scion, to a rootstock so the parts contribute different traits. In apple trees, the scion determines the fruit variety, while the rootstock strongly influences tree size and time to bearing. The resulting tree combines roles from two genetically different individuals.

records.label: HTTP entity tag
records.learning_takeaway: Use an opaque representation validator to detect changes without requiring clients to understand its construction.
records.card: An HTTP entity tag is an opaque label identifying a particular representation for validation. A server may derive it from a version number, hash, or another method, while clients simply compare tags. Strong and weak tags support different comparisons; an ETag need not reveal its construction.

records.label: HTTP method idempotency
records.learning_takeaway: Distinguish repeated intended effects from identical responses or the absence of incidental logging.
records.card: An HTTP method is idempotent when repeating an identical request has the same intended server effect as performing it once. Responses may differ, and servers may still log each attempt. The property helps clients decide when retrying after an interrupted connection will avoid multiplying the requested change.

records.label: HTTP If-Match update preconditions
records.learning_takeaway: Apply a state-changing request only when its representation tag still matches, preventing intervening updates from being overwritten.
records.card: An HTTP If-Match condition can require a representation to retain a matching entity tag before an update proceeds. If someone else has changed it, the precondition can stop an accidental overwrite. The check tests the version instead of assuming the client's earlier copy is current.

records.label: Hubble Space Telescope
records.learning_takeaway: Observing above Earth’s turbulent atmosphere gives Hubble sharper visible-light images.
records.card: Hubble’s position above Earth’s atmosphere avoids the constantly changing refraction that blurs ground-based images. This helped deliver sharp visible-light views of distant objects. Space does not remove diffraction, however: the telescope’s finite aperture still limits the angular detail its optical system can resolve.

records.label: Huffman coding
records.learning_takeaway: Assign variable-length prefix codes using symbol frequencies to minimize expected code length.
records.card: Huffman coding assigns variable-length bit strings to symbols using their frequencies. Frequent symbols can receive shorter codes. The result is an optimal prefix code for the given frequencies, so a decoder can identify consecutive symbols unambiguously without inserting a separator after every codeword.

records.label: Hydroponics
records.learning_takeaway: Grow plants using a nutrient solution without making soil the source of their nutrients.
records.card: Hydroponics grows plants without relying on soil as the nutrient medium. A water-based solution supplies mineral nutrients, while the system must also accommodate the roots’ need for oxygen. Different arrangements support or bathe the roots differently, so soilless growing is more than placing a plant in plain water.

records.label: Hypothalamic–pituitary–thyroid feedback
records.learning_takeaway: Trace TRH and TSH stimulation together with thyroid-hormone feedback.
records.card: Low thyroid-hormone levels stimulate a signaling chain from hypothalamic TRH to pituitary TSH and then the thyroid gland. As thyroid hormones rise, they reduce further stimulation through negative feedback. The system regulates output through returning information, rather than a one-way sequence of commands.

records.label: I Remember (Joe Brainard)
records.learning_takeaway: Repeated opening words accumulate ordinary memories into a book-length structure that also inspired a widely used writing exercise.
records.card: Joe Brainard’s I Remember builds a book through recurring opening words that introduce ordinary recollections. Repetition turns separate memories into an accumulating structure. The work also became a model for a writing exercise, showing how a recognizable formal device can organize both reading and composition.

records.label: Ideal rocket equation
records.learning_takeaway: Ideal velocity change grows with effective exhaust speed and the logarithm of initial-to-final mass ratio.
records.card: The ideal rocket equation links velocity change to constant effective exhaust speed and the logarithm of initial-to-final mass ratio, neglecting gravity and drag losses. At fixed dry mass, adding propellant gives diminishing velocity gains because the extra propellant must initially be accelerated too.

records.label: Imperfect duty
records.learning_takeaway: Distinguish discretion over fulfilling a duty from permission to ignore it.
records.card: In the Kantian distinction discussed here, an imperfect duty remains obligatory while leaving latitude in how it is fulfilled. Flexibility about particular actions does not make the underlying duty optional. This separates discretion within an obligation from supererogation, which concerns morally good action beyond obligation.

records.label: Implied author
records.learning_takeaway: Readers infer an author-image from a work’s stylistic and evaluative choices; this debated construct is not the real writer or narrator.
records.card: The implied author is an image of a work’s maker inferred from its stylistic, aesthetic and evaluative choices. It is not simply the real writer or the narrator. The concept remains debated because textual clues and a reader’s interpretation both contribute to the reconstructed image.

records.label: Implied reader
records.learning_takeaway: A text can presuppose a recipient’s knowledge and values without depicting an actual reader inside its story.
records.card: An implied reader is a recipient-image reconstructed from clues within a text. It concerns the knowledge, assumptions or responses the work appears to accommodate. This differs from an actual reader and from an intended audience known only through the author’s private plans or external statements.

records.label: Impression management
records.learning_takeaway: Shape how others interpret a social performance through behavior, setting, and visible cues.
records.card: Impression management concerns how people present themselves through behavior, surroundings, and visible cues. Goffman's theatrical analogy highlights how different settings invite different performances; a judge's robe and courtroom props help shape expectations. The process need not imply deliberate deception or a completely invented identity.

records.label: Inattentional blindness
records.learning_takeaway: Understand how a visible unexpected event can escape notice during another task.
records.card: Inattentional blindness is missing a visible event while attention is occupied elsewhere. In the basketball-pass counting demonstration described by OpenStax, many viewers failed to notice an unexpected gorilla-costumed figure. The result concerns divided task demands, not an inability of the eyes to receive the image.

records.label: Indiscernibility of identicals
records.learning_takeaway: Understand why genuinely identical things cannot differ in a property.
records.card: The indiscernibility of identicals says that if two names pick out the very same thing, every property of that thing must belong to both referents. It runs from identity to shared properties. The converse claim, that sharing all properties guarantees identity, is a different principle.

records.label: Inert pair effect
records.learning_takeaway: Heavy main-group elements can retain a low-energy valence s-electron pair and form lower oxidation states.
records.card: Some heavy main-group elements form ions that retain their outer s-electron pair instead of losing every valence electron. This inert pair effect helps explain lower oxidation states, such as thallium’s plus-one state, alongside the higher states suggested by its periodic-table group.

records.label: Inertial reference frame
records.learning_takeaway: Distinguish physical interactions from extra inertial-force terms introduced by accelerated coordinates.
records.card: An inertial reference frame lets Newton’s laws describe motion using forces from physical interactions without adding inertial-force terms. Accelerated or rotating frames can still be useful, but require those extra terms. A turning car illustrates how a passenger’s frame differs from an approximately inertial ground frame.

records.label: Information asymmetry
records.learning_takeaway: Distinguish unequal knowledge between parties from uncertainty that both sides share.
records.card: Information asymmetry occurs when one party to a transaction knows more relevant information than another. A used-car seller may know defects the buyer cannot readily observe. This differs from shared uncertainty: both parties can lack information, but asymmetry describes an unequal distribution of what they know.

records.label: Informational social influence
records.learning_takeaway: Understand relying on others as information when a situation is ambiguous.
records.card: Informational social influence occurs when people treat others' responses as evidence about an uncertain situation. If smoke in a theater might be a special effect, nearby people's reactions can guide interpretation. Conformity here reflects reliance on presumed knowledge, rather than only a wish to belong.

records.label: Inharmonicity of musical strings
records.learning_takeaway: Explain why stiff strings have stretched modal frequencies rather than exact harmonic multiples.
records.card: Real instrument strings are not perfectly flexible. Their bending stiffness shifts higher vibration modes farther from exact whole-number multiples of the fundamental. This inharmonicity is especially relevant to plucked or struck strings; periodic bowing can instead draw the vibration into a harmonic pattern.

records.label: Institutionalization
records.learning_takeaway: Understand how shared conventions become established social institutions that outlast the original participants.
records.card: Institutionalization establishes a convention or norm as a durable part of social life. A school functions as more than a building because people recognize roles and shared expectations around it. Those arrangements can predate current participants, showing how socially created institutions can still have real consequences.

records.label: Insulin–glucagon regulation of blood glucose
records.learning_takeaway: Contrast glucose storage and uptake after a meal with glucose mobilization during fasting.
records.card: Insulin and glucagon help keep blood glucose within a usable range. Insulin favors glucose uptake and storage after levels rise; glucagon helps mobilize glucose, including from liver glycogen, when levels fall. Their opposing actions connect changing food availability with the body’s ongoing fuel needs.

records.label: Insurance deductible
records.learning_takeaway: Require an initial out-of-pocket loss amount before the insurance coverage begins paying.
records.card: An insurance deductible is an amount the policyholder pays before specified coverage starts paying. It leaves some loss with the insured party instead of transferring every cost to the insurer. In the textbook's incentive account, retaining that stake can discourage risk-taking that full coverage might otherwise encourage.

records.label: Integer partition function
records.learning_takeaway: Count decompositions of an integer into positive summands while ignoring their order.
records.card: The integer partition function counts ways to write a positive integer as a sum of positive integers when order is ignored. Four has five partitions. Consequently, three plus one and one plus three count as the same possibility, unlike an ordered composition.

records.label: Integral windup
records.learning_takeaway: An integrator can accumulate unusable control demand during actuator saturation, delaying recovery afterward.
records.card: Integral windup occurs when a controller accumulates error while an actuator cannot deliver the requested output because it is saturated. After the command changes, that accumulated demand may take time to unwind. The result can be a delayed recovery even though the actuator’s limits are already known.

records.label: Intention-to-treat analysis
records.learning_takeaway: Preserve original randomized groups when estimating the effect of treatment assignment.
records.card: Intention-to-treat analysis keeps participants in their originally assigned trial groups, even when they do not follow treatment as planned. This preserves the comparison created by randomization for estimating assignment effects. Missing outcome data still require attention; the label alone does not solve that separate problem.

records.label: Inter-rater reliability
records.learning_takeaway: Check whether different observers classify the same behavior consistently.
records.card: Inter-rater reliability concerns agreement between observers evaluating the same event. If two researchers classify a behavior differently, the coding procedure may be inconsistent. Agreement helps establish reproducibility across observers, but by itself does not show that their shared measure captures the intended psychological construct.

records.label: Interest-rate risk in bonds
records.learning_takeaway: Understand why an older fixed-rate bond may need a price discount when newly issued bonds offer higher rates.
records.card: A bond's resale value can change when market interest rates move. If newer bonds offer higher interest, an older fixed-rate bond may need to sell at a discount to attract buyers. This price risk is distinct from an issuer failing to make its promised payments.

records.label: Interleaved practice
records.learning_takeaway: Mix different mathematical problem types so learners must select a strategy instead of repeating one blocked routine.
records.card: Interleaved practice mixes different kinds of problems rather than grouping one type into a long block. In the cited mathematics intervention, students had to choose a suitable strategy for each problem. The challenge is partly recognizing which method applies, not simply carrying out a method already signaled by repetition.

records.label: International Cooperative Alliance
records.learning_takeaway: Explore how an international federation coordinated information, common principles, and trade among otherwise separate cooperatives.
records.card: The International Cooperative Alliance was founded in 1895 to connect cooperatives across countries. Its initial aims included sharing information, defending common principles, and developing international trade. It illustrates how independent member enterprises can coordinate through a federation without becoming a single ordinary business under one owner.
records.primary_subfield: Economic history and documented business cases

records.label: International HapMap Project
records.learning_takeaway: See how patterns of co-inherited DNA variants helped connect genomic variation with disease.
records.card: The International HapMap Project charted common patterns of human DNA variation, especially groups of variants often inherited together. These genomic neighborhoods helped researchers connect variation with disease. Its contribution was a map of shared variation patterns, rather than merely another sequence from a single individual.

records.label: Intrinsic motivation
records.learning_takeaway: Distinguish doing an activity for satisfaction from doing it for an external reward.
records.card: Intrinsic motivation comes from satisfaction in the activity itself, such as baking because it is enjoyable. External rewards can also motivate the same person. Distinguishing these sources helps explain why turning a favorite activity into paid work can sometimes change its appeal.

records.label: Ionic bonding
records.learning_takeaway: Electrostatic attraction holds oppositely charged ions together, with conductivity changing when ions become mobile.
records.card: Ionic bonding holds positively and negatively charged ions together through electrostatic attraction. The ions are constrained in a solid lattice, so they cannot readily carry electric current. Melting the material or dissolving it can free the ions to move and conduct.

records.label: IPM action thresholds
records.learning_takeaway: Distinguish the presence of a pest from a level that warrants an intervention.
records.card: An IPM action threshold marks conditions under which pest management becomes warranted. It may reflect a pest population level or environmental circumstances indicating unacceptable harm. The threshold separates seeing a pest from deciding to intervene, making control a decision based on context rather than mere presence.

records.label: IR8
records.learning_takeaway: Trace a historically influential semi-dwarf rice variety to a specific cross and selection program.
records.card: IR8 emerged from crossing the tall rice variety Peta with the dwarf Dee-geo-woo-gen, followed by selection of useful offspring. Released by IRRI in 1966, it became an influential semidwarf variety. Its history makes crop improvement visible as a sequence of crosses, observations and selection.

records.label: Isle Royale
records.learning_takeaway: Use an isolated island study to distinguish predator effects from climate, disease and food availability.
records.card: On Isle Royale in Lake Superior, a long-running study follows wolves, moose and their environment. Predator numbers matter, but disease, climate and available food also influence population changes. The island illustrates why a predator–prey relationship cannot be understood from two population counts alone.

records.label: Issue preclusion
records.learning_takeaway: Distinguish relitigating a decided issue from repeating an entire claim.
records.card: In US litigation, issue preclusion can bar relitigation of an issue actually litigated and necessarily decided in a valid final judgment. It generally binds a party who had a full and fair opportunity to litigate, with recognized nonparty exceptions. The issue may recur within a different claim.

records.label: Iterative narration
records.learning_takeaway: One narrative statement can gather events that happened repeatedly, compressing habitual experience into a single telling.
records.card: Iterative narration tells once what happened repeatedly. Instead of recounting every separate occasion, a narrative can gather a habit or recurring activity into one statement. The repeated events belong to the story world, while their presentation occurs only once in the telling.

records.label: Jacoby rule
records.learning_takeaway: See how an optional scoring rule encourages use of the doubling cube.
records.card: The optional Jacoby rule makes a gammon or backgammon count as a single game unless a double has been offered. It encourages use of the cube rather than waiting for a multiple-value win. The cited standard match-play rules do not use it.

records.label: James Lind
records.learning_takeaway: Separate a useful controlled comparison from a correct explanation of why the treatment worked.
records.card: In 1747, James Lind compared different remedies among sailors with scurvy; those given citrus improved. Yet he did not understand vitamin deficiency and retained other theories about the disease. His work separates the value of a treatment comparison from a correct explanation of its mechanism.

records.label: James Naismith
records.learning_takeaway: See how indoor space and injury constraints shaped basketball's original design.
records.card: James Naismith devised basketball at Springfield in 1891 to provide an engaging indoor winter activity. Avoiding the rough collisions of outdoor games shaped the design. Elevated peach baskets required players to toss the ball toward a goal rather than charge through it.

records.label: Janissary corps
records.learning_takeaway: The Ottoman elite infantry and household guard drew recruits from state training and was intended to reduce dependence on hereditary nobles.
records.card: The Janissaries were an elite Ottoman infantry corps and household guard. Recruits trained for service to the ruler, including boys taken through devshirme. The sultans intended this force to reduce dependence on hereditary nobles, expecting recruits’ status and privileges to bind them to the ruler.

records.label: Japanese sarasa trade textiles
records.learning_takeaway: Indian cottons designed for Japanese buyers circulated despite restrictions on Japanese overseas travel, showing selective trade rather than total isolation.
records.card: Sarasa textiles made for Japanese buyers show that restrictions on overseas travel did not end foreign exchange. Indian cotton designs were adapted for this market and circulated through trade. Their surviving patterns make selective connections visible within a period often associated with isolation.

records.label: Jensen’s inequality
records.learning_takeaway: For a convex function, averaging before applying the function does not exceed averaging afterward.
records.card: Jensen’s inequality compares two orders of operations. For a convex function and nonnegative weights summing to one, applying the function to a weighted average gives no more than averaging the function’s values. A nonlinear transformation therefore need not commute with taking an average.

records.label: Jidoka
records.learning_takeaway: Stop work when an abnormality appears so defects are addressed without requiring constant human machine-watching.
records.card: Jidoka builds a response to abnormalities into production. Toyota describes machines stopping when something goes wrong, helping prevent defects from continuing unnoticed. The approach can reduce the need for someone to watch a machine constantly, linking productivity to detecting problems rather than simply increasing operating speed.

records.label: Joint consensus in Raft
records.learning_takeaway: Require separate old- and new-configuration majorities during membership changes to prevent incompatible simultaneous majorities.
records.card: Raft changes membership through a transitional joint configuration. Decisions during that phase require separate majorities of both the old and new configurations. This prevents the two memberships from making incompatible decisions independently while allowing servers to learn about the change at different times.

records.label: Jordan curve theorem
records.learning_takeaway: A simple closed planar curve separates the plane into an inside and an outside.
records.card: A simple closed curve in a plane separates it into an inside and an outside. The Jordan curve theorem makes this familiar picture precise: the complement has two connected components, and the curve borders both. Self-intersections would change the problem and are excluded.

records.label: Just-in-time production
records.learning_takeaway: Coordinate production and replenishment with downstream demand to shorten lead times and avoid unnecessary stock.
records.card: Just-in-time production coordinates making and replenishing items with when they are needed. Toyota describes a pull system in which a later process obtains parts already used from an earlier one. This aims to shorten production time and limit unnecessary stock rather than keep every machine producing continuously.

records.label: Just intonation
records.learning_takeaway: Explore why pure small-ratio intervals create compromises when changing keys.
records.card: Just intonation favors intervals described by simple frequency ratios. Yet pure fifths and pure thirds do not fit every chain of notes identically: repeated three-to-two fifths can conflict with a pure third. Fixed-pitch instruments must therefore confront compromises that adjustable voices or strings can handle differently.

records.label: Just-noticeable difference
records.learning_takeaway: See why noticing a change depends on the starting stimulus intensity.
records.card: A just-noticeable difference measures the change needed to distinguish two stimulus intensities. The same added light can be conspicuous in a dark room yet barely noticeable in bright surroundings. This differs from asking whether any light can be detected at all, the question behind an absolute threshold.

records.label: Justified true belief analysis
records.learning_takeaway: Distinguish a belief's truth and justification in a traditional analysis of knowledge.
records.card: The justified true belief analysis proposes that knowledge requires a belief to be true and adequately justified, with those conditions together sufficient. Truth excludes error; justification excludes unsupported lucky guesses. Gettier cases challenge the proposal by combining justification and truth with another kind of epistemic luck.

records.label: Kīlauea
records.learning_takeaway: Explore how a flank eruption and summit collapse can be connected through a magma system.
records.card: Kīlauea’s 2018 eruption linked activity far apart on the same volcano. Magma moved from summit storage toward the lower East Rift Zone, while the summit floor repeatedly collapsed. Increased pressure after collapse could boost the distant eruption rate, revealing a connected underground magma system.

records.label: Karner blue butterfly
records.learning_takeaway: Explore how ant attendance can protect butterfly larvae while the ants receive carbohydrate-rich secretions.
records.card: Karner blue butterfly larvae can exchange a sugary secretion for protection from ants. The ants gain food, while their attendance can reduce threats to the caterpillars. This butterfly offers a concrete example of mutualism, with the particular ant partners varying between locations.

records.label: Karst drainage
records.learning_takeaway: Trace water through fractures enlarged by dissolution rather than assuming it remains in surface streams.
records.card: In karst terrain, water enlarges soluble-rock fractures and can travel through underground openings before emerging at springs. Surface streams alone may therefore miss important drainage routes. Rapid movement through these openings can also carry contamination with little filtration, linking rock structure to water quality.

records.label: Kepler Space Telescope
records.learning_takeaway: Long, continuous stellar-brightness measurements reveal repeated planetary transits across a crowded fixed field.
records.card: Kepler’s original survey repeatedly measured the brightness of stars in one crowded field. Small, recurring dips could reveal planets crossing in front of their host stars. Concentrating on a stable field made long time series possible, turning subtle changes in starlight into evidence about unseen planetary systems.

records.label: Kerf bending
records.learning_takeaway: Create a bend by cutting relief slots while retaining an outer web of material.
records.card: Kerf bending cuts a series of slots into one side of wood while leaving a thin outer layer intact. The remaining web can flex around a curve. Slot spacing and depth affect the result, and the weakened piece usually needs a supporting form or backing to hold its shape.

records.label: Keystone species
records.learning_takeaway: Explain how a predator can maintain community diversity by limiting a space-dominating competitor.
records.card: A keystone species plays an especially important role in its community. On rocky shores, sea stars eat mussels that might otherwise dominate available space. Removing that predator can therefore change which other organisms are able to persist alongside the mussels.

records.label: Khinalig and Köç Yolu
records.learning_takeaway: A mountain village, lowland winter pasture and connecting route together make seasonal mobility visible at landscape scale.
records.card: Khinalig’s cultural landscape includes a mountain village, seasonal grazing areas and the route joining them. Summer and winter locations form parts of one living system. The site demonstrates why a mobile way of life may need to be understood through a connected landscape rather than one settlement.

records.label: Khipu
records.learning_takeaway: Knotted cords with differing colors and structures recorded numerical information used to administer labor, goods and taxation.
records.card: Khipus used knotted cords to record information in the Inka world. Differences in knots, colors and cord arrangements supported numerical administration, including accounts of labor and goods. They demonstrate a system of record keeping whose organization cannot be understood by looking for written alphabetic words.

records.label: Kiichiro Toyoda
records.learning_takeaway: Explore how limited resources shaped his effort to coordinate automobile parts just when production needed them.
records.card: Kiichiro Toyoda advocated coordinating automobile parts just when they were needed while working with limited resources. Toyota's history connects that concern with just-in-time production and later downstream pull arrangements. The case shows how production timing emerged from a concrete coordination problem, rather than from simply demanding faster work.
records.primary_subfield: Economic history and documented business cases

records.label: Knickerbocker Trust Company
records.learning_takeaway: Examine how uncertain solvency, lost clearing support, and deposit withdrawals culminated in a trust company's suspension.
records.card: Knickerbocker Trust Company's 1907 crisis intensified after it lost clearing support and depositors withdrew funds. Potential rescuers could not quickly establish its solvency, and the company suspended operations. The case distinguishes an urgent need for liquidity from having enough information to judge whether rescue lending is sound.
records.primary_subfield: Economic history and documented business cases

records.label: Knitting gauge
records.learning_takeaway: Connect stitches and rows per unit length with the dimensions a knitting pattern will produce.
records.card: Knitting gauge counts stitches and rows within a given length of fabric. A swatch tests the yarn, needles and stitch pattern together before a larger project is made. If the gauge differs from the pattern, the same stitch count can produce a different finished size.

records.label: Knuckleball aerodynamics
records.learning_takeaway: Understand erratic flight from seam-dependent forces varying during the pitch.
records.card: A baseball's seams make its surface aerodynamically uneven. As their orientation changes during flight, the effective location and direction of aerodynamic forces can vary. NASA connects these unsteady forces with the knuckleball's erratic motion, rather than explaining it solely through a steady spin-generated curve.

records.label: Ko rule
records.learning_takeaway: See why immediate recapture must wait for a play elsewhere.
records.card: A ko capture can create an opportunity for immediate recapture that would restore the previous position. The basic ko rule forbids that immediate reply. The player must first play elsewhere, giving the opponent an opportunity to respond or end the local cycle.

records.label: Komi
records.learning_takeaway: Understand points compensating White for playing second.
records.card: Komi compensates the player using White stones for Black's first move in Go. It adds points to White's final score rather than adding stones to the board. The British Go Association's cited default uses seven-and-a-half points; other rules or agreements can use different values.

records.label: Ksar
records.learning_takeaway: A fortified collective settlement groups homes and communal spaces within defensive walls, exemplified by southern Moroccan earthen villages.
records.card: A ksar is a fortified settlement grouping homes and shared spaces within defensive walls. Southern Moroccan examples use earthen construction adapted to their setting. Looking at dwellings together with communal facilities reveals how collective defense and everyday settlement organization could share the same built form.

records.label: L.L.Bean
records.learning_takeaway: Use the textbook's mail-order case to see how guarantees and reputation can reduce buyers' uncertainty without inspecting goods.
records.card: OpenStax uses L.L.Bean's mail-order business as a case of selling goods customers cannot inspect beforehand. A guarantee and a reputation for quality can reduce that uncertainty. The example illustrates how trust supports remote retail, rather than establishing the company's current return policy or every customer's experience.
records.primary_subfield: Economic history and documented business cases

records.label: Laboratory reference intervals
records.learning_takeaway: Explain why being outside a population reference range does not by itself establish disease.
records.card: A laboratory reference interval describes results found in a selected comparison population. Being outside it does not automatically establish disease, and being inside it does not guarantee health. Different laboratories, methods and patient groups can use different ranges, so the reported context matters.

records.label: Lagrange’s group theorem
records.learning_takeaway: Equal-sized subgroup cosets partition a finite group, forcing subgroup order to divide group order.
records.card: Lagrange’s group theorem explains why a subgroup’s size divides the size of a finite group. Its cosets partition the group into equally sized blocks. The divisibility condition is necessary, but it does not guarantee that a subgroup exists for every divisor of the group’s order.

records.label: Lahar
records.learning_takeaway: Distinguish fast volcanic debris-and-water flows from molten lava.
records.card: A lahar is a moving mixture of water and volcanic debris, not a stream of molten lava. It can rush through valleys during an eruption, afterward or even while a volcano is quiet. Recognizing the mixture and its possible timing changes how volcanic hazards are understood.

records.label: Lake-effect snow
records.learning_takeaway: Trace narrow snow bands to cold air gaining heat and moisture over unfrozen lake water.
records.card: Cold air moving across a warmer, unfrozen lake gains heat and moisture. As that air rises, narrow cloud bands can form and deliver lake-effect snow downwind. Wind direction strongly affects where the snow falls, so heavy snowfall can occur close to places receiving very little.

records.label: Lalibela’s rock-hewn churches
records.learning_takeaway: Carved churches, passages and drainage works made a sacred landscape that served as a symbolic alternative to distant holy places.
records.card: Lalibela’s churches were carved into rock and connected through passages and carefully managed drainage. Together they form a sacred landscape rather than a set of isolated monuments. Their arrangement expressed religious meaning while addressing the practical demands of moving through and maintaining excavated spaces.

records.label: Landsat
records.learning_takeaway: Use consistently calibrated imagery to distinguish real long-term land changes from sensor differences.
records.card: Landsat’s repeated satellite observations provide a long record of changes on Earth’s surface. Careful calibration helps researchers compare images across years and distinguish real changes in forests, cities or coastlines from changes in measurement. The archive’s value grows through continuity as well as through individual pictures.

records.label: Language documentation
records.learning_takeaway: Create records of language use and community knowledge that can serve both research and family legacies.
records.card: Language documentation creates records of language use and the knowledge expressed through it. Recording community stories can preserve family histories as well as linguistic forms. Such records may support future work, but making an archive is different from ensuring that people continue learning and using the language.

records.label: Lava tube
records.learning_takeaway: Trace a volcanic cave from a crusted-over lava stream to an emptied conduit.
records.card: A lava tube begins when the surface of a flowing lava stream cools into a crust while molten material continues beneath it. If the lava later drains away, an empty passage remains. The cave records a former flow route rather than a space carved by underground water.

records.label: Le Châtelier’s principle
records.learning_takeaway: Predict how concentration, volume, or temperature changes disturb and re-establish chemical equilibrium.
records.card: Le Châtelier’s principle predicts how equilibrium responds when conditions change. At fixed temperature, compressing a gaseous mixture favors the side with fewer gas molecules when the sides differ. Temperature changes also shift equilibrium, with direction depending on whether the reaction absorbs or releases heat.

records.label: Lead-time bias
records.learning_takeaway: Explain how earlier diagnosis can lengthen measured survival without delaying death.
records.card: Screening can move a diagnosis earlier without changing when a person dies. Survival measured from diagnosis then looks longer simply because the clock started sooner. Lead-time bias explains why improved survival after detection does not, by itself, prove that a screening program saves lives.

records.label: Least collaborative effort
records.learning_takeaway: Model conversational choices by the combined work of both participants through mutual acceptance, rather than minimizing only speaking effort.
records.card: The principle of least collaborative effort proposes that conversational partners minimize their combined work through mutual acceptance of a contribution. A perfectly prepared utterance is not always cheapest overall. A shorter presentation followed by a quick clarification may require less total effort than preventing every possible misunderstanding in advance.

records.label: Leather temper
records.learning_takeaway: Distinguish a hide’s pliability from its thickness when choosing between draping and shape-holding uses.
records.card: Leather temper describes how readily a hide bends, drapes or holds its shape. It is different from thickness: equally thick pieces can feel quite different. A soft garment panel and a firm structured bag may require different tempers, so flexing a sample reveals information a thickness measurement cannot.

records.label: Lectio divina
records.learning_takeaway: Prayerful scriptural reading moves through attention to the text, meditation, prayer and contemplation, with an intended consequence for action.
records.card: Lectio divina is prayerful engagement with scripture through reading, meditation, prayer and contemplation. In the Catholic account cited here, the practice is intended to lead toward action. Its aim is to let attentive reading shape religious life, rather than merely extracting information from a passage.

records.label: Liberties in Go
records.learning_takeaway: Count shared adjacent empty points for an entire connected string.
records.card: A liberty is an empty intersection directly beside a Go stone along a horizontal or vertical line. Connected stones share their liberties as one string. Surrounding every liberty captures the entire string, so adding a connection can change the survival prospects of several stones at once.

records.label: Lichtenstein, Flowers, Parsifal
records.learning_takeaway: Elizabeth Peyton’s monotype brings references to Lichtenstein’s dots, Wagner’s opera and still-life painting into one image, translating mechanically associated marks into handwork.
records.card: Elizabeth Peyton’s Lichtenstein, Flowers, Parsifal combines references to Lichtenstein’s dots, Wagner’s opera and still-life imagery in a monotype. The dots are hand-applied before printing. An editorial reading emphasizes the contrast between mechanically associated marks and their manual realization.
records.primary_subfield: Works, movements and historical design cases

records.label: Linguistic change from above
records.learning_takeaway: Trace consciously noticed adoption of a prestigious outside variant, illustrated by New York City's rhoticity shift.
records.card: A linguistic change from above spreads with social awareness, often through adoption of a prestigious variant from outside a community. Increasing rhoticity in New York English is a textbook example. Above refers to awareness of the change, rather than simply locating its speakers at the top of society.

records.label: Linguistic change from below
records.learning_takeaway: Trace language-system changes that spread below conscious social awareness, such as gradual vowel fronting.
records.card: A linguistic change from below develops largely outside speakers' conscious awareness. The textbook illustrates it with the goose vowel moving forward in Canadian English. Speakers can participate in a shifting pronunciation pattern without noticing it, unlike consciously adopting a prestigious form recognized as different.

records.label: Litotes
records.learning_takeaway: Denying an opposite can make an understated assertion, sometimes giving a speaker an appearance of modesty.
records.card: Litotes makes an understated assertion by denying its opposite. Calling something not unwelcome, for example, can express acceptance with restraint. The wording leaves room for context and tone to determine how much emphasis the speaker intends, rather than stating the positive claim directly.

records.label: Living shoreline
records.learning_takeaway: Stabilize sheltered coasts using vegetation and natural materials while retaining habitat functions.
records.card: Living shorelines use plants and other natural materials, sometimes with low structural elements, to stabilize estuarine coasts. They can buffer waves while preserving habitat and allowing marsh processes to continue. The approach connects erosion protection with ecological functions rather than treating the shoreline only as a rigid boundary.

records.label: Local bridge in a network
records.learning_takeaway: Identify a tie whose endpoints have no mutual neighbor and whose removal makes their shortest connecting path longer.
records.card: A local bridge connects two nodes that have no common neighbor. Removing it leaves no two-step alternative route between its endpoints; reaching the other side takes a longer path, if one exists. This precise edge property helps distinguish network-spanning connections from ties embedded among mutual friends.

records.label: Lock water-saving basin
records.learning_takeaway: Side basins permit part of a lockage’s water to be reused instead of discharged.
records.card: Water-saving basins capture part of the water used by navigation locks so it can be reused. Panama’s 2016 expanded-lock design provided three basins per chamber and specified sixty-percent reuse per lockage. Such storage reduces demand on lake water that also serves surrounding communities.
records.primary_subfield: Transport systems and engineered case studies

records.label: Lottery paradox
records.learning_takeaway: Compare rational acceptance of each likely loser with certainty that one ticket wins.
records.card: If high probability licenses belief, each ticket in a large fair lottery may reasonably be treated as a loser. Combining all those beliefs yields that every ticket loses, although one must win. The lottery paradox challenges combining individually plausible beliefs without restriction.

records.label: LZ77
records.learning_takeaway: Replace repeated byte strings with backward distance and length references within a sliding history.
records.card: LZ77-style compression replaces repeated strings with references to earlier input. In DEFLATE, a reference gives a backward distance and a length, telling the decoder what earlier bytes to copy. Literal bytes handle material without a suitable match in the available history.

records.label: Ma Huan
records.learning_takeaway: A Muslim translator accompanied Zheng He’s fourth voyage, illustrating the role of linguistic and cultural expertise in imperial travel records.
records.card: Ma Huan was a Muslim translator and chronicler who joined Zheng He’s fourth voyage. His role puts written observation alongside travel through foreign ports. As a learning case, it invites attention to the people who recorded and interpreted encounters during imperial expeditions.

records.label: Magna Carta
records.learning_takeaway: The failed settlement of 1215 was reissued in later versions; its later constitutional influence should be distinguished from its baronial setting.
records.card: Magna Carta began as a 1215 settlement between King John and rebellious barons, and its first version failed to secure lasting peace. Later reissues gave it a different career. Its constitutional reputation grew from that subsequent history, rather than arriving fully formed in 1215.

records.label: Malus’s law
records.learning_takeaway: A polarizer transmits an intensity proportional to the squared cosine of its angle to incoming polarization.
records.card: Malus’s law describes linearly polarized light passing through an ideal polarizer. The transmitted intensity equals the incoming intensity multiplied by the squared cosine of the angle between polarization and the filter’s axis. Parallel alignment transmits maximally; perpendicular alignment blocks the light in this ideal model.

records.label: Managed aquifer recharge
records.learning_takeaway: Distinguish deliberate underground replenishment from simply storing surface water.
records.card: Managed aquifer recharge deliberately adds water to underground storage. At Sand Hollow, water spread in a reservoir seeps into the underlying sandstone aquifer. Monitoring water levels, infiltration rates and chemistry helps determine where that water goes and how effectively the recharge system is working.

records.label: Manchester Baby
records.learning_takeaway: See how cathode-ray-tube storage let an experimental 1948 machine hold and run its own program.
records.card: Manchester's experimental Baby computer tested a way to store data electronically in cathode-ray tubes. Patterns of dots represented binary information, including a program held in memory. Its successful run in 1948 demonstrated a stored-program approach that made changing a task different from rewiring a machine.

records.label: Manila galleon trade
records.learning_takeaway: American silver moved west across the Pacific while Asian goods traveled through Manila to Mexico, where imports influenced local artistic production.
records.card: The Manila galleon trade connected Asian commerce with Spanish America across the Pacific. Silver traveled west, while Asian goods passed through Manila toward Mexico. Imported textiles and other objects also influenced local artistic production, making the route a channel of cultural as well as commercial exchange.

records.label: Mansabdari system
records.learning_takeaway: Under Akbar, administrators’ ranks combined civil service and cavalry responsibilities with revenue allocations that could be reassigned.
records.card: Under Akbar, mansabdars held ranks that connected administrative service with responsibility for supplying cavalry. Revenue from assigned land supported them, and allocations could be shifted as their rank or position changed. This tied officeholders’ resources to imperial appointment rather than secure hereditary possession.

records.label: Marine heatwave
records.learning_takeaway: Identify unusual ocean warmth relative to local seasonal history rather than one worldwide temperature threshold.
records.card: A marine heatwave is unusually warm ocean water measured against the normal conditions for that place and season. A common definition requires temperatures above the seasonal ninetieth percentile for at least five consecutive days. The comparison is local and time-specific, not one temperature threshold for every sea.

records.label: Marine stratus
records.learning_takeaway: Explain coastal low-cloud sheets through ocean formation, inland advection and daytime evaporation.
records.card: Marine stratus forms a low cloud layer associated with coastal ocean air. Winds can carry it inland, while daytime warming and mixing with drier air can make it evaporate. Its changing extent reflects both movement of the cloudy air and changes in temperature and humidity.

records.label: Mario J. Molina
records.learning_takeaway: Molina and Rowland showed how chlorine derived from human-made compounds catalyzes ozone destruction.
records.card: Mario Molina and F. Sherwood Rowland connected chlorofluorocarbon use with damage to stratospheric ozone. Sunlight can release chlorine atoms that repeatedly participate in ozone-destroying reactions. Their work illustrates why a small amount of a regenerated reactive species can have a much larger chemical effect.

records.label: Marker-assisted selection
records.learning_takeaway: Select breeding candidates using genetic markers associated with a useful trait.
records.card: Marker-assisted selection chooses breeding material using DNA markers associated with traits of interest. A breeder reads the marker pattern rather than relying only on the trait’s visible expression. The method depends on an established marker–trait relationship, so detecting a genetic difference alone is not enough.

records.label: Markov’s inequality
records.learning_takeaway: Bound the probability of a nonnegative quantity exceeding a positive threshold using its mean.
records.card: Markov’s inequality bounds the chance that a nonnegative random quantity exceeds a positive threshold using only its finite mean. Divide the mean by the threshold to obtain the bound. No specific distribution shape is required, but dropping nonnegativity would invalidate this argument.

records.label: Martingale
records.learning_takeaway: A process’s conditional expected next value equals its present value despite its random future.
records.card: A martingale is a random process with finite expectations whose expected next value, given its history, equals its current value. It can still fluctuate substantially. A symmetric one-dimensional random walk illustrates this: either step is possible, but their conditional average produces no expected change.

records.label: Mastery learning
records.learning_takeaway: Hold learning goals steady while varying time and corrective support before progression to new units.
records.card: Mastery learning holds intended outcomes steady while allowing time and support to vary. Learners work through units, demonstrate sufficient understanding, and receive additional help when needed before progressing. Approaches differ in their thresholds and organization, so aiming for mastery is not itself one uniform teaching procedure.

records.label: Material constitution
records.learning_takeaway: Distinguish a statue from the material constituting it through their possible persistence conditions.
records.card: A clay statue raises a puzzle: the clay seems able to survive squashing, while the statue does not. Does that show two coincident objects, or should their relationship be understood differently? Material constitution investigates this disputed relationship between an object and the matter that constitutes it.

records.label: Matrix organization
records.learning_takeaway: Combine functional and project authority, gaining cross-functional coordination while creating potential dual-boss conflicts.
records.card: A matrix organization gives people reporting relationships along two dimensions, commonly a function and a project. This can connect specialist departments to shared project goals. It also creates potential conflict when two managers make competing demands, so coordination depends on more than drawing intersecting lines on a chart.

records.label: Matrix-tree theorem
records.learning_takeaway: Count a graph’s spanning trees by evaluating a cofactor of its Laplacian.
records.card: The matrix-tree theorem turns counting into a determinant. Form a graph’s Laplacian from vertex degrees and adjacency, then remove the same row and column. For a finite, simple, unweighted, undirected graph, the resulting determinant counts spanning trees, avoiding an explicit listing of every tree.

records.label: Mauna Loa Observatory
records.learning_takeaway: See how representative air sampling and repeated calibration support an atmospheric CO2 record.
records.card: Mauna Loa Observatory’s carbon-dioxide record depends on more than taking repeated readings. Air samples are assessed for background conditions, and the analyzer is frequently checked against reference gases. Reporting carbon dioxide in dry air helps prevent changing water vapor from masquerading as a change in carbon dioxide.

records.label: Maydianne Andrade
records.learning_takeaway: See how competing explanations for redback mating behavior can be tested with observations and experiments.
records.card: Maydianne Andrade investigated why male redback spiders sometimes risk being eaten during mating. Her observations and experiments compared nutritional, remating and paternity explanations. The case shows how an apparently self-defeating behavior can be studied by separating competing hypotheses and measuring reproductive consequences.

records.label: Mean ceramic dating
records.learning_takeaway: An assemblage’s production periods can estimate occupation timing; the method uses multiple ceramics rather than a single object.
records.card: Mean ceramic dating estimates occupation timing from an assemblage of pottery whose production periods are known. Combining the ceramics gives a date estimate for the group. It does not turn every sherd into an exact timestamp for the deposit containing it.

records.label: Meantone temperament
records.learning_takeaway: See how slightly narrowed fifths improve thirds but constrain modulation.
records.card: Meantone temperament narrows fifths to improve the tuning of major thirds. The discrepancy is distributed across a chain of fifths rather than left entirely in the resulting third. This can suit particular keys well, while movement into other keys exposes the compromise's limits.

records.label: Mechanical strain
records.learning_takeaway: Describe deformation as a dimensionless change relative to original size or shape.
records.card: Mechanical strain describes deformation relative to an object’s original dimensions. Stretching a short bar by a millimeter produces more axial strain than stretching a much longer bar by the same amount. This dimensionless measure separates proportional deformation from absolute displacement or the applied force.

records.label: Mechanistic organizational structure
records.learning_takeaway: Coordinate work through hierarchy, standardized procedures, and defined roles where consistency is important.
records.card: A mechanistic organizational structure emphasizes hierarchy, defined roles, and standardized routines. These features make control and consistency central to coordination. It is one end of a design continuum, not a description of every organization with rules; real structures can combine mechanistic and more flexible features.

records.label: Melodic inversion
records.learning_takeaway: Distinguish interval-preserving real inversion from key-preserving tonal inversion.
records.card: Melodic inversion turns an idea's interval directions upside down. A rising movement becomes a falling one. Real inversion preserves the precise sizes and qualities of intervals, while tonal inversion adjusts them to fit the scale or key, allowing the transformed melody to remain within its tonal setting.

records.label: Melodic retrograde
records.learning_takeaway: Hear how reversing note order differs from inverting intervals.
records.card: A melodic retrograde presents notes in the reverse order. It differs from melodic inversion, which reverses the direction of intervals rather than the sequence itself. Reading a tune backward and turning its upward leaps into downward leaps are therefore two distinct ways to transform musical material.

records.label: Memoryless property
records.learning_takeaway: Elapsed waiting does not alter the remaining-wait distribution; exponential and geometric laws provide continuous and discrete examples.
records.card: A waiting-time distribution is memoryless when waiting beyond one point leaves the same distribution for the additional wait. Exponential and geometric laws provide continuous and discrete examples. The condition concerns remaining waiting time given survival so far, rather than an absence of all information about a process.

records.label: Meno's paradox of inquiry
records.learning_takeaway: Question how inquiry can recognize an answer it does not already know.
records.card: Meno's paradox asks how inquiry can work: if you already know the answer, inquiry seems unnecessary; if you do not, how could you recognize it? One response distinguishes partial knowledge from total ignorance. A searcher may know enough to recognize an answer without already possessing it.

records.label: Mental set
records.learning_takeaway: Recognize persistence with a formerly useful approach after circumstances change.
records.card: A mental set is persistence with a problem-solving approach that worked before but is ineffective now. Familiarity can keep a solver repeating the same strategy instead of reconsidering the problem. Functional fixedness is a particular case involving an object's expected use.

records.label: Merton Abbey workshops
records.learning_takeaway: Morris’s workshop site offered river water and grounds for washing and drying fabrics, tying textile production to the practical properties of its location.
records.card: Morris’s Merton Abbey workshops used a site with river water and grounds suitable for washing and drying fabrics. Textile production depended on these practical conditions as well as on design. The workshops show how making patterned cloth joined artistic choices with the resources and layout of a place.
records.primary_subfield: Works, movements and historical design cases

records.label: Metafiction
records.learning_takeaway: Fiction can call attention to its own invented or constructed status, making the reader notice how the work is made.
records.card: Metafiction draws attention to a narrative’s own fictional or constructed status. A work can make readers notice that its world has been invented and arranged. Such reflection concerns fictionality, which differs from a narrator merely commenting on the practical act of telling a story.

records.label: Metanarration
records.learning_takeaway: A narrator can comment on the act of telling without claiming that the story is fictional.
records.card: Metanarration occurs when a narrator comments on the act or process of telling. These remarks may organize the account or draw attention to its communication. They need not announce that events are fictional, so metanarration can also appear in nonfictional narratives.

records.label: Method of initial rates
records.learning_takeaway: Change initial reactant concentrations across trials to infer reaction orders and the rate constant.
records.card: The method of initial rates compares reaction speeds measured soon after mixing different starting concentrations under otherwise matched conditions. Holding one concentration fixed while changing another isolates its influence. Rate ratios reveal reaction orders before the resulting rate law is used to find the constant.

records.label: Method of joints
records.learning_takeaway: Resolve axial truss-member forces by applying equilibrium to one pin joint at a time.
records.card: For an ideal statically determinate planar truss, the method of joints isolates connections and balances forces in each direction. Start at a joint with no more than two unknown member forces. Working through the joints identifies which members carry tension and which carry compression.

records.label: Metonymy
records.learning_takeaway: An associated attribute can stand for the person or thing meant, as an institution may be named through a symbolic object.
records.card: Metonymy refers to something through an associated attribute or object. The substitution works through a recognizable connection rather than literal identity. An institution, for instance, may be evoked through an object linked with its authority, letting a compact expression stand for a wider social relationship.

records.label: Mezuzah
records.learning_takeaway: A parchment text enclosed on a doorpost brings scriptural words into the threshold of everyday domestic space.
records.card: A mezuzah places a parchment inscribed with Torah verses at a doorway, usually within a protective case. The practice brings scriptural words into domestic thresholds. Its meaning depends on the written scroll, not simply on treating the visible container as an ornament.

records.label: Midrash
records.learning_takeaway: Interpretive stories can draw moral or theological meaning from biblical words beyond the immediate narrative setting.
records.card: Midrash can draw moral or theological teaching from biblical wording through interpretive stories and associations. Such readings need not follow only the immediate narrative situation. Comparing them with contextual readings reveals different questions a commentator may bring to the same scriptural passage.

records.label: Mikveh
records.learning_takeaway: A Jewish ritual bath can be studied through its built setting; Cologne’s medieval mikveh reaches groundwater deep beneath the former Jewish quarter.
records.card: A mikveh is a Jewish ritual bath. Cologne’s medieval example descends about sixteen meters to groundwater and stood within a Jewish quarter. This named case offers a way to examine religious practice, access to water and communal architecture together without assuming every bath has the same design.

records.label: Milgram's obedience experiments
records.learning_takeaway: Compare obedience in the original setup with changes produced by proximity and setting.
records.card: Milgram's participants believed they were administering increasingly strong shocks when an experimenter instructed them to continue; the learner actually received none. In the original setting, many continued to the highest level. Changing the setting or bringing the learner closer reduced obedience, limiting any simple universal conclusion.

records.label: Miner’s rule
records.learning_takeaway: Approximate cumulative fatigue damage by adding consumed lifetime fractions while recognizing nonlinear-damage limitations.
records.card: Miner’s rule estimates cumulative fatigue damage by adding the fraction of expected lifetime consumed at each load level. Failure is predicted when the sum reaches one. The linear accumulation assumption is only an approximation; changing crack behavior or strengthening can make actual damage evolve differently.

records.label: Minimal pair
records.learning_takeaway: Use a spoken-language word pair differing in one sound as evidence of contrastive phonemes, without treating failure to find a pair as proof of equivalence.
records.card: In spoken language, a minimal pair consists of words differing in one sound position. English pill versus kill provides evidence that the contrasting sounds belong to different phonemes, since the words have different meanings. Failing to find such a pair does not establish equivalence.

records.label: Mishnah
records.learning_takeaway: An early compilation of Jewish legal traditions forms a textual layer on which later Talmudic discussion comments.
records.card: The Mishnah is a compilation of Jewish legal traditions that forms a foundational layer of the Talmud. Later discussion comments on and works through this material. Distinguishing the earlier collection from its commentary helps readers see how a composite religious text carries different layers of teaching.

records.label: Misinformation effect
records.learning_takeaway: Explore how misleading information after an event can alter later reports.
records.card: Later information can alter how an earlier event is remembered. In Loftus and Palmer's car-crash studies, wording in questions affected speed estimates and later reports of broken glass. The finding shows how post-event suggestions can shape reports, rather than proving that every eyewitness memory is inaccurate.

records.label: Missing fundamental
records.learning_takeaway: Understand why a bass pitch remains audible when a speaker omits its fundamental.
records.card: A small loudspeaker may reproduce a bass note's upper harmonics while barely producing its lowest frequency. Listeners can nevertheless hear the corresponding low pitch. For periodic tones, the spacing between surviving harmonics supplies information about the absent fundamental, so perceived pitch need not match the lowest audible component.

records.label: Miter lock gate
records.learning_takeaway: Paired V-closing gates use buoyant hollow construction to reduce hinge loads while retaining water.
records.card: Miter lock gates close as a pair forming a wide V across a chamber. In Panama’s original design, hollow, watertight lower halves provide buoyancy that reduces hinge loading. This reduces effective gate weight while the structure must still resist water-pressure forces.
records.primary_subfield: Transport systems and engineered case studies

records.label: Mixed-member proportional representation
records.learning_takeaway: See how constituency representation combines with a party-proportional seat total.
records.card: Mixed-member proportional representation combines constituency representatives with party-list seats intended to make overall representation proportional. In New Zealand's version, voters choose a local candidate and a party separately. The party vote largely determines each party's total seats, while electorate winners take individual constituency seats.

records.label: Möbius inversion formula
records.learning_takeaway: Recover an arithmetic function from sums over its divisors using Möbius-weighted cancellation.
records.card: Möbius inversion recovers an arithmetic function from the sums of its values over divisors. A second divisor sum, weighted by the Möbius function, cancels the accumulated contributions. The formula turns information about totals over divisors back into information about the original individual values.

records.label: Möbius strip
records.learning_takeaway: A half-twisted band creates a one-sided nonorientable surface with a single boundary.
records.card: A Möbius strip can be made by joining the ends of a band after giving one end a half-twist. The result has one continuous side and one boundary curve. Its nonorientability distinguishes it from an ordinary untwisted band, despite their similar local appearance.

records.label: Mode locking in bowed strings
records.learning_takeaway: See how periodic bowing can enforce harmonic motion despite inharmonic string resonances.
records.card: A bow alternately sticks to and slips against a string, sustaining a nearly periodic motion. That nonlinear drive can pull the string's slightly mismatched resonances into harmonic frequency ratios. The resulting steady note can therefore be more harmonically regular than the freely vibrating string's natural modes.

records.label: Modern roundabout
records.learning_takeaway: Curved approaches and entry-yield rules lower speeds and reduce vehicle conflict points.
records.card: A modern roundabout channels entering vehicles through curved approaches and gives circulating traffic priority. Lower speeds and fewer crossing conflicts can reduce severe collisions. Its safety mechanism depends on the geometry and entry-yield rules, rather than merely placing a circular island in the middle of an intersection.
records.primary_subfield: Transport systems and engineered case studies

records.label: Molecular solid
records.learning_takeaway: Neutral molecules form solids whose melting behavior depends on intermolecular attractions.
records.card: Molecular solids consist of neutral molecules held near one another by intermolecular attractions. Their melting temperatures vary with those attractions: small nonpolar molecules can freeze only at very low temperatures, while larger or polar molecules may remain solid at much warmer temperatures.

records.label: Molly houses
records.learning_takeaway: Georgian meeting places allowed queer social networks and gender expression under laws and policing that made participants vulnerable.
records.card: Molly houses were meeting places associated with queer social life in Georgian London. They offered spaces for companionship and forms of gender expression while exposing participants to hostile policing and prosecution. Their history joins everyday sociability with the dangers created by criminalization.

records.label: Money bills under the Parliament Acts
records.learning_takeaway: Compare the Lords' restricted role over money bills with other public bills.
records.card: Under the UK Parliament Acts, a Speaker-certified money bill can reach Royal Assent without Lords consent after a month without unamended passage. It must already have passed the Commons and reached the Lords at least a month before session-end; the Commons can direct otherwise.

records.label: Monotype
records.learning_takeaway: Ink or paint worked on a flat plate transfers under pressure to damp paper, typically yielding a single impression whose marks can be changed before printing.
records.card: A monotype transfers ink or paint from a flat plate to paper, usually producing one principal impression. The artist can alter the marks before printing rather than relying on a permanently carved image. This makes preparation on the plate a direct part of the image’s improvisation.

records.label: Moore's paradox
records.learning_takeaway: Explain why asserting a fact while denying belief in it sounds self-defeating.
records.card: Moore's paradox concerns the oddness of asserting a fact while denying that one believes it. The combination need not be logically contradictory: someone else could truthfully describe that situation. The puzzle is why the speaker's own present assertion appears to undermine the position it expresses.

records.label: Moral hazard
records.learning_takeaway: Trace how protection from losses can change behavior after insurance is in place.
records.card: Moral hazard describes how protection from consequences can change behavior after an agreement. Insurance may reduce the incentive to prevent a loss when another party pays much of the cost. Insurers use monitoring and cost sharing to address this problem, although they cannot observe every risky action.

records.label: Moral luck
records.learning_takeaway: Investigate how moral assessment can depend on circumstances outside an agent's control.
records.card: Moral luck names a tension in judging people: responsibility seems to require control, yet praise and blame often depend on factors outside their control. Two equally reckless actions can have different outcomes. The puzzle asks whether, and how, those differences should affect moral assessment.

records.label: Morris worm
records.learning_takeaway: See how self-propagating code disrupted network services without destroying stored files in the 1988 incident.
records.card: The Morris worm spread across the early Internet in 1988 and disrupted computers and services without destroying their files. Its impact illustrates that availability can fail even when stored data remains intact. The incident also prompted organized response efforts, including an early computer emergency response team.

records.label: Mortise-and-tenon joint
records.learning_takeaway: Connect a fitted projection, its matching recess and seated shoulders with a strong wooden joint.
records.card: A mortise-and-tenon joint fits a projecting end of one piece into a matching recess in another. Close-fitting faces provide contact for bonding, while the shoulders seat against the receiving piece. The arrangement connects shape and fit with joint performance, rather than relying on an end-to-end butt connection alone.

records.label: Mosaicism
records.learning_takeaway: Distinguish genomic differences arising within descendants of one fertilized egg from chimerism.
records.card: A person can have genetically different groups of cells that all descend from the same fertilized egg. This is mosaicism: a change arising during development is inherited by that cell’s descendants. Its effects depend on the variant and which cells carry it.

records.label: Mulching
records.learning_takeaway: Explain how a surface covering changes evaporation, weed growth and soil temperature.
records.card: Mulching covers the soil surface with a chosen material. The layer can slow evaporation, reduce light available to weeds and alter soil temperature. Those effects depend on the material, so a gardener’s choice of covering changes more than the appearance of the bed.

records.label: Multi-column index
records.learning_takeaway: Order index entries by several columns so combined constraints avoid filtering unrelated intermediate matches.
records.card: A multi-column index orders records using several fields together. In SQLite's fruit example, indexing fruit and state lets the database locate California oranges directly instead of first finding all oranges and rejecting other states. Column order determines how that combined ordering can be used.

records.label: Musical diminution
records.learning_takeaway: Distinguish proportional rhythmic shortening from changing only some durations.
records.card: Musical diminution shortens the rhythmic values of a motive or phrase, commonly by halving every duration. The pitch sequence can remain recognizable while the idea unfolds faster. Some uses of the term are less exact, referring more generally to a passage rewritten with shorter note values.

records.label: Musical phase shifting
records.learning_takeaway: Compare gradual desynchronization with discrete shifts of a repeated pattern.
records.card: Phase shifting changes the alignment of repeated musical patterns. One part can retain its timing while another gradually runs ahead, or a performer can jump directly to the next rotation. Reich's Piano Phase and Clapping Music demonstrate these different ways of reorganizing the same recurring material.

records.label: Mutualism
records.learning_takeaway: Recognize interspecific exchanges in which both partners benefit, as in ant-tended butterfly larvae.
records.card: Mutualism is an interaction between species in which both participants benefit. Ants attending Karner blue butterfly larvae provide protection and receive carbohydrate-rich secretions in return. Examining what each partner gains turns a vague picture of cooperation into a testable account of a biological exchange.

records.label: N-of-1 trial
records.learning_takeaway: Compare interventions repeatedly within one person rather than assuming a group average fits everyone.
records.card: An N-of-1 trial compares intervention and control periods repeatedly within the same person, often in randomized order. This can reveal an individual response that a group average obscures. It works best when effects can change or fade between periods, rather than permanently carrying into later comparisons.

records.label: Narrative eventfulness
records.learning_takeaway: A change becomes especially eventful when interpreted as significant or unexpected against a story’s cultural and situational expectations.
records.card: Narrative eventfulness concerns how a change becomes significant, surprising or unusual within a story’s context. Merely changing state is not enough for this stronger sense. Characters, narrators or readers interpret the change against expectations, so the same occurrence can acquire different importance in different settings.

records.label: Narrative levels
records.learning_takeaway: A character’s act of telling can establish a further story level, creating nested relations between narration and narrated worlds.
records.card: Narrative levels describe the relationship between an act of telling and the story world it presents. A character who begins another story can introduce a further level. The model tracks these thresholds, including relationships that exist even without an obvious frame tale.

records.label: Narrative paralepsis
records.learning_takeaway: A narrative can reveal information beyond its established focalization norm; identifying this excess depends on the particular text.
records.card: Narrative paralepsis supplies information that exceeds a particular text’s established focalization norm. The exception is defined against the work’s own pattern of disclosure. Identifying it therefore requires attention to narrative coherence rather than a universal rule about what a narrator could plausibly know.

records.label: Narrator review in oral history
records.learning_takeaway: Giving narrators an opportunity to review an interview before release connects historical access with consent and the terms of participation.
records.card: Offering a narrator the chance to review an interview before public release can connect historical access with informed participation. The Oral History Association recommends building this opportunity into the process when possible, alongside clear expectations about preservation, access and the project’s timetable.

records.label: Natural-breaks map classification
records.learning_takeaway: Grouping similar values and separating large gaps creates dataset-specific classes that may hinder direct comparisons across maps.
records.card: Natural-breaks classification groups similar values and places boundaries near larger gaps in the data. The resulting classes can reveal internal clusters, but their thresholds depend on the particular dataset. Maps classified separately this way may therefore be difficult to compare directly through their legends.

records.label: Neapolitan chord
records.learning_takeaway: Recognize the flattened-supertonic major chord as a chromatic predominant.
records.card: The Neapolitan chord is a major chord built on the lowered second scale degree. In classical tonal analysis it commonly appears in first inversion and serves a predominant function. Its distinctive chromatic color therefore has a directional role, helping prepare the approach to dominant harmony.

records.label: Negative space
