records.learning_takeaway: Unmarked areas around or within depicted forms can describe an object, as blank chair shapes do in Ruth Asawa’s 1965 lithograph Chair (TAM.1558-II).
records.card: Negative space is the area around or between depicted forms that helps shape a composition. In Ruth Asawa’s 1965 lithograph Chair, unmarked gaps suggest chairs among patterned marks. These spaces show how an image can describe an object through areas left open.

records.label: Networked team structure
records.learning_takeaway: Coordinate task-focused teams through flexible relationship networks rather than relying primarily on fixed reporting lines.
records.card: A networked team structure organizes work around flexible connections among task-focused teams. Teams may initially be assigned, then find additional collaborators and resources as the work develops. The distinctive feature is this evolving task arrangement, rather than treating every informal workplace friendship as an organizational design.

records.label: Neutral axis in beam bending
records.learning_takeaway: A bending beam has a zero-axial-stress line between tensile and compressive regions.
records.card: Under simple elastic beam bending, fibers on one side are stretched while those on the other are compressed. The neutral axis marks where the axial bending stress changes sign and becomes zero. Finding it helps locate the regions where tensile or compressive failure may begin.

records.label: Neutral theory of molecular evolution
records.learning_takeaway: Separate neutral genetic variation and drift from the claim that all evolution is nonadaptive.
records.card: The neutral theory of molecular evolution emphasizes mutation and genetic drift in explaining much genetic variation. When alternative gene versions do not differ in fitness, chance can change their frequencies. This does not mean all variation is neutral or that natural selection is unimportant.

records.label: New York Clearing House
records.learning_takeaway: See how membership-based mutual liquidity support helped some banks while initially excluding distressed trust companies.
records.card: During the Panic of 1907, the New York Clearing House supported member banks with loans and later loan certificates. Trust companies outside its membership initially lacked that access. The case shows how an institution can provide collective liquidity while its eligibility boundary leaves other connected institutions exposed.
records.primary_subfield: Economic history and documented business cases

records.label: New Zealand MMP threshold
records.learning_takeaway: Explore two alternative routes to eligibility for proportional representation.
records.card: New Zealand's MMP system gives parties two routes to parliamentary eligibility: at least five percent of the party vote or an electorate victory. The alternative route means a party below the percentage threshold can still qualify through local success. These are New Zealand's rules, not universal MMP requirements.

records.label: No-false-lemmas condition
records.learning_takeaway: Evaluate the proposed repair that knowledge cannot be inferred from false premises.
records.card: The no-false-lemmas condition proposes repairing justified true belief by excluding beliefs inferred from false premises. It blocks some Gettier examples, but deceptive perceptual environments pose a further challenge. A belief can apparently be accidentally true without having been inferred from any false proposition.

records.label: No-till farming
records.learning_takeaway: Reduce soil disturbance by establishing crops without full-width tillage.
records.card: No-till farming establishes crops while limiting soil disturbance and retaining previous plant residues at the surface. Planting directly into that cover differs from turning the whole field before sowing. The practice changes both how soil is worked and how residues remain part of the growing environment.

records.label: Normalization across string concatenation
records.learning_takeaway: Recheck normalization at concatenation boundaries because joining normalized strings can require reordering or composition.
records.card: Joining two normalized Unicode strings does not guarantee that the result stays normalized. A combining mark at the boundary may need reordering or composition with the preceding text. Software can therefore need to normalize the join even when both original pieces were already normalized.

records.label: Normalization for choropleth maps
records.learning_takeaway: Dividing a count by a relevant denominator distinguishes prevalence or intensity from the size of a region’s population.
records.card: Normalizing a count divides it by a relevant denominator before mapping it. Cases per resident, for example, answer a different question from total cases. The choice helps distinguish prevalence from population size, although the denominator must fit the comparison the map is intended to make.

records.label: Normative social influence
records.learning_takeaway: Distinguish joining a group to gain acceptance from believing its answer is correct.
records.card: Normative social influence draws people toward a group's position because acceptance matters. Someone may publicly give an answer they privately doubt to avoid ridicule or fit in. Agreement in this case need not mean believing the group has better information about the question.

records.label: Numerical and qualitative identity
records.learning_takeaway: Distinguish being one and the same object from being perfectly alike.
records.card: Numerical identity means being one and the same thing; qualitative identity means being alike in qualities. The distinction matters for change: a persisting object can remain the same object while its features alter. Similarity of appearance alone does not settle whether two descriptions pick out one thing.

records.label: NuSTAR
records.learning_takeaway: High-energy X-ray observations reveal black-hole dynamics and enabled a precise spin measurement.
records.card: NuSTAR uses high-energy X-rays to study regions around black holes, exploding stars, and active galaxies. Its observations have helped estimate black-hole spin, illustrating how radiation from an object’s surroundings can carry information about the object itself.

records.label: Nutrient-film technique
records.learning_takeaway: Circulate a shallow nutrient stream past roots while retaining access to oxygen.
records.card: Nutrient-film technique moves a shallow stream of nutrient solution through channels containing plant roots. The solution circulates back toward a reservoir while roots retain access to air. The arrangement differs from deeply immersing the whole root system, and depends on keeping that moving supply available.

records.label: Oasis settlement
records.learning_takeaway: Reliable managed water lets settled agriculture and habitation persist within desert landscapes, as archaeological evidence at Al Ain illustrates.
records.card: An oasis settlement joins habitation and agriculture to a dependable local water supply within an arid region. At Al Ain, irrigation works and settlement remains record this relationship over time. Water management helps explain how settled life could persist in an otherwise demanding desert landscape.

records.label: Observer's paradox in sociolinguistics
records.learning_takeaway: Recognize that systematically recording everyday speech may change the very speech researchers want to observe.
records.card: The observer's paradox in sociolinguistics is that researchers want to study how people speak when they are not being observed, yet must observe them to collect evidence. A recording or unfamiliar interviewer can change self-monitoring, so natural rapport helps but cannot guarantee completely unmonitored speech.

records.label: Ocean acidification
records.learning_takeaway: Connect absorbed atmospheric CO2 with more hydrogen ions and less available carbonate.
records.card: When seawater absorbs carbon dioxide, chemical reactions increase hydrogen ions and reduce the availability of carbonate ions. Ocean acidification can therefore make building some shells and skeletons more difficult. The change concerns a shift in ocean chemistry, not a claim that seawater has become acidic in everyday terms.

records.label: Ode to the West Wind
records.learning_takeaway: Shelley adapts interlocking tercets into five sonnet-like units, each closing with a couplet.
records.card: Shelley’s Ode to the West Wind adapts terza rima into five units resembling sonnets. Interlocking tercets lead into closing couplets, joining forward movement with repeated moments of closure. The poem offers a specific case of reshaping an inherited rhyme pattern for a different design.

records.label: Offside in association football
records.learning_takeaway: Distinguish occupying an offside position from committing an offside offence.
records.card: An offside position is judged when a teammate plays or touches the ball, but position alone is not an offence. Penalization requires the specified involvement in active play. A player receiving the ball directly from a goal kick, throw-in or corner kick commits no offside offence.

records.label: Ofuda
records.learning_takeaway: A shrine tablet bearing a kami or shrine name supports veneration in the home, extending a visit into domestic religious life.
records.card: Ofuda are shrine tablets of paper or wood bearing a kami’s or shrine’s name. Commonly placed on a household altar, they are understood by practitioners to extend sacred protection into the home. The object links domestic veneration with the shrine from which it was received.

records.label: Omamori
records.learning_takeaway: A portable shrine amulet is often selected for a particular request and carried as an expression of a kami’s protection.
records.card: Omamori are small protective amulets associated with shrines and particular requests, such as seeking good fortune or avoiding danger. Often carried in bags, they are understood to hold a kami’s presence. Their portability connects a shrine visit with a person’s ordinary movements and concerns.

records.label: One Art
records.learning_takeaway: Bishop’s villanelle moves from small losses toward personal loss; an editorial reading hears increasing strain in its repeated assurance.
records.card: Elizabeth Bishop’s One Art moves from small misplaced things toward more intimate loss within a villanelle’s returning lines. An editorial reading hears the repeated assurance becoming harder to sustain. The poem offers a way to examine how formal repetition can expose strain as well as control.

records.label: Open repair request
records.learning_takeaway: Request help with an unclear message without specifying which part caused difficulty.
records.card: An open repair request signals that something in the previous message was unclear without identifying the troublesome part. A brief Huh? is one example. Because the speaker receives little information about the problem, resolving it may require repeating or reformulating more of the earlier utterance.

records.label: Open security design
records.learning_takeaway: Keep protection dependent on guarded keys rather than secrecy of the mechanism, enabling public review.
records.card: Open security design keeps protection from depending on attackers being ignorant of how the mechanism works. Specific keys or passwords remain secret instead. This separation allows the design to be examined by reviewers without assuming that publishing its structure necessarily defeats the protection.

records.label: Optical mixing
records.learning_takeaway: Neo-Impressionists separated colored strokes in the hope that their interaction in the viewer’s eye would produce more vibrant effects than physically mixed pigments.
records.card: Neo-Impressionists placed separate colored strokes beside one another in the hope that they would interact in the viewer’s perception. They sought effects different from physically mixing pigments beforehand. Understanding optical mixing here means examining an artistic strategy and its historical ambitions, rather than assuming literal pigment fusion.

records.label: Oral-history interview lead-in
records.learning_takeaway: Recording participant names or pseudonyms, date, setting and proposed subject preserves the interview’s context for future users.
records.card: An oral-history lead-in records basic context at the start of a session: who is speaking, when and where it happens, and the intended subject. Appropriate names or pseudonyms preserve identification while avoiding unnecessary exposure, such as stating a private home address.

records.label: Organic organizational structure
records.learning_takeaway: Distribute decisions and rely on adaptive coordination when work and circumstances change quickly.
records.card: An organic organizational structure gives people more room to coordinate and make decisions as circumstances change. Authority is less tightly concentrated, and work relies less exclusively on fixed routines. The idea describes a flexible design orientation, rather than simply naming the friendships that arise inside any workplace.

records.label: Organizational formalization
records.learning_takeaway: Specify roles, responsibilities, and accountability to different degrees instead of leaving all coordination to emergent relationships.
records.card: Organizational formalization describes how explicitly roles, duties, and accountability are defined. A highly formalized system spells them out closely; a looser one relies more on relationships that emerge through work. Formalization is a matter of degree, distinct from whether an organization has any structure at all.

records.label: Orientable surface
records.learning_takeaway: Local tangent-space orientations can be chosen continuously across an orientable surface.
records.card: An orientable surface admits a consistent choice of orientation across its tangent planes. That choice can vary continuously as you move across the surface. A Möbius strip shows what can go wrong: its half-twist prevents a locally chosen side from remaining globally consistent.

records.label: Original order in archives
records.learning_takeaway: Preserving a creator’s record sequence can retain evidence of how the records functioned, rather than replacing it with a modern subject arrangement.
records.card: Original order preserves the arrangement a record creator used, when that order can be established and remains meaningful. Keeping the sequence may reveal how an office or person worked. Rearranging everything by a modern subject scheme can erase those functional connections.

records.label: Oscillator quality factor
records.learning_takeaway: Lower damping produces a narrower resonant response and more selective frequency discrimination.
records.card: An oscillator’s quality factor describes how sharply it responds near resonance. With light damping, oscillations persist and the resonance peak is narrow; stronger damping broadens it. A tuned radio circuit uses a narrow response to select one frequency while reducing its response to nearby ones.

records.label: Othello
records.learning_takeaway: Understand how a placement changes ownership of intervening discs.
records.card: Othello changes the ownership of pieces already on the board. A player places a disc to bracket an uninterrupted line of opposing discs, then flips those discs to their color. The winner has more discs when neither player can make a legal move.

records.label: Other-initiated conversational repair
records.learning_takeaway: Signal trouble with another speaker's message so the original speaker can repeat, clarify, or confirm it.
records.card: Other-initiated repair occurs when a listener signals trouble with someone else's message and the original speaker helps resolve it. The response may repeat words, clarify a missing detail, or confirm an interpretation. This creates a collaborative detour aimed at restoring understanding so the conversation can proceed.

records.label: Otoacoustic emissions
records.learning_takeaway: Use tiny cochlear sounds as evidence about inner-ear function while considering transmission blockages.
records.card: The cochlea can produce very quiet sounds when its sensory hair cells respond to stimulation. An otoacoustic-emission test records these responses through a probe in the ear canal. Weak or absent emissions need careful interpretation because outer- or middle-ear problems can also obstruct the returning sound.

records.label: Otto cycle
records.learning_takeaway: A simplified spark-ignition engine cycle converts heat into net work represented by enclosed pressure-volume area.
records.card: The Otto cycle idealizes a spark-ignition piston engine through compression, rapid heat addition, expansion, and heat rejection. Heat is added and removed at fixed volume in the model. The enclosed area on its pressure–volume diagram represents net work, after accounting for work spent compressing the gas.

records.label: Overdiagnosis
records.learning_takeaway: Distinguish detecting a real condition from finding one that would ever have harmed the patient.
records.card: Overdiagnosis occurs when testing finds a real condition that would never have caused symptoms or harm during a person’s life. The finding is not necessarily a false-positive result. Detecting it can still expose someone to unnecessary investigations or treatment, so more diagnoses need not mean better health.

records.label: Overlong UTF-8 encodings
records.learning_takeaway: Reject longer-than-permitted encodings so alternate byte sequences cannot bypass character-based security checks.
records.card: An overlong UTF-8 sequence uses more bytes than the encoding permits for a character. Accepting such sequences can make one character appear in multiple byte patterns. Security checks may reject a forbidden normal encoding yet overlook an invalid alternative that a later parser interprets identically.

records.label: Palampore
records.learning_takeaway: Indian hand-painted cotton bedcovers commonly organized luxuriant flowers around a central tree and were tailored to European markets.
records.card: A palampore is a large Indian painted cotton textile often used as a bedcover or hanging. Many export examples arrange abundant flowers around a central tree. Their designs show how makers shaped local techniques and motifs for the tastes of distant buyers.

records.label: Panic of 1907
records.learning_takeaway: Trace how runs on institutions outside the main clearing-house support network disrupted wider financial-market liquidity.
records.card: The Panic of 1907 spread through trust companies that were important lenders but largely outside New York's clearing-house support network. Runs on their deposits disrupted wider market liquidity. The episode shows how vulnerability can grow at institutional boundaries, rather than remaining confined to the first troubled bank.
records.primary_subfield: Economic history and documented business cases

records.label: Pantoum
records.learning_takeaway: Lines recur in new stanza positions, so changing context and punctuation can shift their meaning.
records.card: A pantoum repeats lines in new positions across successive stanzas. The words return, but their neighbors and grammatical connections can change. Following those shifts shows how a fixed pattern of recurrence can generate new meanings without requiring every repeated line to be rewritten.

records.label: Paper grain direction in bookbinding
records.learning_takeaway: Connect aligned paper fibers with easier folding along the grain and unequal expansion when adhesive wets the sheet.
records.card: Machine-made paper often has fibers preferentially aligned in one direction, called its grain. Folding across that direction can produce uneven creases, and moisture from adhesive causes greater expansion across the grain. These directional differences matter when arranging folds and glued parts in bookbinding.

records.label: Paris law for fatigue crack growth
records.learning_takeaway: In the middle growth regime, an empirical power law links crack advance per cycle to stress-intensity range.
records.card: Paris law estimates fatigue-crack growth in an intermediate growth regime. Crack advance per loading cycle follows an empirical power of the stress-intensity range. The fitted constants depend on the material and conditions, and the law does not describe every near-threshold or final rapid-fracture stage.

records.label: Park Grass Experiment
records.learning_takeaway: Interpret a long-term grassland experiment in light of treatment design and changes in measurement methods.
records.card: Park Grass has studied grassland responses to fertilizer and liming since the nineteenth century. Its long record is not a single unchanging protocol: later liming subplots and changes in harvesting affect comparisons. Reading the experiment requires the treatment and measurement history alongside the hay-yield numbers.

records.label: Parliament Act 1911
records.learning_takeaway: Connect the 1909 budget conflict with replacing most Lords vetoes by delay.
records.card: The Parliament Act 1911 followed the Lords' rejection of the 1909 budget. It replaced their veto over most Commons public bills with delay, while excluding bills extending Parliament beyond five years. The 1949 Act shortened that delay, showing how legislative power shifted between the chambers.

records.label: Parliamentary sovereignty
records.learning_takeaway: Explore Parliament's legal supremacy in the UK and its relationship with institutional reforms.
records.card: Parliamentary sovereignty is the UK's principle that Parliament is the supreme legal authority and can make or repeal laws. One Parliament cannot generally prevent a later Parliament from changing its legislation. Institutional reforms may constrain how power is exercised without, in this account, extinguishing that legal principle.

records.label: Parthenocarpy
records.learning_takeaway: Distinguish fruit formation without pollination in selected cucumber varieties from ordinary pollination-dependent fruit set.
records.card: Some greenhouse cucumber varieties can form seedless fruit without pollination, an example of parthenocarpy. Pollinating those varieties may instead introduce seeds. The case separates fruit development from seed production, while reminding growers that a pollination rule useful for one cucumber type may not fit another.

records.label: Password salting
records.learning_takeaway: Add per-password salt before costly hashing to prevent shared passwords from routinely producing identical stored hashes.
records.card: Password salting adds a separate value when a password is hashed for storage. Different salts help prevent equal passwords from routinely producing equal stored hashes. A suitable password-hashing scheme also makes each guess costly; salting and computational expense address different parts of an offline guessing attack.

records.label: Patronage-based surplus distribution
records.learning_takeaway: Allocate cooperative surplus in proportion to member transactions rather than only in proportion to invested capital.
records.card: Patronage-based surplus distribution returns cooperative benefits in proportion to members' transactions with the cooperative. This differs from distributing returns solely according to invested capital. The cooperative principles also allow surplus to support reserves, development, or other approved purposes, so member payouts are not the only permitted use.

records.label: Paul Signac
records.learning_takeaway: Signac helped carry Neo-Impressionism forward through theoretical writing and through watercolor experiments that extended its investigation of color.
records.card: Paul Signac helped develop and promote Neo-Impressionism through both artistic practice and theoretical writing. His later exploration of watercolor extended his investigation of color into a different medium. The case shows a movement continuing through explanation and experiment after the death of its leading innovator, Seurat.
records.primary_subfield: Works, movements and historical design cases

records.label: PCR inhibition in eDNA samples
records.learning_takeaway: Explain why a negative molecular detection can reflect assay inhibition rather than species absence.
records.card: A negative eDNA test may mean the assay was inhibited, not that the species was absent. Substances such as humic acids can interfere with PCR. An internal positive control helps reveal this problem by checking whether DNA amplification succeeds inside the tested sample.

records.label: Pectin gelation
records.learning_takeaway: Explain fruit-spread setting as a network whose requirements depend on the kind of pectin used.
records.card: Pectin molecules can form a network that gives fruit spreads their gel structure. Setting conditions depend on the pectin formulation: conventional types rely on appropriate sugar and acid, while other types can work with little or no sugar. Substituting one formulation blindly can therefore change the result.

records.label: Pedal point
records.learning_takeaway: Hear a held note change harmonic status while surrounding chords move.
records.card: A pedal point holds one note while surrounding harmonies change. It begins as a chord tone but can become a non-chord tone against later chords. Often heard in the bass, it can also appear higher up, creating continuity while its harmonic meaning shifts.

records.label: Peer Instruction
records.learning_takeaway: Sequence an individual conceptual answer, peer explanation, a second vote, and instructor feedback during class.
records.card: Peer Instruction inserts conceptual questions into a lecture. Students first commit to individual answers, explain their reasoning to nearby peers, then answer again before the instructor explains. The sequence gives discussion a specific job: compare reasons and reconsider an answer, rather than simply listen to another mini-lecture.

records.label: Perceptual closure
records.learning_takeaway: Explore how incomplete parts can be perceived as a complete object.
records.card: Perceptual closure is the tendency to see a complete object from incomplete visual parts. Broken arcs can look like a circle rather than unrelated segments. The perceived whole therefore contains an organization that is not supplied by a continuous drawn outline.

records.label: Percy Lavon Julian
records.learning_takeaway: Julian used plentiful plant sterols to make steroid compounds more accessible through chemical synthesis.
records.card: Chemist Percy Lavon Julian developed ways to obtain useful steroid compounds from plentiful plant materials. Working with soybean sterols helped make progesterone and other hormones more accessible. His work shows how changing a chemical starting material can reshape the practical scale of production.

records.label: Perpetual check in shogi
records.learning_takeaway: Compare ordinary repetition with repeated checks that make the checking player lose.
records.card: Repeated checking is not a safe route to a draw in shogi. Under the Japan Shogi Association's cited explanation, if continuous checks produce the same position four times, the player giving those checks loses. Ordinary repetition without continuous checking is treated differently.

records.label: Peshat
records.learning_takeaway: A contextual reading asks what biblical words mean within their surrounding narrative, while commentators can disagree about that plain sense.
records.card: Peshat seeks a text’s plain or contextual sense by attending to how its words work within the surrounding passage. That does not make interpretation automatic. Commentators can disagree because their assumptions shape what they take to be the most straightforward reading.

records.label: Phishing-resistant authentication
records.learning_takeaway: Bind cryptographic authentication to the real verifier or channel so an impostor cannot relay a reusable output.
records.card: Phishing-resistant authentication binds the authentication process to the legitimate verifier or communication channel. An impostor cannot simply relay a captured output to sign in elsewhere. NIST therefore distinguishes cryptographic verifier binding from manually entered one-time codes, whose outputs can be relayed despite being temporary.

records.label: Photogram
records.learning_takeaway: In the described paper process, opaque objects leave light areas while translucent objects can yield intermediate tones during direct exposure.
records.card: A photogram places objects on light-sensitive paper and exposes it directly. In the process described here, opaque objects leave light areas while translucent ones can produce intermediate tones. The image records contact and light transmission rather than a camera’s view of a scene.

records.label: Photographs of British Algae
records.learning_takeaway: Anna Atkins arranged algae directly on sensitized paper for cyanotype images, combining botanical naming with the visual traces of individual specimens.
records.card: Anna Atkins’s Photographs of British Algae arranged specimens directly on sensitized paper to make cyanotype images. Botanical names accompanied the delicate traces. The project brings scientific identification together with the visual decisions involved in placing an individual specimen against the blue photographic field.

records.label: Photogravure
records.learning_takeaway: A light-sensitive gelatin resist helps etch varying depths into a printing plate, whose ink-bearing recesses reproduce photographic tones.
records.card: Photogravure translates a photographic image into an intaglio printing plate. A light-sensitive gelatin resist helps produce etched recesses of differing depth, which hold varying amounts of ink. Those differences reproduce tonal variation through printing rather than through a conventional photographic paper image alone.

records.label: Photoperiodism
records.learning_takeaway: Explain seasonal plant responses through the duration of light and darkness rather than temperature alone.
records.card: Plants can use the duration of light and darkness as a seasonal signal. Photoperiodism helps regulate events such as flowering or winter-bud formation, with different species responding differently. A plant’s calendar can therefore depend on day–night timing, rather than only on whether the weather is warm.

records.label: Piano Phase
records.learning_takeaway: Follow two repeated patterns as one pianist gradually changes their alignment.
records.card: Steve Reich's Piano Phase makes a repeating twelve-note pattern change through alignment rather than replacement. A second pianist gradually increases speed relative to the other part, causing the patterns to slip out of phase. The process lets different combinations emerge from recurring material.

records.label: PID control
records.learning_takeaway: Combine present error, accumulated error, and error-rate feedback to regulate a system.
records.card: In a basic formulation, PID control combines three responses to error: proportional action responds to present error, integral action accumulates it, and derivative action responds to its rate of change. Adjusting their gains changes how a system approaches its target, including persistent offset, overshoot, and settling.

records.label: Pillow lava
records.learning_takeaway: Recognize rounded lava forms as evidence of rapid cooling in water.
records.card: When lava flows into water, its exposed surface cools rapidly, producing rounded forms known as pillow lava. These shapes can survive within ancient rock. Recognizing them helps geologists infer that molten rock once met water, rather than assuming every lava flow formed in open air.

records.label: Pisaster ochraceus
records.learning_takeaway: Explore why ochre sea-star predation on mussels helps preserve rocky-shore diversity.
records.card: The ochre sea star, Pisaster ochraceus, feeds on mussels along rocky shores. By limiting mussels that would otherwise occupy much of the available surface, it helps other organisms retain space. This makes its feeding behavior a useful case of a predator shaping community diversity.

records.label: Pitch (tar-derived material)
records.learning_takeaway: Explain how tar-derived pitch can shatter under a quick blow yet flow extremely slowly over years.
records.card: Tar-derived pitch can feel solid and break under a quick hammer blow, yet flow over much longer times. The University of Queensland’s pitch-drop experiment demonstrates this contrast: material placed in a funnel slowly forms drops over years, with the flow rate affected by temperature.

records.label: Pitch (music)
records.learning_takeaway: Relate perceived high and low notes to their ordering on a keyboard.
records.card: Pitch is a sound's perceived highness or lowness. On a piano, moving right produces higher notes. For periodic musical tones, doubling the vibration frequency raises pitch by an octave, showing why musical intervals depend on frequency ratios rather than equal additions of hertz.

records.label: Planar graph
records.learning_takeaway: Planarity means some crossing-free drawing exists, even if another drawing of the same graph crosses.
records.card: A graph is planar if it can be drawn in a plane without edges crossing except at shared vertices. One messy drawing does not disprove planarity: another arrangement might remove the crossings. The distinction concerns the existence of a suitable drawing, not its first appearance.

records.label: Plaque with equestrian ọ́bà and attendants
records.learning_takeaway: The enlarged ruler and smaller attendants on this Benin brass palace plaque use relative size to make rank visible.
records.card: This Benin brass palace plaque makes its ruler larger than the surrounding attendants. Size expresses rank within the composition rather than simply reproducing natural proportions. The mounted figure and accompanying people show how a particular court artwork can organize political relationships visually.

records.label: Pochoir
records.learning_takeaway: Brushing pigment through a stencil without a screen creates hand-colored impressions that can retain visible brush marks.
records.card: Pochoir applies color by hand through a stencil, without the mesh used in screen printing. Brushes can leave visible traces as pigment passes through the cut openings. The process combines a repeatable shape with variations created by the way each impression is colored.

records.label: Poisson process
records.learning_takeaway: Model independent event counts in disjoint intervals at a constant rate.
records.card: A constant-rate Poisson process has independent event counts in nonoverlapping time intervals. For very short intervals, one-event probability is approximately proportional to duration, while multiple events become negligible by comparison. Random clusters can occur even though the model’s average event rate stays constant.

records.label: Polder landscape
records.learning_takeaway: Draining and enclosing wet land creates inhabitable agricultural space that depends on a maintained network of dykes, canals and drainage.
records.card: A polder landscape is enclosed and drained land whose usability depends on water management. Dykes, canals and drainage works make fields and settlement possible, while requiring continued maintenance. Reclamation therefore creates a lasting relationship between the land’s apparent stability and the infrastructure that controls water.

records.label: Population bottleneck
records.learning_takeaway: Explain why rapid numerical recovery need not restore lost genetic diversity.
records.card: A population bottleneck sharply reduces the number of individuals contributing genes to later generations. Chance can eliminate variants during that small-population period. Even if numbers subsequently rebound, the lost diversity need not return, as the history of heavily hunted northern elephant seals illustrates.

records.label: Positive predictive value
records.learning_takeaway: Explain why a positive test is less convincing when the target condition is rare.
records.card: Positive predictive value is the probability of having a condition after a positive test. Even with unchanged sensitivity and specificity, it falls when the condition is rarer in the tested population. A positive result therefore gains meaning from both test performance and the starting prevalence.

records.label: Prasad
records.learning_takeaway: Offerings made to a deity can later be shared among worshippers, connecting devotion with communal distribution.
records.card: Prasad connects offerings made to a deity with their later sharing among worshippers. In many pujas, food or other offerings move through this ritual sequence. Receiving and distributing them joins an individual act of devotion with a shared material practice within the community.

records.label: Pratimoksha
records.learning_takeaway: A monastic code adds extensive rules for ordained Buddhists beyond ethical precepts shared with lay followers.
records.card: The Pratimoksha is a code of Buddhist monastic discipline governing ordained practitioners. It extends beyond the basic ethical precepts shared with lay followers. Distinguishing these layers shows how common commitments coexist with more detailed obligations attached to a particular religious role.

records.label: Prayer wheel
records.learning_takeaway: A rotating cylinder encloses written mantras, joining textual devotion with repeated physical motion in Tibetan Buddhist practice.
records.card: A Tibetan Buddhist prayer wheel contains rolls of written mantras within a rotating cylinder. Turning it joins repeated bodily motion with devotional text, even when the words remain enclosed. Wheels range from handheld objects to larger stationary installations, giving the practice several material forms.

records.label: Preface paradox
records.learning_takeaway: Examine believing each researched claim while reasonably expecting some mistake in the whole book.
records.card: An author can reasonably believe each carefully researched claim in a book while admitting that the book probably contains an error. Combining all the individual beliefs conflicts with that admission. The preface paradox tests how rational confidence in particular claims fits with recognition of one's fallibility.

records.label: Prefix-free code
records.learning_takeaway: Decode concatenated codewords unambiguously because no codeword is another codeword's prefix.
records.card: A prefix-free code gives each symbol a bit string that is never the beginning of another symbol's complete code. A decoder follows bits until it reaches a symbol, then starts again. Variable-length messages can therefore be separated into codewords without additional boundary markers.

records.label: Preliminary injunction
records.learning_takeaway: Explore temporary relief before final judgment and why irreparable harm matters.
records.card: A preliminary injunction provides court-ordered protection before final judgment. In US federal practice, the cited test considers likely success, likely irreparable harm, competing hardships and the public interest. The question is whether interim relief is justified while the dispute remains unresolved, not whether the applicant has already won.

records.label: Prepared piano
records.learning_takeaway: Hear how objects placed between piano strings transform its available timbres.
records.card: A prepared piano changes its sound through objects placed beneath or between its strings. John Cage used such physical alterations to expand the instrument's available timbres. The keys remain a familiar interface, while the altered vibrating system produces sounds unlike those of an unprepared grand piano.

records.label: Prequestioning
records.learning_takeaway: Ask questions before exposure to focus study, while preserving attention to material the questions do not cover.
records.card: Prequestioning asks learners questions before they encounter new material. This can activate relevant knowledge and direct attention to what they need to learn. The cited guide cautions that selective reading may neglect material not covered by the questions, and its classroom evidence for this recommendation was limited.

records.label: Presentism
records.learning_takeaway: Explore the thesis that only temporally present objects exist.
records.card: Presentism holds that only temporally present objects exist. Merely past or future objects are excluded from its inventory of reality, though abstract entities may fall outside time. The claim concerns existence itself, not simply which events people can currently observe or remember.

records.label: Pressure thrust
records.learning_takeaway: A nozzle’s exit-pressure mismatch contributes force in addition to exhaust momentum flux.
records.card: Pressure thrust is the force contribution from a difference between nozzle-exit and ambient pressure. With uniform exit pressure, it equals that difference times exit area, alongside momentum-flow thrust. Equal pressures remove this term, but need not remove the engine’s remaining thrust.

records.label: Principal–agent problem
records.learning_takeaway: Analyze conflicting interests when one party relies on another's behavior or attributes that contracts cannot fully guarantee.
records.card: A principal–agent problem arises when one party depends on another's action or attributes, but their interests differ and a contract cannot fully guarantee the desired result. Employers may value effort that is hard to verify. The framework separates who wants the outcome from who controls the relevant behavior.

records.label: Principle of accountability in sociolinguistics
records.learning_takeaway: Count every eligible variant to form a denominator instead of counting only the interesting pronunciation.
records.card: The sociolinguistic principle of accountability requires counting all occasions when a variant could occur, not only the instances that attract attention. Ten examples in one setting may represent a lower usage rate than eight in another. The relevant denominator makes comparisons across speaking contexts interpretable.

records.label: Principle of least privilege
records.learning_takeaway: Give each program and user only necessary permissions to limit accidents and the code requiring trust.
records.card: Least privilege gives each user or program only the authority needed for its job. If an error or misuse occurs, fewer permissions limit what can be damaged. The principle also reduces the number of privileged components that must be examined when investigating an unexpected access path.

records.label: Private-value auction
records.learning_takeaway: Model each bidder's value as personal and unaffected by learning others' valuations, an idealized limiting case.
records.card: A private-value auction models each bidder's valuation as personal: learning that someone else values the object highly does not change one's own value. It is an idealized case. A house, for example, may mix personal enjoyment with resale concerns that introduce a common-value component.

records.label: Proactive interference
records.learning_takeaway: Understand how an older memory can obstruct recall of newly learned information.
records.card: Proactive interference occurs when older learning gets in the way of remembering newer information. After changing phone numbers, you might keep giving the old number automatically. The direction matters: an established memory is obstructing access to its more recently learned replacement.

records.label: Problem of closeness in double effect
records.learning_takeaway: Examine when a harmful side effect seems inseparable from the agent's chosen means.
records.card: The problem of closeness challenges the line between intended means and foreseen side effects. A harmful result may be so closely connected with an agent's chosen means that calling it unintended seems artificial. The difficulty is classifying the action without already assuming the moral verdict.

records.label: Problem of temporary intrinsics
records.learning_takeaway: Ask how one persisting object can possess incompatible intrinsic properties at different times.
records.card: The problem of temporary intrinsics asks how one persisting object can have incompatible intrinsic properties at different times. A metal plate may change from round to square. Explaining that change requires an account of what it means to possess a property at a time.

records.label: Procedural memory
records.learning_takeaway: Distinguish remembering how to perform a skill from verbally recalling its instructions.
records.card: Procedural memory is expressed in skilled actions, such as balancing on a bicycle or driving. Practice can improve performance even when a person cannot fully describe the knowledge guiding it. This distinguishes remembering how to do something from consciously reporting facts or past events.

records.label: Puja
records.learning_takeaway: Offerings and visual interaction with deity images are common elements of Hindu puja; practices vary with the deity and community.
records.card: Puja is a Hindu form of worship that can bring a devotee into a ritual encounter with a deity. Images, visual attention and offerings often participate in the encounter. Practices vary with the deity and community, and pujas can occur at home, in temples or elsewhere.

records.label: Pulmonary surfactant
records.learning_takeaway: Connect surfactant deficiency with air-sac collapse and difficult breathing in premature newborns.
records.card: Pulmonary surfactant helps the lungs remain expanded so air sacs can participate in breathing. Premature newborns may have too little, allowing lung collapse and making breathing much harder. The example connects a substance within the lung with the mechanical ability to keep air spaces open.

records.label: Pulse oximetry
records.learning_takeaway: Estimate blood oxygen saturation from light passing through tissue.
records.card: A pulse oximeter shines light through tissue to estimate blood oxygen saturation. A small sensor can provide this information without drawing arterial blood. The reading is an estimate, however, and factors including poor circulation, cold skin or skin pigmentation can affect its accuracy.

records.label: Pure-tone audiometry
records.learning_takeaway: Map the quietest tones a person detects at different frequencies.
records.card: Pure-tone audiometry measures the quietest tones a person can detect at different pitches. Through headphones, sounds are presented while the listener signals when they hear them. The resulting pattern separates sensitivity across frequencies, rather than reducing hearing to a single yes-or-no ability.

records.label: Qibla
records.learning_takeaway: A shared orientation toward Mecca organizes Muslim prayer; a mosque’s mihrab indicates this direction rather than being the direction itself.
records.card: Qibla is the direction toward Mecca used in Muslim prayer. It coordinates worshippers’ orientation across very different locations. A mosque’s mihrab indicates that direction, but the niche and the direction are different things: one is an architectural marker of the other.

records.label: Quantile map classification
records.learning_takeaway: Putting equal numbers of geographic features in each class can separate close values or combine widely different values.
records.card: Quantile classification places roughly equal numbers of mapped features in each class. This spreads observations across the legend, but nearby values can fall on opposite sides of a class boundary. Conversely, quite different values may share a class when the data are unevenly distributed.

records.label: Quantum tunneling
records.learning_takeaway: A quantum state can transmit through a finite barrier that forbids passage at the same classical energy.
records.card: Quantum tunneling allows a particle’s wave state to extend through a finite potential barrier higher than its total energy. Some amplitude can emerge beyond the barrier even when a classical particle would turn back. The transmission probability depends on the barrier’s width, height, and particle energy.

records.label: Quotient group
records.learning_takeaway: Cosets of a normal subgroup become group elements, collapsing selected distinctions while preserving an operation.
records.card: A quotient group replaces a group’s individual elements with cosets of a normal subgroup. Multiplying those cosets gives a new group whose elements each represent an entire collection of original elements. The construction organizes selected distinctions into classes while retaining an algebraic operation.

records.label: Raft consensus algorithm
records.learning_takeaway: Separate leader election, log replication, and safety to make a replicated-log consensus algorithm easier to understand.
records.card: Raft manages a replicated log by electing a leader that receives commands and sends entries to followers. Its design separates leader election, log replication, and safety rules. This decomposition was chosen to make the protocol easier to understand while preserving agreement when machines stop or become disconnected.

records.label: Rain shadow
records.learning_takeaway: Trace contrasting mountain rainfall through rising moist air and descending dry air.
records.card: Moist air rising over a mountain cools and can release precipitation on the windward side. After crossing the summit, descending air warms and becomes drier. This rain-shadow effect helps explain why nearby places on opposite sides of a mountain can have sharply different rainfall.

records.label: Ramp metering
records.learning_takeaway: Regulate freeway entry to break up merging platoons and reduce flow breakdown.
records.card: Ramp metering uses entrance-ramp signals to regulate freeway entry. Breaking up merging platoons can reduce sudden mainline braking and improve traffic flow. Metering also creates waiting queues, so its design must account for ramp storage and effects on adjacent streets.
records.primary_subfield: Transport systems and engineered case studies

records.label: Ramp-queue spillback management
records.learning_takeaway: Balance freeway entry control with finite ramp storage so queued vehicles do not block adjacent streets.
records.card: A ramp meter can protect freeway flow while allowing its waiting queue to spill into nearby streets. Queue detectors and available storage therefore matter. Increasing the release rate can relieve the ramp but worsen freeway conditions, making queue management a balance between connected parts of the road system.
records.primary_subfield: Transport systems and engineered case studies

records.label: Ramsey number
records.learning_takeaway: Find when every sufficiently large graph must contain a chosen clique or independent-set pattern.
records.card: A Ramsey number gives the smallest vertex count that forces either a clique of one chosen size or an independent set of another in any simple undirected graph. The party analogy treats vertices as people and edges as mutual acquaintance.

records.label: Random walk
records.learning_takeaway: Repeated random steps form paths whose behavior changes with dimension and allowed movement.
records.card: A random walk builds a path from successive randomly chosen steps. The allowed directions, step lengths, and surrounding space define the model. Walks on a line, a plane, or a lattice can behave differently, so specifying the rules matters as much as calling the motion random.

records.label: Randomized controlled trial
records.learning_takeaway: Use chance-based assignment and a comparison group to assess an intervention’s effects.
records.card: A randomized controlled trial uses chance to assign participants to an intervention or comparison group. Comparing outcomes helps separate the intervention’s effects from differences that might influence who receives it. Randomization is a design tool; clear follow-up and careful analysis are still needed for a trustworthy result.

records.label: Randomized election timeouts
records.learning_takeaway: Spread election starts probabilistically so competing candidates are less likely to repeatedly split votes.
records.card: Raft randomizes election timeouts so followers are less likely to start competing elections simultaneously. After a split vote, candidates wait for new randomized timeouts before trying again. Spreading their attempts helps one candidate obtain a majority before others begin another round.

records.label: Rashi
records.learning_takeaway: His verse-by-verse commentary combines attention to plain meaning with selected interpretive stories that address textual difficulties.
records.card: Rashi’s biblical commentary often proceeds verse by verse, noticing questions raised by the wording. His stated approach joins attention to contextual meaning with selected interpretive stories that help settle textual difficulties. The combination shows why plain reading and inherited commentary need not be mutually exclusive.

records.label: Ravishing DisUnities: Real Ghazals in English
records.learning_takeaway: This anthology assembled English ghazals with varying fidelity to the inherited form, making formal adaptation visible across poets.
records.card: Ravishing DisUnities collected English ghazals under Agha Shahid Ali’s editorship, with poems differing in their fidelity to the inherited form. The anthology makes adaptation visible across writers. Its variety lets readers compare what happens when autonomous couplets and recurring verbal patterns are maintained or loosened.

records.label: Rayleigh criterion
records.learning_takeaway: Compare overlapping diffraction patterns to estimate when two point sources are just resolvable.
records.card: The Rayleigh criterion conventionally treats two point sources as just resolved when one diffraction maximum meets the other’s first minimum. For an ideal circular aperture much wider than the wavelength, increasing aperture size or shortening wavelength reduces the corresponding angular separation.

records.label: Reaction order
records.learning_takeaway: Reaction orders are experimentally determined concentration exponents and need not match balanced-equation coefficients.
records.card: Reaction order describes how a measured reaction rate depends on concentration. Doubling a reactant with order two multiplies its contribution to the rate by four. Orders can be zero, fractional, or negative, and do not generally follow the balanced equation’s coefficients.

records.label: Reaction quotient
records.learning_takeaway: Compare the current reaction quotient with its equilibrium value to predict net reaction direction.
records.card: A reaction quotient summarizes a mixture’s current composition using products and reactants raised to their stoichiometric powers. Comparing it with the equilibrium constant predicts which reaction direction will dominate. Unlike the equilibrium constant at fixed temperature, the quotient changes as the mixture reacts.

records.label: Reduced penetrance
records.learning_takeaway: Explain why not everyone carrying a disease-associated variant develops that condition.
records.card: Carrying a disease-associated genetic variant does not always mean developing the condition. Reduced penetrance describes this incomplete appearance among people with the variant. Genetic background, environment and lifestyle may contribute, making a family’s inheritance pattern harder to interpret than a simple all-or-nothing prediction.

records.label: Reduplication
records.learning_takeaway: Repeat all or part of a linguistic form to express a grammatical or meaning contrast.
records.card: Reduplication repeats part or all of a linguistic form to express a grammatical or meaning contrast. In Halq'eméylem, one pattern derives meanings such as being disposed to an action. English salad-salad provides a different example: repetition can emphasize a prototypical instance rather than simply pluralizing something.

records.label: Reference groups
records.learning_takeaway: Distinguish groups used as comparison standards from groups someone actually joins.
records.card: A reference group supplies a standard people use to compare themselves with others. It need not be a group they actually belong to: admired athletes or an older sibling's friends may serve that role. Several reference groups can matter at once and convey competing expectations.

records.label: Regulatory sandbox
records.learning_takeaway: Distinguish supervised, limited testing from exemption from regulation.
records.card: A regulatory sandbox permits supervised testing of an innovation within defined limits. The UK's Financial Conduct Authority typically uses small, time-limited trials with real consumers. Acceptance does not remove authorization requirements or exempt a firm from national law, distinguishing controlled experimentation from unrestricted permission to operate.

records.label: Relative identity
records.learning_takeaway: Explore the proposal that identity must answer same what rather than identity without qualification.
records.card: Relative identity proposes that asking whether two things are the same requires specifying the kind of thing: the same what? On Geach's view, things might be the same under one classification but different under another. This contested proposal challenges treating identity as a single unqualified relation.

records.label: Renal countercurrent multiplication
records.learning_takeaway: Explain how opposite flows and unequal permeability build a medullary concentration gradient.
records.card: Fluid travels in opposite directions through neighboring limbs of the kidney’s loop of Henle. The descending limb allows water to leave, while the thick ascending limb moves salt outward without water following. These differences help build the medullary concentration gradient used to recover water.

records.label: Renal myogenic autoregulation
records.learning_takeaway: Explain how pressure-induced contraction of an afferent arteriole stabilizes renal flow.
records.card: The kidney’s incoming arteriole responds directly to pressure changes. Rising pressure stretches its smooth muscle, which contracts and increases resistance; falling pressure permits relaxation. This local myogenic response helps stabilize renal blood flow without requiring a fresh instruction from nerves or circulating hormones.

records.label: Renin–angiotensin–aldosterone system
records.learning_takeaway: Connect reduced renal pressure with vasoconstriction and sodium retention through a hormonal cascade.
records.card: Reduced pressure at the kidney can trigger renin release and a cascade producing angiotensin II. This constricts vessels and stimulates aldosterone, which promotes sodium retention; water retention then supports blood volume. The renin–angiotensin–aldosterone system connects circulation with the kidney’s handling of salt and water.

records.label: Repetitive narration
records.learning_takeaway: A single event can be recounted more than once, allowing repeated tellings rather than repeated occurrences to structure a narrative.
records.card: Repetitive narration recounts more than once an event that happened once. The repetition belongs to the telling, not to the occurrence. Separating those counts distinguishes several accounts of one event from a story in which similar events happen repeatedly.

records.label: Replay-resistant authentication
records.learning_takeaway: Use freshness challenges or one-time outputs so recording a past authentication does not enable successful reuse.
records.card: Replay-resistant authentication makes a recorded earlier exchange insufficient for another successful login. Fresh challenges, nonces, or appropriately checked one-time outputs can demonstrate that an exchange is current. A reusable password alone lacks that property because the same secret is presented again each time.

records.label: Replicated log
records.learning_takeaway: Retain an ordered command history across replicas and repair disagreements before applying committed entries.
records.card: A replicated log records commands in a shared order across machines. In Raft, a leader sends entries to followers and uses log information to identify disagreements. Committed entries can then drive deterministic state machines, separating the agreement on history from execution of that history.

records.label: Replicated state machine
records.learning_takeaway: Execute the same ordered commands deterministically on several replicas to obtain matching states and outputs.
records.card: A replicated state machine keeps several machines consistent by giving them the same ordered commands. If each replica executes those commands deterministically, their states and outputs match. The difficult coordination work is agreeing on the log despite failures, rather than independently guessing what state each machine should hold.

records.label: Reputation in markets
records.learning_takeaway: Make future business valuable enough that sellers have a reason to preserve buyers' trust.
records.card: A seller's reputation can make future business depend on how current customers are treated. Passing off a poor-quality product may earn money now but lose repeat customers and recommendations later. This gives buyers a reason to consider the seller's ongoing stake, alongside the product they can inspect.

records.label: Research debriefing
records.learning_takeaway: Understand why concealed research purposes must be explained after deceptive studies.
records.card: Research debriefing explains a study after participation, especially when its purpose was concealed. Participants receive an honest account of the research question, the use of their data and why deception was used. The explanation helps restore information that the study deliberately withheld during the task.

records.label: Resource mobilization theory
records.learning_takeaway: Explain collective organizing partly through acquiring time, money, and people rather than grievances alone.
records.card: Resource mobilization theory explains social movements partly through their ability to obtain time, money, and participants. Grievances alone do not describe the practical work of organizing transport, meetings, or sustained action. The perspective directs attention to the resources and connections that make collective efforts possible.

records.label: Resource partitioning
records.learning_takeaway: Explain how different food, places or feeding times can reduce direct competition.
records.card: Species can reduce direct competition by using different foods, different parts of a habitat or different feeding times. Resource partitioning separates their ecological niches even when they live nearby. The key distinction is how resources are used, rather than simply how many species are present.

records.label: Respiratory compensation for metabolic acidosis
records.learning_takeaway: Connect increased ventilation with lower carbon dioxide and partial correction of low blood pH.
records.card: When metabolism makes the blood too acidic, increased ventilation can remove more carbon dioxide. This shifts the carbonic-acid balance and helps raise pH toward its usual range. Respiratory compensation can limit the disturbance, but it does not itself remove the underlying metabolic cause.

records.label: Restricted repair request
records.learning_takeaway: Target a specific missing or unclear component so the original speaker can give a focused clarification.
records.card: A restricted repair request identifies a particular part of a message that needs clarification. Asking Who? narrows the trouble to a person reference instead of rejecting the whole utterance. This gives the original speaker a more focused task, such as specifying the missing identity or repeating that component.

records.label: Retroactive interference
records.learning_takeaway: Understand how later learning can obstruct access to older information.
records.card: Retroactive interference occurs when newer learning makes older information harder to recall. After learning a replacement address, you might struggle to recover the previous one. The direction reverses proactive interference: what was learned later now obstructs access to what was learned earlier.

records.label: Reviewability of communication
records.learning_takeaway: Use persistent messages that an addressee can revisit, changing the need and cost of repetition during coordination.
records.card: Reviewability is a communication medium's ability to leave messages available for the recipient to inspect again. Written or recorded messages can support checking details that ordinary unrecorded speech leaves behind only briefly. This changes the effort needed for grounding, and differs from the sender's ability to revise before sending.

records.label: Rhythmic augmentation
records.learning_takeaway: Recognize a motive whose durations expand proportionally while its pitch pattern remains recognizable.
records.card: Rhythmic augmentation stretches a musical idea in time while preserving its relative durations. A motive in quarter notes might return in half notes, with every value doubled. This differs from simply adding notes at the end: the existing pattern itself occupies more time.

records.label: Riparian forest buffer
records.learning_takeaway: Connect streamside vegetation with filtering runoff, stabilizing banks and shading aquatic habitat.
records.card: A riparian forest buffer places trees, shrubs or other perennial vegetation beside water. The strip can filter runoff, stabilize banks and shade aquatic habitat. Its effectiveness depends on site conditions and continuity, so the presence of a few trees alone does not guarantee the same conservation benefit everywhere.

records.label: Risk pooling
records.learning_takeaway: Combine many uncertain individual losses into a shared pool funded by premiums.
records.card: Risk pooling combines many people's uncertain losses so premiums can fund the claims that actually occur. An individual may face a large bill even when the group's average loss is manageable. How people are grouped and priced matters, especially when their risks differ or are privately known.

records.label: Rochdale Pioneers
records.learning_takeaway: See how pooling resources, honest retailing, democratic membership, and shared profits formed an influential cooperative model.
records.card: The Rochdale Pioneers pooled scarce resources to sell basic goods through a cooperative shop in 1844. Customers became members, gained a democratic voice, and shared in profits connected with their custom. The case links retail trust and access to goods with a different arrangement of ownership and control.
records.primary_subfield: Economic history and documented business cases

records.label: Role conflict
records.learning_takeaway: Distinguish incompatible obligations between different roles from excessive demands within one role.
records.card: Role conflict occurs when obligations associated with different roles pull in incompatible directions. A parent may need to collect a sick child while an employer expects work on a deadline. The problem concerns competing roles, rather than only having too many demands inside one role.

records.label: Role-set
records.learning_takeaway: Recognize that one social status can carry several distinct role relationships and expectations.
records.card: A role-set is the array of role relationships attached to a particular social status. Being a student, for example, involves more than one expectation or relationship. The concept differs from simply listing all the separate statuses a person holds, such as student, worker, and family member.

records.label: Role strain
records.learning_takeaway: Recognize competing or excessive demands within a single role even without a clash between separate roles.
records.card: Role strain arises when the demands inside a single role become difficult to satisfy together. Parenting, for example, includes care, organization, transport, and guidance. A person can experience that pressure without also holding a conflicting job role, which distinguishes strain from conflict between separate roles.

records.label: Rollback journal
records.learning_takeaway: Preserve old database content before overwrite so an uncompleted transaction can be undone.
records.card: A rollback journal saves original database content before a transaction overwrites it. If the transaction must be undone, the saved content can restore the earlier state. This differs from SQLite's write-ahead-log mode, which preserves the main database while appending new changes elsewhere.

records.label: Rootstock dwarfing
records.learning_takeaway: Explain why the same apple variety can grow to different sizes on different rootstocks.
records.card: A dwarfing rootstock can limit an apple tree’s size while its scion determines the fruit variety. If a buried scion forms its own roots, the rootstock’s dwarfing influence can be lost. Tree size therefore depends partly on which root system supports the grafted shoot.

records.label: Rule of lenity
records.learning_takeaway: Explore construing unresolved criminal-law ambiguity in a defendant's favor.
records.card: In US criminal law, lenity favors the defendant when a statute remains ambiguous. It concerns interpreting a penal law's reach, rather than deciding whether evidence proves the conduct. Its rationale includes reserving the definition of crimes and punishments to lawmakers instead of judicial expansion.

records.label: Rule of Saint Benedict
records.learning_takeaway: A monastic rule organizes manual labor, reading and communal prayer into a repeated rhythm of shared life.
records.card: The Rule of Saint Benedict organizes monastic life around shared obligations, including manual labor, reading and communal prayer. Repetition gives the day a religious structure. Its influence came through adoption by communities, turning a written rule into a recurring pattern of work, worship and collective discipline.

records.label: Sakichi Toyoda
records.learning_takeaway: Connect his self-stopping loom experiments with the later manufacturing principle of detecting abnormalities at their source.
records.card: Sakichi Toyoda's loom work connects a named invention history with jidoka. Toyota describes looms that stopped automatically when yarn broke or ran out, reducing the need for constant watching. The lesson is a design response to abnormal conditions, rather than automation understood only as continuous unattended operation.
records.primary_subfield: Economic history and documented business cases

records.label: Salisbury convention
records.learning_takeaway: Explore restraint by the Lords toward government bills promised in an election manifesto.
records.card: The Salisbury convention restrains the House of Lords from voting down government bills promised in an election manifesto. It helps an elected government advance its announced program even without a Lords majority. This convention concerns how a chamber exercises its powers, rather than a new statutory voting procedure.

records.label: Sand Hollow Reservoir
records.learning_takeaway: See why engineered recharge performance can change as gradients and clogging evolve.
records.card: Utah’s Sand Hollow Reservoir stores water at the surface while also allowing it to infiltrate the underlying Navajo Sandstone aquifer. Monitoring showed recharge rates changing over time, with clogging and hydraulic conditions among the likely influences. The site illustrates why recharge performance must be measured after construction.

records.label: Sangha
records.learning_takeaway: Buddhist monastics and lay followers sustain reciprocal relationships of material support and teaching, although the term’s boundaries vary.
records.card: Sangha names the Buddhist community, sometimes specifically monastics and sometimes a wider community including lay followers. Monastics and laity can sustain reciprocal relationships: teaching and guidance flow one way, while food and other material support flow the other. The term’s boundaries depend on context.

records.label: Sassi of Matera
records.learning_takeaway: Cave dwellings, churches and workshops developed with the ravines and limestone plateau instead of replacing their topography.
records.card: Matera’s Sassi developed through cave dwellings, churches and workshops integrated with ravines and a limestone plateau. Building and excavation worked with the terrain’s existing forms. The settlement illustrates how an inhabited landscape can grow by adapting geological spaces rather than replacing them with an entirely separate urban grid.

records.label: Scanning tunneling microscopy
records.learning_takeaway: Use the strong gap-dependence of tunneling current to map a conducting surface with atomic detail.
records.card: A scanning tunneling microscope brings a sharp conducting tip extremely close to a biased conducting sample. Electrons tunnel across the gap, and current changes strongly with tip–surface separation. Monitoring that current while scanning reveals atomic-scale structure through electronic behavior rather than ordinary reflected-light imaging.

records.label: Screening in economics
records.learning_takeaway: Let a less-informed party investigate or set requirements to learn hidden characteristics before a transaction.
records.card: Screening is an effort by the less-informed side of a transaction to learn relevant hidden characteristics. A buyer may have a mechanic inspect a used car, or an employer may check references. This reverses the initiative in signaling, where the better-informed party supplies an observable indication.

records.label: Scribing to fit
records.learning_takeaway: Fit a new component to an irregular existing surface by transferring its contour onto the workpiece.
records.card: Scribing to fit transfers the contour of an existing surface onto a new workpiece. A cabinet panel beside an uneven wall, for example, can be marked to match that wall’s profile. The method handles irregularity directly instead of assuming that every surrounding surface is straight.

records.label: Secchi disk
records.learning_takeaway: Use a simple black-and-white visual target to assess water clarity.
records.card: A Secchi disk uses a contrasting black-and-white target to assess water clarity. It offers a simple visual way to compare how readily something can be seen through water. Clarity matters because it influences how much light can reach submerged plants and other photosynthetic organisms.

records.label: Second-order reaction half-life
records.learning_takeaway: For a single-reactant second-order law, lower initial concentration produces a longer half-life.
records.card: For a reaction whose rate is proportional to one reactant’s concentration squared, the half-life depends on the starting concentration. As the mixture becomes more dilute, consuming half of what remains takes longer. A half-life alone cannot determine its rate constant without concentration information.

records.label: Second-price sealed-bid auction
records.learning_takeaway: Award the item to the highest bidder but charge the second-highest submitted bid.
records.card: A second-price sealed-bid auction gives the item to the highest bidder but charges the second-highest bid. The allocation rule resembles a first-price auction, while the payment rule differs. Also called a Vickrey auction, it separates the winning offer from the amount the winner actually pays.

records.label: Seismic tomography
records.learning_takeaway: Treat inferred Earth-interior structure as a model constrained by coverage, data quality and uncertainty.
records.card: Seismic tomography infers structures inside Earth from seismic information. Its models can address targets ranging from fault zones to the whole planet, but their usefulness depends on data quality, geographic coverage and uncertainty. A tomographic image is therefore an interpreted model, not a direct photograph underground.

records.label: Seki
records.learning_takeaway: Recognize mutual survival when either attack would allow the opponent to capture.
records.card: Seki is mutual survival in Go without each group having two independent eyes. Neighboring groups share a shortage of liberties, and either player's attempt to capture can allow the opponent to capture first. Leaving the position alone therefore preserves both sides' stones.

records.label: Self-efficacy
records.learning_takeaway: Distinguish believing one can complete a task from valuing its reward.
records.card: Self-efficacy is a person's belief that they can carry out a particular task. In Bandura's account, this belief helps shape the challenges people attempt and their persistence after setbacks. Believing an outcome is valuable differs from believing one has the capability to achieve it.

records.label: Self-explanation
records.learning_takeaway: Generate one's own causal or logical explanations during study rather than merely repeating the presented answer.
records.card: Self-explanation asks learners to produce their own account of why an idea or solution works. The aim is to connect steps to causes, principles, or reasons rather than merely say them aloud. The IES guide encourages explanatory questions and feedback instead of treating repetition of an answer as understanding.

records.label: Self-incompatibility in fruit crops
records.learning_takeaway: Understand why some fruit trees need pollen from a different compatible variety to crop well.
records.card: Some fruit varieties cannot reliably set fruit using their own pollen and need a different compatible variety nearby. Hybrid plums provide an example, whereas some European plums are self-compatible. Planning pollination therefore requires matching varieties, not merely counting the number of trees in the garden.

records.label: Self-reference effect
records.learning_takeaway: Investigate why relating information to oneself can improve later remembering.
records.card: The self-reference effect is a relative memory advantage for information connected to oneself. Material considered in personally relevant terms can be remembered better than less self-relevant material. It is studied as an influence on encoding, linking what information means to a person with later remembering.

records.label: Semantic compositionality
records.learning_takeaway: Explain how a novel expression's meaning depends on its parts and how those parts are combined.
records.card: Semantic compositionality explains how unfamiliar expressions can be understood from familiar parts and the way they are combined. It applies to sentences and to complex words. Knowing each piece is not enough on its own: different structures can organize the same pieces into different meanings.

records.label: Semantic entailment
records.learning_takeaway: Test whether one sentence being true necessarily makes another true by looking for contradiction under denial.
records.card: A sentence entails another when the first cannot be true while the second is false. If someone sighed, for example, they emitted a breath. Adding a denial of the entailed claim produces a contradiction, unlike a merely suggested interpretation that the speaker can cancel.

records.label: Senet
